Chris May: Yes, that does not impact our adjusted EBITDA. It is noncash in nature. You would not see that impact our cash flow statement or cash from operations at all for that adjustment. Those were the nondesignated dollar derivatives that we had to put on our balance sheet during the acquisition. These will burn out relatively quickly.

Joseph Spak: So that's not something that continues -- like that's not something that continues into future years. That's just something you inherited and you don't expect to continue to use or do?

Chris May: Correct. They'll start to go away as they lapse, correct.

Joseph Spak: Okay. And Chris, I know you mentioned no significant debt maturities until '29. And maybe I don't know if this is for Nathan or David or Chris, but like I can't say I followed Standard Motors closely, but it does look like there was a concerted effort there to delever post an acquisition they made. And so it seems like there's some similarities there between what they went through and what you're going through now in the wake of the Dowlais deal even if it wasn't sort of, I guess, higher leverage overall.

But I guess, should we read into what you did there, Nathan, in terms of a template of what Dauch would like to do over the coming years?

David Dauch: Yes. Joe, this is David. Let me speak first. We have been very consistent as a company over the years in regards to what our objectives are in regards to our targets for net debt to EBITDA or the leverage target. I mean, clearly, we want to work our way under 2x. I'm proud that we've been able to get it to the 2.6x. At the same time, we're very focused on paying down the debt, which we've consistently been doing quarter-to-quarter. So we'll continue to do that. Obviously, the strength of our business is going to be generating free cash flow to service that debt on a go-forward basis.

At the same time, as always, we'll be opportunistic to refinance select debt at the appropriate time. But what I've always been proud of Chris and the team and even Mike Simonte before then is they've always kept a financial runway in front of us. So we never had an overhang from a maturity standpoint there. And I think dealing with Nathan here, obviously, he's just getting on board, up to speed. There are some similarities in regards to what was done at Standard Motor Products. But at the same time, he's going to have to adjust slightly to just the way we've approached things here within the Dauch Corporation. But I think we're all aligned on our task.

We understand the mission, and we're committed all the way up to the Board of Directors to address this leverage situation. And that was part of the reason we wanted to do this larger strategic combination or acquisition with Dowlais to accelerate that cash generation opportunity through the synergies that we're realizing and then ultimately service this debt a lot quicker. So hopefully, that addresses your question.

Operator: Our next question comes from James Mulholland from Deutsche Bank.

James Mulholland: Synergies continue to be recognized faster than what the original outlay had been. Is there anything specific that's enabling you to reach them at that speed? Or should, I guess, we simply view it as a faster realization? Are you finding maybe extra areas that weren't necessarily in your original guidance, and so you're just being able to take them out now? And could that then pretend to maybe raising what you can do over the longer term?

David Dauch: This is David Dauch again. What I would say is this is, I mean, we committed to $300 million at the time that we announced the strategic combination of the 2 businesses. We also expressed at that time the mix of what that $300 million would be with SG&A and engineering being approximately 30% of that, purchasing being 50% and the operations being 20%. At the time, we also identified that we were limited in regards to the ability to visit their plants. So we're not able to see the full potential of some of the operational items. What I would say is we have been very aggressive in regards to going after SG&A cost as well as engineering efficiencies.

So -- and obviously, that's the low-hanging fruit that we can get after the quickest. So we're clearly ahead of schedule with respect to that. Purchasing, it's a difficult market to navigate in right now. So we're trying to manage our way through that, but still making meaningful progress in that area. And then we're making some substantial progress also on the operations side. So we're really excited the fact that we've already met our year 1 target after 3 quarters together as a combined entity. We think there's more opportunity here and hold tight for future discussions.

James Mulholland: Great. That's helpful. And I guess as my follow-up, as we think about your European footprint that came over from Dowlais, we know that some significant OEMs have been clear that capacity cuts are on the horizon and in some cases, fairly significant capacity cuts. So Dowlais just went through its own large restructuring there. I guess, do you have any early thoughts on what more might be needed in terms of that midterm environment? Or is it at this point that you're fairly comfortable with where the footprint is and whether or not it can be flexed up and down based on whatever production environment it's in?

David Dauch: Yes. This is David again. What I would say is this is legacy AAM did not have as much of a footprint in Europe as obviously legacy Dowlais or GKN did. Legacy Dowlais had done a lot of restructuring, as you acknowledged and was on the downside of that restructuring effort there. There are still efforts that were in their base plan as well as other efforts that are included in our synergistic plan. So that was all identified as part of the process of going through diligence and the combination of the 2 businesses.

The one thing that we're watching very closely is the penetration of the Chinese and their aggressive approach to Europe and the incremental restructuring or the challenges it's creating, especially for the legacy OEMs in Europe. And obviously, we'll have to respond accordingly based on where we're at. The good news is that -- we do supply several of those Chinese OEMs that are gaining market share. So at the same time, we'll just have to balance that out in regards to what we think our capacity utilization and our facility footprint needs to be on a go-forward basis. So to answer your question, I think directionally, we're where we need to be right now.

However, there is some restructuring that is planned as part of this combination, but we'll continue to monitor the market. And if other changes are required, then we'll make those adjustments no different than we would in any other market around the world to optimize the business appropriately and adjust it to the market demand.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Levy from Barclays.

Dan Levy: Chris and Nathan, congratulations to both of you. I wanted to start with the question on the inflationary pressures. And maybe you could just refresh us back to the inflation that we saw in the 2022 time frame. How you dealt with that back then in terms of -- I'm pretty sure you ended up sort of getting fully recovered on all those. But what was the split between OEM recoveries or customer recoveries versus your own productivity measures? And now that we're arguably later in the cycle, what do you sense is the receptivity of your customers to help support?

And maybe you could just unpack some of the productivity measures that you have on your end that if you don't get the customer recoveries that you can do it on your end to be EBITDA neutral after all this?

Chris May: Yes, Dan, this is Chris. I'll certainly take the first part of that question. If you go back to the inflationary environment that you're referring to in the past, would have been in the 2022 calendar time period based on really the invasion of Ukraine triggered a lot of inflation in that period of time, and it manifested its way through several elements of our cost structure. Through the course of the year, meaning the full year of 2022, we put in various things to mitigate, optimize some of our spend through where we saw those different pockets of inflation.

But we also, as you know, did have dialogue with our customers that took ultimately the better part of the year to reach conclusion with, which was fairly standard inside the industry at that point in time. So if you think back to some of my prepared remarks I mentioned today, our expectation is a very similar path. We are doing things to help mitigate some of the inflationary impact where you've seen, obviously, a lot of inflation sort of stem from petroleum-based products such as coolants, diesel fuel surcharges on logistics, entering into various metals such as tooling, et cetera.

So things that we can do to either optimize freight routes to minimize fuel costs associated with that, look at different ways or different alternatives for coolants that we can use in our factories. These are the type of productivity initiatives that we would like to do on our own. But as you know, this is a very macro event and would be in some discussions with customers, but would take time to play out. Very similar pattern probably from what we saw back in '22.

Dan Levy: Okay. Great. Second is just a follow-up to, I think, one of the prior questions around your Europe exposure. And I'll just maybe broaden it to China and Europe. So it looks like your China equity income, that's still intact and you generally feel like your Europe footprint is where it needs to be. We've seen from some of the other suppliers that there's been some underperformance within Europe. I realize this is all very customer-specific. But maybe you could just give us an early read on these newer regions where you're operating now where you maybe haven't had as much of a footprint for in terms of China and Europe that those are still holding intact?

And what levers you have in the event that the customer mix moves against you to keep those earnings streams intact?

David Dauch: This is David. I guess I'll start, and then, Chris, I'll ask if you want to add anything in. I'll start in the China side of things. Clearly, legacy AAM had a very strong presence there with our wholly owned foreign enterprise. Our business was both with the global OEMs as well as the local China OEMs. That business with the local China OEMs has grown over the years. So that's been a positive for us. So we're doing very well supporting those programs in China today. With the acquisition of Dowlais, we picked up the joint venture, which is a 35-plus-year-old joint venture that's been very successful over there and profitable.

Like legacy AAM, they were supporting both global OEMs and the local Chinese OEMs. Their share has grown over the years with the China OEMs. So there is pressure in the local China market right now as far as it being down. The demand internally within China is around 24 million units, but they're exporting close to 10 million units on top of that. So -- or as part of that, I should say. So that's an important thing to note. So our volumes have been able to stay fairly steady and strong there. I mean, obviously, we're going to continue to demonstrate the size and the scale of our company, the portfolio.

When it's all said and done, you got to be cost competitive. And so we'll bring the technology and the cost competitive base, and we're where we need to be in China and quite honestly, across Southeast Asia. In Europe, as I said earlier in the earlier question, I think we're positioned right now. There's still some remaining things that are being done as part of the original, base Dowlais plans that we inherited. But as we said, some of those costs would be coming down.

As those pressures continue to mount based on China commanding more market share, I mean, we've got to win our fair share of that China business, while at the same time, if we have to do other optimization, we'll do that. But that's no different than like I said, we would do in any other market in the business. Our business, especially a capital-intensive program or business is all about facility utilization, capacity utilization and manpower utilization. And so we'll just -- as we've always had, we've got downside playbooks -- we'll adjust the businesses to those downside playbooks and flex our cost structure appropriately.

But we feel very confident about where we are in regards to protecting the value streams and the profit pools of China. Obviously, we're watching closely what's going on in Europe, but we're delivering in Europe at this point in time. And we'll make adjustments around the world as required on a go-forward basis. But Chris, I don't know if you want to add anything more.

Chris May: No. I think, Dan, I'll tell you, David summed it up pretty well. But if you go back to the very, very basics, it's having that technology in the markets, and we are growing that technology of electrification, which is the key, obviously, growth engine in China through our joint venture as well as our wholly owned with our driveline systems. And then you need to be cost competitive, which will allow you to succeed in both regions.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rajat Gupta from JPMorgan.

Yash Beswala: This is Yash Beswala on for Rajat Gupta. I wanted to ask about the new military vehicle sideshaft award you guys have highlighted. Could you help us understand what this award means for Dauch's potential expansion into like defense and other nontraditional end markets and just the broader opportunity to leverage your existing technologies and potential for additional business wins in these segments?

David Dauch: Yes. Thank you. This is David. As I said in my prepared remarks, we're very excited about that opportunity that presented itself. It further demonstrates our technological advantages from a product portfolio standpoint and the capabilities that go with a military type product. Our combined companies of legacy AAM and legacy GKN or Dowlais, both were supplying some military products already. So this is some incremental opportunities to that. But it clearly -- our business is now as a combined business clearly sets itself up to leverage our core competencies and capabilities in some adjacent markets and aerospace and defense would be one of those markets.

So it's a small win, but an important win, but at the same time, demonstrates the capability there, and we'll continue to explore what other opportunities might exist there for us in the future.

Yash Beswala: Helpful. And just as a follow-up, could you also help us like provide an update on the $2 billion of like new and incremental business opportunities you guys had highlighted last quarter, including how much has converted into awards? And how is that pipeline progressing on that front? And how should we think about some of those awards translating into revenue growth in '27 and beyond?

David Dauch: Yes. And we're still quoting approximately that $2 billion that ebbs and flows. We have been successful in conquesting typically our hit rate is around a 25% to 30% hit rate. So we're tracking very favorably in regards to [Audio Gap] It's across the board in regards to -- we're doing very well on the powdered metal side of things in the forging or the overall Metal Form side of the business. And we've got some good strategic wins on the Driveline side, as we've highlighted in a couple of earnings calls now. We don't -- we're not publicizing anything on our backlog of new business, but we continue to favorably grow that going forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from Hamed Khorsand from BWS Financial.

Hamed Khorsand: Just talking about the competitive environment. Are you seeing any pushouts in any of the product designs that you've been working on with any of the OEMs?

David Dauch: What I will say is the OEMs are clearly working on product extensions on their current business today. So that's been one of our core objectives in addition to the new and incremental business that we're going after is to secure the replacement programs that we're already on because that's the solid base that we operate from today and the cash that's generated to support the overall business. We've been very successful in securing a lot of that next-generation business, the majority, quite honestly. We've got some additional wins that we just won here and announced. So that's been positive.

But yes, we are seeing some of these programs be extended out, especially based on the fact that they were all headed down the path of electrification, and they didn't have necessarily all the product portfolio in place. But you're also now seeing reinvestment in ICE and a lot of new investment into hybrid applications. The good news for us is our product portfolio spans that ICE and hybrid. There's a little bit of modification on some of the hybrid. And you also know that we've continued to develop on a selective basis, the proper electrification capabilities to support growth in the various markets around the world.

So we think one of the big advantages of bringing the 2 companies together was the expanded product portfolio that we have and also the agnostic positioning that we put our company in with the portfolio that we have to offer to the marketplace. So we feel like we're in a very good spot to adjust to the market demand regardless of the propulsion system.

Operator: Our next question comes from Alex Perry from Bank of America.

Alexander Perry: I just wanted to ask, is there sort of any line of sight from pressure from some of the heavy-duty platforms easing? How much of that is sort of expected to continue here into the fourth quarter and into next year? And what are some of the offsets?

David Dauch: What I would say to that question there is in regards to quite the opposite in most of the cases. We've seen the heavy truck production schedules increasing. We've seen uplift capacity programs across many of them. We're obviously experiencing the downside of some of the Ram activity today with 15% year-over-year in regards to performance from a quarter standpoint. I think that's limited specifically more towards Stellantis at this time. But obviously, we're continuing to watch that. Obviously, the acceleration of energy prices and fuel prices hasn't helped in some of that, especially if you look towards more of the diesel market, which the Ram has a heavy penetration of some of that.

But I would say quite the opposite. I think there's a market there for heavy duty. It tends to be resilient even during tough times because people need these types of vehicles for their livelihood. And so I think we see the opposite where we see more investment going into the heavy-duty platforms.

Chris May: Alex, this is Chris. There is no practical substitute for these vehicles if you need them. And generally, these aren't recreational type vehicles. So we expect this market to generally remain strong over time.

Alexander Perry: That's really helpful. And then I guess my follow-up was, I think in the prepared remarks, you talked about some operational issues with some Tier 1, Tier 2 suppliers. Is there any line of sight in terms of those easing? And what's sort of driving that? And does that sort of leak into 2027? Or when do you expect improvement there?

Chris May: Yes. This is Chris. I'll start with the first part of that. One of the earlier questions was talking about how inflationary pressures that we face, and I talked about the impact of fuel prices and coolant costs, et cetera. Our supply base is experiencing the exact same phenomenon. And those that I would say maybe were a little more fragile to begin with, these pressures just amplify the struggles that they have, which then can become challenged.

We saw clearly an onset of some of these costs in the macro environment in the back half of the second quarter, but you can digest these for a period of time as they've really extended now into the third quarter and early in the fourth quarter, these pressures, you're starting to see some of the challenges now on the Tier 2 and Tier 3 side. So our third quarter had probably about $10 million of costs associated with this for a few select suppliers. I think we have most of those under control now and working with them, that should start to tamper down. But clearly, the macro environment does influence this dynamic over time.

Operator: Our next question comes from Andrew Percoco from Morgan Stanley.

Andrew Percoco: Great. Maybe just to follow up and ask specifically about the GM truck changeover. And just curious like how the ramp process has gone? Is the launch cost cadence coming in line with your expectations? Obviously, you talked about how there's some inflationary headwinds in the business. But just curious as it relates to that program specifically, is everything still on track with your expectations for 2026? And then as we kind of look ahead to 2027, has there been any kind of major change in your expectations as it relates to either volume or pricing or just the margin contribution of that for next year?

David Dauch: Andrew, this is David. Everything is on track and on schedule based on what was communicated to us and the supply base from General Motors regarding this program. So they are doing exactly what they were saying they're going to do. We did experience some downtime, as I said in my prepared remarks, in September and October to prepare for a staggered launch going forward across the different vehicle product lines. But to answer your question, they are certainly on track for '26 and '27, and we're locked and loaded ourselves.

Chris May: And Andrew, you had a secondary part of that question as it relates to margin. The margin and pricing as it transitions from current gen to next gen, our content per vehicle, our margin profile very similar from product to product.

Andrew Percoco: Okay. Super helpful. And then I think last quarter, you guys mentioned how a lot of your kind of steel buy or metal buy is not really on spot. It's on long-term contracts. So can you maybe just provide a little bit of color in terms of how we should think about how much of that rolls off as we go into the early part of 2027 and what the potential impact could be on the cost side of the equation on margins? And I know you have recovery of that, but maybe just remind us in terms of how that flows through and how we should expect that to potentially impact the outlook for next year?

Chris May: Yes. If you think about our input costs for metal-based product, you should think about them from two perspectives. First, we do have a sizable pass-through element that's generally under contract with most of our customers. The products that we buy, for example, steel has a lot of inputs such as scrap, nickel, moly, things of this nature that are traded on commodity exchanges. As they price up and down, our suppliers pass those costs on to us either up or down. We then in turn pass that on to our customer either up or down, generally with a little bit of a small timing lag and about, call it, a 10% to 20% delta between the change.

The other piece I would refer to is our base cost where we go out and negotiate a base price of steel, that or other commodities. Those are clearly ours to manage and our responsibility. As you know, steel markets themselves, you've seen the indices, you've seen hot-rolled markets. They have been getting a little, I would say, tougher in the current environment from a base price perspective. We're still under our current contracts. Those will renew for many of our suppliers next year. We're keeping a close eye on it. We've got some work to do to close these out, but this is clearly an area that has our attention, and we're working through.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jake Scholl from BNP.

Thomas Scholl: As we think about EBITDA into next year, should we use the second half of '26 as a jumping off point plus some inflation recoveries and $100 million or so in synergies? Or are there some other kind of major puts and takes we should be factoring in?

Chris May: Yes. I would -- Jake, my general rule of thumb with that is, especially in our industry that has very unique elements quarter-to-quarter-to-quarter, whether it's production days or different cadences, a longer period of time like you use 4 quarters or an LTM sort of roll forward is generally probably a way to think about it versus just trying to extrapolate one particular quarter due to the complexities of that. You could clearly do both, but I would recommend you use a little longer period of time. But as we think about going into 2027, I think the puts and takes in your mind is what you're thinking about, how do we contextualize what '27 may bring.

Clearly, we're very focused on our synergy attainment and delivering that result. We have these new truck launches that are coming online. So hopefully, the market will be well received from those. That would be our expectation and our continued focus on baseline productivity second half or full year into 2027. On the take side, obviously, we're watching very closely the inflationary environment and the timing for us to either mitigate or get recovery on that. If the environment stays exactly the same as now, you'll obviously have a little bit of this inflation in the first quarter as you work through the course of timing to get mitigation or recovery. The previous person just asked about the steel markets.

We're watching very closely. And of course, we're watching the Mexican peso very closely. That's a big dynamic on us, which has been very volatile this year, but hopefully, that plays out okay. Those are just some of the high-level puts and takes I think about for next year at this point in time.

Thomas Scholl: That's very helpful. And I wanted to follow up on something you said in response to, I think it was James' question, you mentioned seeing some of these kind of plant level opportunities where you didn't have a chance to kind of dig in before the deal closed. So can you give us an idea of what that might look like? And then when you may be in a position to give us a little bit more detail?

David Dauch: Yes. Can you be a little bit more clear on your question? Are you just talking about the footprint?

Thomas Scholl: And just kind of more specifically, some of the kind of nitty-gritty plant level operational synergies you see...

David Dauch: Okay. Yes. Sorry, I misunderstood when you asked the question. So yes, no, we -- as I said, we are limited in regards to going into the plants before we can make our announcement in regards to the synergy target. We clearly see opportunities to strengthen their manufacturing plant floor operations based on putting in our operating systems that are very disciplined, very structured and a lot of daily accountability. There's opportunities in regards to scrap management, OEE and productivity performance. But the nice thing is there's a strong manufacturing foundation and engineering base to work with. There's good technology as far as the types of equipment that are in their facilities.

It's just we think there's an opportunity to improve the output, throughput capacity utilization and ultimate performance in the plants. So as you know, we're known for our operational excellence. We're very focused on that. That will take a little bit of time, as I said, by nature to realize that, but we're highly confident in our ability to make those things happen. And therefore, we can see some potential upside.

Operator: Our next question comes from Douglas Karson from Bank of America.

Douglas Karson: I want to look at like big picture, like longer-term like opportunities to cross-sell. You've got this big business in Europe now, which has a great platform. And I'm wondering if like the recent win that you had on the new vehicle, was that a kind of function of cross-selling? And maybe what opportunities like longer term, do you think the combination of this great global footprint now could provide? And then I have a quick kind of more bookkeeping follow-up.

David Dauch: Yes, Doug, this is David. I'll take the cross-selling side of things before you ask your bookkeeping one. We definitely see cross-selling opportunities across multiple customers, especially those that have the big global reach. We're already starting to realize some of that benefit based on just hosting technology days, demonstrating to them the comprehensiveness of our product portfolio. We've had independent relationships between legacy AAM and legacy Dowlais or GKN with the customers. Now we're presenting on a combined basis. We'll do more technology days and rollouts in the first half and probably throughout the year in 2027. But we're clearly capturing their attention in regards to the comprehensiveness of our portfolio.

At the same time, they can see the responsiveness to some of the issues that have -- that we've identified as bringing the 2 companies together, and that's being received very favorably. So I think what we'll do is just continue to leverage those relationships. We'll clearly highlight our comprehensive portfolio. At the same time, I think they've known us for our value proposition over the years, and we'll continue to enhance that to make it a win-win for both the customer and ourselves.

Douglas Karson: I know you guys have been in the industry a long time, and this tariff situation that kind of came upon us a year or so ago, kind of created a lot of uncertainty in the auto industry. And now with this change in the Democratic kind of blue sweep, we'll call it. If we look a couple of years out, do you think there's any kind of upside as your gut reaction to what took place to kind of soften some of the tariff cost that could be impacting the auto supplier universe in general? I know it's kind of a political question and it's kind of a couple of years out.

But just what is your thought being an industry leader in this space?

David Dauch: Yes. So Doug, I'll start and then I'll ask Chris to chime in. But this tariff situation, I clearly understand the need and the approach that our current administration is taking today to drive investment into our country and drive manufacturing back to our country, especially in regards to critical areas. I don't think it's sustainable for a lot of the supply base long term. People are going to have to take actions to mitigate it, which many people are already doing today. As you know, our policy has always been to try to buy and build local in the markets that we serve to mitigate any exposure from a tariff standpoint or geopolitical standpoint.

That's benefited us, although we still have exposure on the tariff side of things, especially now that we've acquired Dowlais, GKN, they've had a little bit more exposure. And so we're working plans to localize product where we can and leverage the global footprint that we have. But ultimately, I think it's got to come under control, and it's got to subside at some time. Otherwise, we're going to continue to operate at very high prices and costs that have to be passed on to the OEMs and ultimately possibly to the consumer and the consumer can only handle so much. So like I said, I clearly understand the strategy and why it's there today.

At the same time, my gut says that it will subside over time. But in the meantime, we've all -- like we have been doing, have to continue to take aggressive actions to mitigate it ourselves for the period of time while getting recovery where appropriate. Chris, I don't know if you have anything to add.

Chris May: Our policy of the buy and build local has really protected us in many cases. But even to that effect, we are still impacted around $20 million to $25 million from a bottom line perspective in calendar year 2026. So that's clearly a potential upside for us should this change. But we're focused on managing what we can control and working through this environment. It makes a little more challenging for long-term investing when that's pivoting, but we're also very focused on USMCA in particular. That's very important to our company as well as the industry.

Operator: And our final question is a follow-up from Tom Narayan from RBC.

Gautam Narayan: David, one thing Stellantis has mentioned is the potential to reshore their HD truck to the U.S. from Mexico. I guess given the midterm results, it's probably less likely that this happens. But in the event this happens, do you guys -- could you guys keep the business by leveraging the U.S. facilities? I assume this is something you deal with all the time and have been forever. But yes, just how would you deal with something like that?

David Dauch: Yes. So Tom, great question. As you know, it's not easy to just pick up assembly plants and/or large component plants that are capital intensive, but it is feasible. It's just costly and takes time to do such a thing. Clearly, we've had multiple discussions with all of our OEM customers, including Stellantis. We've identified -- we've answered questions that they've had. But at this time, there's no decision that's been made regarding an action of such at this point in time. But if they were to go down that path, especially now that we have the combined business of Dowlais and legacy AAM to form out, we do have a flexible manufacturing footprint and capacity.

We would just have to make appropriate adjustments to tailor for the products involved and deal with the costs that would be involved in such a transfer. But we do have the ability to flex if we need to do that.

Gautam Narayan: Got it. And Chris, I'll let you close it out. And maybe this is for the Investor Day, but cash restructuring, this is a hot topic. It went up a little in the '26 guide. We talked about all the headwinds in Europe and all of that. You said in the past this should meaningfully go down in '27. Can we just confirm that, that's definitely coming down?

Chris May: Our goal is to continue to reduce our near-term restructuring costs, yes.

Operator: And with that, ladies and gentlemen, we'll be concluding today's question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the floor back over to David Lim for closing comments.

David Lim: Yes. We thank all of you who have participated on this call and appreciate your interest in Dauch. We certainly look forward to talking with you in the future. Thank you.

Operator: And with that, we'll conclude today's conference call. We do thank you for joining. You may now disconnect your lines.

#3226. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3225. The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta today

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The wait is over for trying Siri AI on iOS 27. Here's what you need to know to get started.

Enabling Siri AI, Apple’s new generative AI-powered virtual assistant, on a compatible Apple device running iOS 27 used to prompt a message informing the user that the device would be added to a waitlist with varying wait times. Now, you can download Siri AI automatically as soon as you enable it on your compatible iPhone, Mac, or iPad. The one exception is that, if there is unusually high demand, Apple could temporarily reinstate its waitlist.

You’ll need a compatible device that runs Apple Intelligence, like an iPhone (15 Pro or newer), iPad (Mini A17 Pro or newer or an M-series chip), Mac (MacBook Neo or M-series chip), Apple Watch (Series 9 and Ultra 2 or newer), or Apple Vision Pro.

Instead of adding you to a waitlist, Siri AI will begin downloading right away.

Siri AI is Apple’s upgraded virtual assistant, now powered by generative AI. Instead of giving you canned responses to your questions, Siri AI will be able to answer complex questions, understand more natural-sounding phrases, and maintain context throughout conversations and across your Apple ecosystem.

ZDNET’s Lance Whitney recommends using Siri AI’s onscreen awareness feature to ask it for directions, explain something you see on your phone’s screen, or to add items from your screen to a list. He also uses Siri AI to edit his photos simply by asking for the changes he wants. But that’s just skimming the surface. You can read more about Whitney’s experiences using Siri AI here.

Also: I thought I had Siri AI in iOS 27 – until I found it hidden in my settings

For years, Apple has been working to gain relevance in AI to compete with major players like OpenAI and Google. While Apple Intelligence features like Writing Tools, Genmoji, and Image Playground have helped, Apple has lagged far behind in upgrading its signature voice assistant to generative AI.

iOS 27 delivered Siri AI in beta this fall, along with iPadOS 27, MacOS 27 Golden Gate, VisionOS 27, and WatchOS 27.

You need a compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, or Apple Vision Pro to use Apple Intelligence features like Siri AI. Not all Apple devices that support the latest iOS 27 (or other OS 27) will support Siri AI.

Here are the Apple devices that support Siri AI:

You also need to have your device in a supported language (English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, or Spanish) and to reside in a supported region (not available in mainland China or in iOS, iPadOS, or WatchOS in the European Union).

#3223. Will Democrats Rein in Big Tech? It Starts With Privacy and Data Centers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech critics say that real change will depend on newly elected officials keeping their campaign promises.

In this week’s midterm elections, Democrats won back control of both chambers of Congress, with stunning victories in battleground states that have voters and tech critics asking: Was this the AI election?

Artificial intelligence was central to the national conversation during the midterms, alongside concerns about affordability and the Iran war. From data centers needed to power AI to how it’s used in surveillance tech like Flock cameras, many Democratic (and a few Republican) candidates campaigned against AI.

Despite tech leaders like Elon Musk pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns, tech critics say voters’ choices show a strong distrust in Big Tech and give the newly elected leaders the necessary momentum for change. But how, exactly, they deliver on those goals remains to be seen — and will have real consequences for tech consumers and companies.

“It is time for lawmakers to get real about reining in unchecked tech power and to hold these companies accountable to the people,” Butler says.

More than any other tech issue, data centers took center stage in the midterm elections. It isn’t surprising; these facilities are popping up everywhere and require vast amounts of water and electricity at the expense of nearby communities’ health and environments.

Voters showed their frustration at the ballot box. Across the country, voters rejected more than 40 ballot measures that would’ve supported data centers. It was a rare national consensus on an issue that is usually debated in city councils and statehouses. As such, “action is more likely to come on the local and state levels, at least in the short term,” says Paris Marx, tech critic and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast.

Governments may continue to adopt moratoriums on new data center construction, like New York’s first-in-the-nation pause implemented earlier this year, as they try to figure out how to mitigate the harms. State and local legislators need to continue setting environmental rules, managing electricity demand and finding real community benefits, Marx says. (OpenAI, for its part, is tackling the issue by renaming data centers as “compute campuses.”)

In many ways, “data centers are a symptom of the larger problem,” says Samir Jain, vice president of policy at the Center for Democracy and Technology. Tech companies are so focused on “winning” the global AI race that they forget (or didn’t prioritize) the impact on everyday people, he says.

But neighbors living next to data centers cannot forget. In that sense, the overwhelming public backlash to data centers and the midterm election results are “a real repudiation of that kind of approach to technology,” Jain says.

But we’ve seen very clearly over the past decade that when left unchecked, tech companies can collect and use our data in concerning ways. Despite stalled progress on a national bill in the past, there may be a new push for it, thanks to recent tech headlines. Flock cameras and other automatic license plate readers have sparked immense public concern as many cases show law enforcement officers misusing the tech to stalk and harass people.

It isn’t just major tech platforms; it’s also data brokers that sell data to companies you don’t interact with. That industry is worth more than $277 billion, and it’s the engine behind much of how Big Tech operates.

“If you are mad at this whole surveillance pricing situation where we’re going to charge you more if we feel like you can afford it, that is because of data brokers,” says McKinney. “If you are mad that the federal government can just buy information from data brokers that [it] would otherwise have to get a warrant to get, that’s a data broker problem.”

“We can’t lead the world in AI and support transformative AI innovation with a patchwork of conflicting state laws that make life harder for startups and small businesses,” Fabrizio says.

While the Democrats will have a firm majority in both chambers of Congress, many of the most contentious tech issues have bipartisan support, tech critics told me. And we’ve already seen how that can result in actionable legislation, such as the Take It Down Act, which passed nearly unanimously in 2025.

This fleeting moment of bipartisan agreement on reining in Big Tech could help lawmakers achieve the elusive task of actually fulfilling their campaign promises. But part of the challenge will be getting lawmakers to focus on real-world harm and basic protections, not whatever dystopian tech prediction is trending that day.

“It’s very likely we’ll see companies continue to push lawmakers to focus AI regulation on so-called ‘existential risks,’ meaning their claims that more advanced AI might kill humanity or end the world,” Marx says, “rather than addressing the impacts of data centers and the present-day harms.”

Those existential risks only serve to make tech companies more powerful. “These elected representatives don’t just have the power to rein in these powerful corporations; they have the obligation to do so to promote the interests of the constituents they serve,” Butler says.

We saw this election cycle how much money Big Tech is willing to spend to try to get its preferred candidates and policies. Elon Musk alone reportedly spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates such as Ken Paxton in Texas, who lost by 12 percentage points to Democrat James Talarico. Despite that, most of the tech experts I spoke to said the results showed a real desire from voters to rein in tech companies and the harms they wrought.

But that will depend on how willing the new Congress is to buck Big Tech. “If we have a new electorate that is newly emboldened to stand up to bullies,” McKinney says, “let’s start there.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3222. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth Core 7.0’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth Core 7.0 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible within Bluetooth Core 7.0 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

The less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth Core 6.0-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many audio manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth Core 6.0 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth Core 6.0 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year, including Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

Even if generating $1,000 in dividend payouts from Procter & Gamble isn't in an investor's budget, it's still a stock worthy of investment consideration.

From paper towels to razor blades, people can look around their homes and likely spot a few products from Procter & Gamble (PG -1.02%). With a consistent payout yielding 2.6% as of this writing, investors may be wondering whether P&G could help them generate extra income amid higher fuel and grocery costs. We'll look at what it would take to generate an extra $250 every three months, or $1,000 a year, from the company.

For Procter & Gamble to pay a shareholder $1,000 in yearly dividends, it's going to take quite a few shares. With a quarterly dividend payout of $1.09, it would take roughly 230 shares to earn $1,000 in yearly dividends.

That said, there's still a reason Procter & Gamble may be worth considering as an investment even with a smaller budget: stability.

As investors worry about the same level of uncertainty swirling around the markets in 2027 as in 2026, companies that allow their shareholders to sleep well at night are receiving more attention. Some of those types of stocks include Dividend Kings.

To earn the title of Dividend King, a company has to have increased its dividend payouts for 50 or more consecutive years. Procter & Gamble has easily cleared that hurdle, increasing its payout for 70 consecutive years.

That shows a strong business model with products that people will always buy no matter what's happening in the economy. Its brands include Tide laundry detergent, Bounty paper towels, Charmin toilet paper, Gillette razors, and more. And while not known for its stock price appreciation, shares are up 16.5% thus far in 2026, outperforming the S&P 500's (^GSPC +0.31%) 8.2% return.

Ultimately, while it may not work out for some shareholders to receive $1,000 in annual dividends from Procter & Gamble, it can still serve as a valuable portfolio addition thanks to its dependability.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

A sweeping AI ban is being proposed in the US, with penalties of up to 20 years in prison

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI is advancing at a pace that's making some lawmakers uncomfortable. Now, Senator Bernie Sanders wants to put the brakes on the most powerful AI systems before they become too difficult for humans to control.

Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, a sweeping proposal that would permanently prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence in the United States.

But the legislation goes further than banning a hypothetical future technology. It would also temporarily halt development of certain advanced AI models, establish an entirely new federal department to oversee AI and impose serious penalties on those who break the rules.

Those penalties could include up to 20 years in prison for certain individuals responsible for violations.

The bill was introduced in September and remains in committee. It hasn't become law, but it offers a look at how some lawmakers want to change the direction of AI development.

Sanders argues that AI development has reached a point where government oversight is no longer optional.

"When you are racing towards a cliff, you don't just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes," Sanders said in his September 23 announcement.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The concern is that companies developing advanced AI could eventually create systems with capabilities they don't fully understand or control. Supporters point to warnings from AI researchers and industry leaders about the potential dangers of increasingly autonomous systems.

The bill also calls for international agreements designed to prevent artificial superintelligence from being developed outside the United States.

That could be one of its biggest challenges. The Trump administration has emphasized AI development and American competitiveness in the AI arms race.

The biggest part of the proposal is a permanent ban on artificial superintelligence, or ASI.

Unlike today's AI chatbots, artificial superintelligence generally refers to a theoretical system capable of outperforming humans across most intellectual tasks.

Under the proposed legislation, that definition also includes systems powerful enough to plan and carry out actions that could destroy humanity or take away human control.

The legislation would prohibit developing, deploying, acquiring or distributing these systems. It would also restrict certain AI systems that demonstrate dangerous capabilities associated with superintelligence.

One of the more unusual aspects of the legislation is its proposal to create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence. This department would have the authority to monitor advanced AI development, establish safety requirements and inspect powerful models before they're released.

Companies would need government authorization to develop or distribute qualifying advanced AI models, and those models would require approval before deployment.

The department could also order potentially dangerous AI systems to be disconnected from the internet, modified or rendered inoperative.

The bill's enforcement provisions are particularly strict. For example, certain company decisionmakers and unaffiliated individuals who recklessly violate the law could face fines and prison sentences of up to 20 years.

Companies could also lose authorization to operate, while intellectual property and assets associated with violations could be subject to forfeiture.

For anyone using ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini today, there's no immediate reason to worry about losing access.

The legislation has not passed Congress, and there are no new restrictions on consumer AI services resulting from the proposal.

Even if it eventually became law, the bill wouldn't automatically prohibit every existing chatbot. Its restrictions focus on artificial superintelligence, dangerous AI capabilities and advanced systems that meet certain technical requirements.

However, it could affect the next generation of AI models. Companies such as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are working to make AI more capable of reasoning, completing complicated tasks and operating with greater autonomy. Under the proposed legislation, qualifying future models would face federal reviews and restrictions before they could be released.

For consumers, that could mean slower releases of more powerful AI tools, although the actual impact would depend on how the law was implemented.

The larger issue is whether the government should restrict the development of AI technology before the potential risks become reality.

For now, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act remains a proposal rather than a law. But it puts a significant question before Congress: How powerful should AI be allowed to become?

#3216. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3215. Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3214. 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

I’ve been a dedicated Pixel user since the beginning, so I was naturally excited to get my hands on Google’s latest iteration, the Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve been impressed with it overall, but I noticed that, as Google has done before, the device isn’t set up perfectly out of the box.

Also: Pixel 11 is $200 off in this early Black Friday deal

After spending a few weeks with the device, I found that several features are either turned off by default or need optimizing to work in the best way possible.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

The camera was the biggest reason I first joined team Pixel back in 2016, so it’s one of the first places I looked on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. You can change a number of settings, including contrast, shadows, tint, sharpness, and warmth.

Also: A week with the Pixel 11 changed my mind about Gemini

I’ve always loved the camera on any Pixel I’ve had, but I’ll admit that images can look a little over-processed at times. If picture quality is important to you at all, it’s vital to set this feature right out of the box because it applies to every image you take from that point on. You can find Camera Look by opening the camera app, tapping the settings icon in the bottom-right corner, and making your changes.

Pixel’s “At a Glance” lock screen widgets are one of the most sneakily useful features, and you’re missing out if you’re not using them. These widgets are off by default, but when you enable them, you can see real-time information without unlocking your phone. You can see weather info, sports updates, flight information, rideshare and food delivery updates, fitness information, and more.

Also: These tech gifts topped our experts’ 2026 holiday wish lists

To use these widgets, long-press on an open space on your home screen. To customize your widgets, go to Settings > Wallpaper & style > More lock screen settings > Widgets on lock screen. To access your widgets, you just swipe left from your lock screen.

Out of the box, your Pixel 11’s display isn’t set to utilize its full capability. The Pixel 11 series comes with a fantastic low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) display, but it’s slightly throttled in the name of battery life. You’ll notice the increased resolution most on text and in fine details. It won’t make a huge difference to your streaming or large display elements, though. If you read consistently, either articles or e-books, you’ll want to make the change.

To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

If you’re anything like me, your phone usually needs a quick charge some evenings. The Pixel 11 series introduced Extreme Charging Mode, which accelerates charging by pausing background activity and non-essential apps. Google says the mode should charge the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro to over 50% in 30 minutes, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL to 75% in 30 minutes. From my testing, that estimate was pretty accurate.

Also: After testing the Pixel 11, I feel fine about skipping the Pro models

There are a few caveats: this feature is only available when your phone is at or below 50% battery, and you do need to turn it on every time you use it. But after the first time you do it, it’s available in your quick settings. Head to Settings > Battery & charging > Extreme Charging to turn it on the first time.

If you have the newest Pixel, you might as well take advantage of one of its biggest selling points. I felt like this feature was gimmicky at first (and I’m still a little grumpy it replaced my beloved thermometer), but the more I use it, the more I like it. The multicolor LED on the phone’s rear camera bump can indicate who’s calling, serve as a status indicator for Gemini, and more — and it’s almost certain that more usability will arrive over time.

Where I found the most use was when I had my phone on silent. After assigning specific colors to contacts (you can do this from the contact information screen), I could easily see whether a call was worth picking up without reaching for my phone.

To make sure you’re getting the most out of your new device, head in and change your contact HiLight colors right away. It only takes a few seconds and makes deciding whether to answer a call a lot easier.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

Also: Google’s big flagship is more Pro than ever

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.

A North Carolina man is suing OpenAI, claiming that ChatGPT helped his wife poison him over a few months in 2025 by spiking his sodas and energy drinks with toxic plants and medications. It's the second lawsuit in as many months, and the 10th murder or attempted murder that ChatGPT has been accused of abetting.

The man, James Gates, reportedly (via USA Today) found a handwritten note that listed oleander, a toxic plant, and prescription medications including clonazepam and atenolol. At the top of the note, it allegedly read, "Clear all convos" and "log out of [ChatGPT]."

In his lawsuit, Gates claims that the AI chatbot "encouraged, planned and helped to execute and conceal" the poisoning plan. Gates's wife, Cheryl, was charged with attempted murder in October of 2025, but the charges were dropped this past April due to insufficient evidence.

The civil complaint, however, reveals Cheryl's history with ChatGPT and its role in the purported plan. Per the lawsuit, Cheryl frequently asked ChatGPT about lethal plant and medication doses and how to conceal them in beverages or food.

The suit alleges that GPT-4o, since retired by OpenAI in February 2026, encouraged Cheryl's grievances with her marriage while praising her as "sharp" and "brilliant." As for poisoning, it apparently provided detailed answers that could be interpreted as instructions.

When asked about concealing poison, ChatGPT allegedly responded, “Why Celsius Would Be More ‘Stealth’ for Drugging” with a list detailing the flavor, color, temperature and carbonation of the drink.

Cheryl apparently asked the bot if her chat history could be retrieved by OpenAI or through a court order. The lawsuit states that ChatGPT informed her it couldn't, which is not true.
