#3197. Regency Centers (REG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record occupancy, raised guidance, and a 2027 refinancing headwind in focus.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Regency Centers Corporation (REG -1.89%) reported quarterly results marked by record high occupancy and an upward revision of full-year financial guidance. Management reported that strong tenant demand and a scarcity of high-quality retail space have enabled the company to achieve historic peaks in both total portfolio and shop-level occupancy. The company is actively shifting focus toward 2027, providing early indications of mid-3% Same Property NOI growth while accounting for headwinds from debt refinancing and the normalization of bad debt expenses. Management stated that the ground-up development platform remains a primary differentiator, providing a visible source of external growth independent of volatile transaction markets. The company maintains a conservative balance sheet with leverage below its target range and significant liquidity to fund a pipeline that has expanded to approximately $700 million in in-process projects.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to Regency Centers Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Kathryn McKie, Vice President, Investor Relations. Thank you. Please go ahead.

Kathryn McKie: Good morning, and welcome to Regency Centers' Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Lisa Palmer, President and Chief Executive Officer; Mike Mas, Chief Financial Officer; Alan Roth, Chief Operating Officer; and Nick Wibbenmeyer, Chief Investment Officer. As a reminder, today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements about the company's views of future business and financial performance, including forward earnings guidance and future market conditions. These are based on the current beliefs and expectations of management and are subject to various risks and uncertainties. It is possible that actual results may differ materially from those suggested by these forward-looking statements we may make.

Factors and risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements may be included in our presentation today and are described in more detail in our filings with the SEC, specifically in our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q filings. In our discussion today, we will also reference certain non-GAAP financial measures. The comparable GAAP financial measures are included in this quarter's earnings materials, which are posted on our Investor Relations website. Please note that we have also posted a presentation on our website with additional information, including disclosures related to forward earnings guidance. Our caution on forward-looking statements also applies to these presentation materials.

As a reminder, given the number of participants we have on the call today, we respectfully ask that you limit your questions to one. Please rejoin the queue if you have any additional follow-up questions. Lisa?

Lisa Palmer: Thank you, Kathryn. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Our team delivered another great quarter. We generated strong same-property NOI and FFO growth, driven by solid operating fundamentals and accretive capital allocation. Demand for space remains robust and our tenant base is strong, supported by the resiliency of consumers in the communities surrounding our centers. Our ground up development platform remains a key differentiator for Regency. We have been expanding our pipeline for years and our team continues to build on that momentum, sourcing high-quality projects across the country. We remain disciplined in the current higher interest rate environment focused on investments that create meaningful earnings growth and long-term value for our shareholders.

Our sector-leading national development platform provides us with a visible source of investment opportunities outside of the transaction markets. Our strong growth so far this year has allowed us to once again increase our full year outlook. We raised our dividend this quarter by 6%, a meaningful increase that extends our long track record of dividend growth, reflecting our performance and the confidence we have and the durability of our cash flows. Looking more broadly and ahead to 2027 and beyond, the fundamentals of our business remain strong. The performance of our portfolio continues to demonstrate sustained strength in tenant demand.

Our neighborhood and community centers anchored by top grocers and focused on necessity, service, convenience and value are well positioned to continue thriving. Our development platform remains the driving force behind our external growth. And we are investing in and leveraging new technologies across our organization, making our team more productive and effective and allowing us to make better, faster decisions. As I close, what sets Regency apart hasn't changed, a high-quality portfolio in strong suburban trade areas, a leading national development platform, a fortress balance sheet and the best team in the business. We are executing on our strategy and have confidence in our ability to drive growth and sustained long-term value for our shareholders in 2027 and beyond.

Alan Roth: Thank you, Lisa, and good morning, everyone. The strength of our results in the third quarter and throughout 2026 reflects the hard work of our team and robust operating fundamentals across our portfolio. Same-property NOI increased 5.1% in the third quarter and 4.4% year-to-date, supported by continued occupancy gains, strong rent growth and disciplined execution. Our same property portfolio reached a new historic high of 97% leased with shop occupancy also reaching a record 94.6%, driven by broad-based tenant demand. Equally encouraging, commenced occupancy increased to 95.1%, yet another historic high as we continue converting our SNO pipeline into rent-paying tenants.

The combination of strong retailer demand as well as ongoing scarcity of both high-quality space and new supply continues to bolster our negotiating position across our portfolio. Cash rent spreads were 12% in the quarter, including negotiated renewal spreads at 15%, while GAAP rent spreads reached 22%. Nearly all of our new shop leases now include annual rent steps of 3% or higher, strengthening our contractual rent growth well into the future. And importantly, we are capturing this rent growth while remaining disciplined with our leasing capital spend. Overall, our tenants remain healthy, and the underlying indicators remain encouraging. Collections are strong, receivables remain below historic levels.

Bankruptcy impacts have been minimal this year, and both foot traffic and tenant sales performance remains solid. And while we have continued visibility to the benefit of commenced occupancy into 2027, growth opportunities extend well beyond the remaining vacancy in our portfolio. We're leasing space earlier, often while it's still occupied, reducing downtime between tenants and accelerating rent commencement. We're capitalizing on mark-to-market opportunities as leases roll taking advantage of supply-demand dynamics through negotiated renewals and embedding strong contractual rent steps into our leases. And we will continue to unlock redevelopment opportunities that improve merchandising, strengthen the competitive positioning of our centers and create value.

Our team continues to deliver, and I'm excited about the runway we have to keep driving NOI growth. With that, I'll hand it over to Nick.

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Thank you, Alan, and good morning, everyone. We continue to see significant positive momentum across our investment platform. During the third quarter, we started several new development and redevelopment projects, made great progress executing on our in-process pipeline, sourced new opportunities and acquire high-quality properties. Year-to-date through October, we started more than $280 million of projects including more than $100 million in the third quarter alone, and we continue to expect starts to approach $400 million by year-end. Our ground up starts in the quarter included a Whole Foods-anchored project in Southern California, and shortly after quarter end, we broke ground on a Sprouts-anchored project in Northern California.

Each of these developments pairs a leading grocer with a premier suburban location, which are exactly the types of projects our platform is designed to deliver. Our in-process pipeline currently stands at approximately $680 million with expected blended return of 9%. We continue to have great momentum leasing up these projects, which is allowing us to bring project NOI online and driving the significant total NOI growth we've seen this year. This success can be seen in the $158 million of projects we've completed so far this year, including the shops at SunVet on Long Island in the third quarter.

This Whole Foods-anchored center has been met with tremendous enthusiasm from both retailers and the community with a merchandising mix that includes Nordstrom Rack, Sephora, Shake Shack and Warby Parker among others. On the transaction side, we acquired more than $100 million of properties in the third quarter, bringing our year-to-date total through October to over $170 million. These included a Stop & Shop anchored center in Northern New Jersey, and a Market Basket-anchored property in suburban Boston. We funded several of these acquisitions with joint venture capital alongside a long-standing partner with whom we have additional capacity to invest.

We continue to source attractive acquisition opportunities, but it remains a competitive transaction market and today's rising interest rate environment creates additional challenges. That said, because we don't exclusively rely on acquisitions to drive our external growth, we can remain patient and selective, pursuing only the opportunities that truly meet our standards for quality and accretion. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to keep building and delivering accretive developments and sourcing high-quality acquisitions that create meaningful growth and value for our shareholders. Based on our deep grocer relationships, a proven track record, ample access to capital as well as sustained strong demand. Mike?

Michael Mas: Thank you, Nick, and good morning, everyone. As you've heard from the team, Regency delivered exceptional results in the third quarter, reflecting the continued fundamental strength of our portfolio and the accretive impact of differentiated capital allocation. Year-to-date, same-property NOI growth is 4.4%, driven by continued growth in occupancy, robust new and renewal leasing, high tenant retention and strong tenant health. Beyond the same property pool, year-to-date total NOI growth is 7.6% with this metric capturing NOI from our ground-up development projects. The strength of our operating results and our ability to accelerate development NOI allows us to once again raise our current year guidance.

We've increased the midpoint of our same-property NOI growth rate to 4.75% or higher, and we've also raised the midpoint of core operating earnings per share, which now calls for full year growth of 5.7% at the midpoint. Looking ahead to next year, while we'll hold full guidance for our fourth quarter call, I do want to share a couple of early indications. Following 2 outstanding years of same property NOI growth, we expect 2027 to be another great year for internal growth as our portfolio is well positioned to benefit from continued strong fundamental trends.

As we sit here today, we anticipate next year's same property NOI growth to be in the mid-3% area, reflecting continued high levels of occupancy, strong rent growth benefiting from our pricing power, steady tenant health and positive contribution from redevelopment. With respect to our long-term target earnings growth rate, we anticipate the refinancing of our maturing debt early next year will have an impact of somewhere in the area of 150 to 200 basis points. Rates have certainly shown some volatility recently. But given where borrowing costs are today, our bias would be towards the lower end of this range. Again, much more to come on 2027 earnings with our full suite of guidance in February.

Moving to our capital and liquidity position. In an environment where balance sheet strength matters more, we are comforted to be in a position of financial strength. Our total leverage currently stands just below our target range, and we have A ratings from both Moody's and S&P. We have substantial availability on our $1.5 billion credit facility and continue to generate strong free cash flow, allowing us to fund our growing external growth pipeline without the need to issue equity or sell properties. We also benefit from additional investment capacity available to us through our long-tenured joint venture partner relationships. This flexibility allows Regency to continue investing accretively and remain opportunistic. In summary, we have had an exceptional year.

Our operating fundamentals are very strong, evidenced by our same-property NOI growth rate. Our development pipeline is providing new, sustained total NOI growth and our balance sheet supports the flexibility to continue investing accretively even through a more uncertain rate environment. We look ahead with confidence in the underlying strength of Regency's portfolio and in our team's ability to deliver attractive, durable growth over the long term. With that, we'd be happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions]. Today's first question is coming from Michael Goldsmith of UBS.

Michael Goldsmith: I appreciate the early indication of the 2027 growth numbers. Right now, you just took your '26 same-property NOI growth to more than 4.25%. And for next year, you're pointing at the mid-3s. So is there -- are there any factors that are in play that would suggest that same property NOI would decelerate? Maybe you can talk through the puts and takes on the same property NOI for next year.

Alan Roth: Sure. Michael, I appreciate the question. So I think I'll start with occupancy, which is where you should start any time you're talking about the direction of our same property growth. As I mentioned on the call in my prepared remarks, we will continue to expect to maintain this very high level of occupancy that we've delivered so far this year. But the increases will be moderating. It's just kind of natural to expect that to occur just as a real brief reminder. And I think to congratulate the Regency team, 2025, we've moved our average commenced occupancy by about 150 basis points. We moved it again this year, and we expect to move it by about 80 basis points.

And I would say that leaves about, I don't know, somewhere in the area of 40 to 50 basis points to move it next year. More to come on the details of that. But that is kind of a natural occurrence of our portfolio as you reach these historical highs that we find ourselves in. Together with that, you benefit from expense recoveries. So we have been benefiting from higher levels of expense recovery rates in '25 and now on to '26, and we'll continue to have some of that up in '27 as well. We are calling for an 87% or 88% recovery rate going forward, which is, again, kind of matching our historical highs.

And then the only other kind of on the downside, I would highlight is we are about 25 basis points on bad debt expense this year, incredibly low. In the third quarter, we had a very low bad debt expense rate. I would say, as we sit here today and it's early, I would plan for something more in the historical averages, which is something approximated or approaching 50 basis points, so that would be incorporated into that 3.5% area that I identified for next year.

Operator: The next question is coming from Jamie Feldman of Wells Fargo.

Conor Peaks: This is Conor on with Jamie. Maybe on ground-up development, can you talk about yields in the next wave of opportunities relative to the 7% plus on the recently announced projects? Are stronger rents and faster leasing creating room for yields to improve or are higher land costs kind of absorbing that upside?

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes. Conor, I appreciate the question. This is Nick. You're absolutely right. I mean, let's just start with the tremendous work our team has been doing over the last several years building this just unbelievable development pipeline that we're now seeing come online and build our in-process to now approaching $700 million. And so as you articulated, our in-process are 7% plus on our ground-up developments. And our teams have been pushing hard to try to get towards the higher end of that 7% plus and they're continuing to push. Do I think we're going to see the gap out at 8%-plus? No.

I think the 7% to 8% range is where they're landing because to your point, there's a lot of inputs, including land cost. But at 7%-plus, we still feel really good with that spread compared to, one, our cost of capital to create real accretion; and two, compared to what those assets would be worth in the private market from an NAV standpoint, so feel really good about those assets. I also feel really good about how we derisk those. I just want to remind everybody, we have a lot of pre-leasing done on those assets before we close. We're fully entitled and we have construction bids in hand.

And so as you've seen us bring these projects online, our teams have done an amazing job holding those yields and improving on the margin in many cases compared to what we thought when we closed on those transactions.

Lisa Palmer: I'd love to just come over the top. And as Mike complemented the operating team to complement our development team. Our conviction in development is as strong as it's been. It remains a key differentiator for us, and it is an important part and driver of long-term growth. And Nick hit on that in terms of the spreads over market cap rates. And we are mindful of our cost of capital. I don't want -- our head is not in the sand on that, and we'll remain disciplined in what we pursue. But the fundamentals supporting development today are still really constructive, as Nick said.

Operator: The next question is coming from Samir Khanal of Bank of America.

Samir Khanal: I guess maybe, Mike, if you can provide an update, expand a little bit on your comments about the transaction market, kind of what are you seeing broadly given the volatility in rates where our unlevered IRRs today? And any comments on pricing or cap rates would be helpful.

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes, Samir, this is Nick. As Mike alluded to in his opening comments, it's volatile out there. There's no question about that. And so we're still in the early innings of what is that going to mean for the transaction market. As you can appreciate, many deals that are closing now were priced 60, 90 days ago. But early indications are -- and this is what you always see in volatility, quality matters. And so early indications are really core grocery-anchored assets with good growth profiles continue to have a lot of demand as there is fund flow into our asset class.

And it does appear those assets that did have a little bit more challenges Potentially, we're going to have a little bit more leverage. Those may be getting retreated in the market from a pricing standpoint. But again, early innings and all indications are our asset classes are still very much in high demand, and so -- but more to come over the next 90 days as assets reprice here.

Operator: The next question is coming from Todd Thomas of KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Todd Thomas: I just wanted to follow up on your comments around the early indication for 2027 same property NOI growth in the 3.5% range. Base rank contribution continues to improve. That was up 4% from 3.7% last quarter. And you talked about the runway from converting the SNO pipeline to rent paying tenants. So are you anticipating any known vacates or occupancy pressure in '27? And then related to your comments on bad debt, is the assumption simply a normalization from current levels? Or is there anything specific? Any specific tenant issues or anything like that, that you're contemplating?

Alan Roth: Todd, I appreciate the follow-up. I would characterize the plan as we sit here today again as being kind of occupancy neutral. We have done an incredible job, and I congratulate the team again on raising our eye level on where occupancy can be in this portfolio, which, by the way, also includes delivering now an incredible amount of redevelopment activity. And I would characterize next year as being kind of occupancy neutral, but opportunity to continue to compress that SNO spreads, right? So I do think we can continue to move commenced occupancy closer to percent leased. I would characterize the ULI change as a normalization.

I don't -- we are not seeing any evidence of tenant health concerns at all. I just can't help but look over my shoulder at a historical average and compare that to where we are today and think -- and not at least think that it could normalize back to historical levels. The teams are doing an incredible job on the leasing front. Pushing rate, using their leverage where we have it, and we have a lot of it today given the tailwinds in the marketplace, given the lack of availability in high-quality centers. And that could evidence itself in a little bit of pressure on bad debt expense. And we'll just be prudent to plan for that.

But to this point, haven't seen a rapid impairment of tenant health.

Operator: The next question is coming from Ronald Kamdem of Morgan Stanley.

Ronald Kamdem: Great. Just following up on that, but going more into the portfolio. Just wondering if you could talk a little bit about just what you're seeing in terms of foot traffic and then some of the categories that are outperforming and updated thoughts on categories that you're reducing exposure to at this point?

Alan Roth: Ronald, thank you for the question. It's Alan. So when I look back at the quarter, there are some really great retailers that we signed multiple leases with. And I think, as you know, the food category tends to be sort of the leader in transactions quarter-over-quarter, but Cava, Paris Baguette, Chipotle, just to sort of name a few on that front. Health and wellness is a key sort of sector that we've been talking a lot about for the last number of years. And we continue to lean into that with 13% of our ABR combined on fitness and medical.

And so when you look back at that quarter again, where were there multiple transactions signed, SweatHouz, IVX Health , JETSET Pilates, all really just great small shop retailers that are filling the portfolio. And then from a milestone perspective, we signed our 75th lease with TJX again, another phenomenal retailer. So there's just a lot of really great operators that are out there. As Mike had mentioned, we are leasing a lot of occupied space right now. The pipeline is deep, it's healthy. And at these occupancy levels, that is another certainly key focus that we continue to drive rents on some of that occupied space.

Operator: The next question is coming from Michael Griffin of Evercore ISI.

Michael Griffin: So I saw that Kroger announced plans to expand their store fleet pretty notably over the next couple of years. And as a key partner of theirs, I'm wondering how Regency could stand to benefit from this? Could this be incremental ground-up developments, redevelopments of existing stores? And then as you look at kind of the grocery landscape broadly, I realize that being with the right grocer in the right market is really paramount. But does the environment feel better for openings there into the next few years? And then how can Regency benefit as a result?

Lisa Palmer: Nick, I'll just take -- I'm going to address the latter and then let you finish with the beginning of the question. I appreciate you answering the question yourself in your question. We certainly always pay attention to the grocers. They're an important part of our business. And as many of you know, because you probably did see it on social media, I've been with the company for 30 years now. And for all of those 30 years, grocery, the grocery business is extremely competitive and that environment just becomes more and more so. And the traditional grocers are facing more competition from the specialty grocers from different means of customers getting their groceries delivered to them as well.

So the competitive pressures are not being reduced in any way, and we never minimize that. But I think it's really important because it's something that we always talk about to really distinguish between the performance of the grocer chains and the underlying value of their best-performing stores. And our strategy is to focus on to own, to develop the stores that will be the best performing stores in their portfolio.

And we continue to believe and grocers continue to believe that a physical presence is important for them to be successful across all delivery methods -- or across all delivery of their goods to the consumers, whether they walk in the store, order online and pick up or have it delivered.

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes, Michael, I'll just add to that. The specifics regarding Kroger, without a doubt look, we love when important relationships we have, doubled down on what Lisa just said, and reinforce that net new stores and brick-and-mortar is important to them. We believe that as well as just Lisa articulated. And so you think about Kroger, yes, we've had a long-standing relationship and a lot of development and redevelopments with Kroger. And so any incremental demand they have is a benefit for Regency. And you could look -- as we talk right now, we just reopened a teardown rebuild store in Westchester, Ohio with Kroger, phenomenal redevelopment.

We're building a King Soopers, which is a Kroger brand in Colorado, new development in Lone Tree, Colorado. And so we are very engaged with Kroger. We're excited to see them ramp back up their store program. And I think incrementally, again, if you just look over our shoulder, look, we started just over $250 million of developments and redevelopments in '24. In '25, we started over $300 million. We've given ahead and this year, it should be in the $400 million range. And so incrementally, as these grocers lean back into store programs, it is beneficial to our development and redevelopment program. So we're appreciative of those relationships.

They're very important to us, and that's why I'm excited about our future investment program.

Operator: The next question is coming from Greg McGinniss of Scotiabank.

Greg McGinniss: I wanted to keep on the grocers, the strength in Kroger, but that's kind of offset potentially a bit by Albertsons talking about reviewing its real estate. Just curious if you can touch on how your banners with them are performing, whether you see that as any risk or not, just given the quality of your assets?

Alan Roth: Greg, thank you for the question. I think Lisa did a really nice job articulating the fact that our stores, when we look at their performance, are trending above with the banners average volumes are. And again, I think that's a testament to the markets that we're operating in, how we deliberately think about merchandising and operating these assets. And we feel really, really good about the overall health of our supermarkets. Some of them, as we talked about Albertsons came out and said they're working to improve their stores, recognizing that grocery competition is, in fact, fierce. But again, we would bring it back to the overall quality of our real estate. It's great.

They, too, are also an important relationship, not just Kroger. Certainly, Whole Foods, Publix, there's a whole host of them, Sprouts, et cetera. And we're staying close to all of them as we do with all of our key retailers, not just the grocers. So we certainly remain very encouraged by the locations and performance of those stores.

Operator: The next question is coming from Juan Sanabria of BMO Capital Markets.

Juan Sanabria: Just hoping to maybe shift gears a bit. Thinking about some of the trends across retail real estate more broadly, it does seem that landlords just trying to take advantage of eyeballs and foot traffic across their platforms. So just curious on your latest initiatives on media or advertising opportunities that I think would be pretty unique, given daily and weekly traffic to your centers.

Alan Roth: Juan, thank you for the question. I think I love the media advertising capabilities because I know Eric Davidson, our group would love to have the shout out to his White Box Series that I think has got over 1 million YouTube views on it. Look, there is certainly an environment of landlord leverage in today's environment at 97%, we are leaning in, and there's a lot of things that certainly we're doing. There's a transition more to fair market value options. There's a transition to no options in many instances. A lot of nonmonetary provisions that there's an opportunity to certainly improve that gives more flexibility for leasing decisions and redevelopment decisions in our assets.

But again, I think one important thing that Regency has always done is we're very deliberate in how we think about merchandising our assets how we think about place making, connecting with the community. And in today's environment. Again, we try to hone in on everything that can really make that asset sustainable in the long term. And so we continue to feel really good about how the teams are focused on various things. And I think that's evidenced in the results. I appreciate the question.

Operator: The next question is coming from Haendel St. Juste of Mizuho Securities.

Ravi Vaidya: This is Ravi Vaidya on the line for Haendel. I wanted to ask about your capital deployment optionality. With leverage below your long-term range of 5% to 5.5%, and what appears to be a disconnect from private market cap rates of maybe 100, 150 bps. Why not buy back stock here? How should we think about your capital deployment optionality, particularly for larger portfolio deals with your peers doing some larger deals such as the Summit and Slate?

Lisa Palmer: Appreciate the question. We have leveraged free cash flow that, as Nick said, still have really great opportunities to put into our development pipeline and it's our in-process development as well as redevelopments. And those returns are still greater than the returns we would receive buy back stock. Stock buybacks have been and will always continue to be a tool in our toolbox and when we do have the availability of capital to use it and when the returns are more attractive than what they would be versus our developments and/or acquisitions, we will utilize it. That's not the case today.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Sydnie Rohme of Barclays.

Sydnie Rohme: I've got kind of a bigger picture one on supply. For a developer that's starting from scratch today and buying land and building at current costs, what rent does a new center needs to make sense versus the roughly $38 per foot you're getting on new leases? And how long does that gap sort of keep new supply out in your opinion?

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Sydnie, I appreciate the question. This is Nick. I hope you can appreciate it, it's difficult to answer because it's so market-specific and site-specific. And so it is our job as our teams do a tremendous job around the country sourcing these land deals. Our job is to put all the inputs into the pro forma to make sure it's a risk-adjusted return we're comfortable with. And so certain markets have higher land costs, as you can appreciate, higher construction cost. And so there is no unfortunate easy button to hit of what the rent needed to make those deals pencil. It really is market by market. But as you can see, we -- I'm comfortable saying both are true.

We are getting more than our fair share of development opportunities. Our teams are doing a tremendous job putting all those inputs into the pro forma, making sure we're getting a risk-adjusted return of north of 7%, which we articulated, we're very comfortable with in this environment. But at the same time, we also know how extremely difficult those opportunities are to find and to make pencil. And that is why even with all of our relationships, even with all of our knowledge, we do believe we are the best in the business at it. We know how difficult it is. And so we don't see a massive amount of supply coming online.

I do think there's a pretty material delta from those economics making sense for a massive amount of supply to come online. And so we're confident on both ends. We're confident on our ability to grow our development pipeline like we have been, and we're confident on the operating side that we're going to continue to have leverage given the limited amount of overall supply coming into the market.

Operator: The next question is coming from Michael Mueller of JPMorgan.

Unknown Analyst: This is Jacob on for Mike. Keeping on the development theme, some of your recent activity has been tied to master plan communities. Can you tell us if working with these developers gives you more visibility into starts 3 to 5 years out? And does it give you any more visibility in the shadow pipeline as well?

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes, I really appreciate the question, Jacob. You're absolutely right. We've had a tremendous amount of success working with master plan developers just for the reason you articulated. Number one is they are planning years in advance which works to our benefit to work with them as a partner to plan. Arguably their most important amenity and many of these projects is what is the retail center going to be. As you're well aware, new homeowners really want to know where they're going to grocery shop. It's an important part of our everyday lives.

And so being able to work with what they see as best-in-class developer, grocery-anchored tenant is an important attribute that they are selling to their future homebuyers. And so also, given the previous question Sydnie asked, they're a little less concerned about the specific land value on that one parcel of land when they're working with thousands of acres. And so they are a little more realistic on land value to make sure they're bringing in the absolute best-in-class grocery operator. So it's a win-win scenario from our perspective. They know we're going to bring the best operator possible to their development.

They know we're going to develop it all cash and they know we're going to own it and care about it long term. And so if you're a master plan developer, I say it all the time, I don't know how you wouldn't pick us to be your retail partner. So very important part of our development program. We take those relationships very, very serious. And to your point, it gives us the confidence as we are working on our shadow pipeline that we're going to be able to continue to have our development starts to be in the same ZIP code that we're seeing this year.

Operator: The next question is coming from Craig Mailman of Citi.

Craig Mailman: I just want to go back to the comments just on the forward demand pipeline for spaces that are leased. Just kind of want to see if there's any takeaways that you could give on where spreads are trending? Are they strengthening or kind of stay the same? And then just kind of longer term, I know we've chatted a little bit on this call about just the vertical makeup in the portfolio.

Like long term, are there any changes that you would like to see from a remerchandising standpoint to just bolster the sustainability of cash flows or bring down bad debt long term as you look to replace some of these tenants who are maybe struggling or just overall strength in the center?

Alan Roth: Craig, it's Alan. I appreciate the question. So from a forward demand perspective, look, our pipeline remains very strong. And merchandising, as I said, has always been a deliberate strategy. I think what I would look to maybe a bit first is the retention rate. Again, and this sort of ties into the supply-demand dynamic that we're in right now. But we were at 84%, and that's a peak. And we do not manage to a number on a retention basis. It's really more of just an outcome. And I would say that I'm very comfortable and it is healthy to take some space back and we do that intentionally via this sort of proactive leasing some occupied space.

And I don't want to make this such a huge prevalent theme, but it's an important one in that we have $2 million of incremental signed snow pipeline that is on space that is occupied right now. And so that ties directly into your point of why are we doing it. We're doing it because we believe we can get a better operator that should drive better foot traffic, which will drive higher sales, which will drive higher rent for the rest of the asset. And it's an accretive transaction, hence, the incremental add to our ABR, so it's a key focus.

It's something we've done in the past, and we will certainly continue to do in the future, particularly at 97% leased, where we'll take advantage of that tailwind of driving revenue.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question is coming from Linda Tsai of Truist.

Linda Tsai: Do you feel pricing power is more concentrated in the starting front or higher contractual escalators?

Alan Roth: Linda, no, I appreciate that question. It's all about gap rent from my perspective. And I think, look, it is an art, not a science. There are instances where you're driving a higher initial rent spread. But at the end of the day, on a collective basis, we're focused on both. And I think when you look at our new deals for the quarter, we were at, what, just north of 30% in terms of GAAP rent spreads. When you look at our shop embedded rent steps 100% of our new shop deals did include rent steps. And we're at that point where 90% of them are over 3%, 20% of them were over 4%.

And so the teams are really clicking on all cylinders in terms of the combined long-term sustainable growth in both spreads and steps.

Operator: Thank you. At this time, I'd like to turn the floor back over to Ms. Lisa Palmer for closing comments.

Lisa Palmer: Yes, we thought that maybe perhaps someone else was trying to ask.

Operator: I did see somebody come in, but they removed themselves.

Lisa Palmer: Okay. Perfect. Thank you so much. I appreciate everyone's time today. Have a -- we'll see many at NAREIT in just a couple of weeks, and enjoy the weekend. Thank you.

#3196. Pet Insurance on Your Mind? Buy It Now, Not Later

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3195. Good Riddance: Tesla to End Cybertruck Production in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tesla says it will wind down its most notorious model at Gigafactory Texas to make room for its self-driving Cybercab.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced the end of the brand’s most ostentatious model, the Cybertruck, in a post on X late Thursday night. Tesla will begin winding down production of the wedge-shaped pickup at its Texas Gigafactory “around the middle of next year,” Musk said, to boost manufacturing capacity for its Cybercab robotaxi.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

The Cybertruck will not be missed by many. Sales have been so low that Tesla doesn’t even separate them out in its financials — lumping it into an “Other models” column — with experts estimating numbers significantly lower than Tesla’s built-out manufacturing capacity and far below Musk’s sales goals. Meanwhile, Tesla and Musk have increasingly shifted their focus to AI, robotics and autonomy as the brand’s future.

Tesla unveiled the edgy, all-electric pickup truck at an event in 2019, and the cracks were already beginning to show in many of Musk’s most outlandish claims surrounding the truck. (In the case of the “bulletproof” glass, the cracks literally showed.)

After multiple delays, deliveries finally began in 2023. Musk had spent the intervening four years baffling people by making (and subsequently retracting) many truly bizarre statements about the EV’s capabilities, but the first nail in the Cybertruck’s coffin was the starting price, which had ballooned to $60,990, up from the initial $40,000 target touted at debut.

Over its lifetime, the Cybertruck struggled to meet even the most basic expectations, contending with reliability issues, multiple recalls and a penchant for eating its owners’ fingers. It didn’t help that the sci-fi-styled EV arrived around the same time Musk became deeply involved in US politics and policy, and has become known as something of a rolling dog whistle for those who agree with the billionaire’s increasingly unpopular ideologies.

Customers were presented with a niche EV that was more expensive than expected, unsafe, unreliable, unpopular and unattractive. It’s no surprise that sales have suffered, with some experts predicting that since its arrival on US roads, Tesla has sold only about 10% of Musk’s Cybertruck goals. That’s despite Tesla building out an estimated 125,000-unit annual manufacturing capacity at the Texas Gigafactory where the truck is built, leaving the automaker with a huge stock of unsold, unwanted inventory sitting on its lots. One of Musk’s other companies, SpaceX, bought $131 million worth of Cybertrucks last year.

The Cybertruck’s 2027 wind-down will make way for increased capacity for the fully autonomous Cybercab, which debuted in 2024 and is slated to ramp up production in Texas next year. Pitched as a robotaxi that you could own for “under $30,000,” Tesla began offering rides in its steering-wheel-free Cybercab in limited parts of Austin in early September — a stunt that immediately prompted a federal investigation into whether the self-driving vehicle meets federal safety standards.

The Cybertruck joins the Model S and X on Tesla’s 2026 chopping block. The electric sedan and SUV were discontinued in January to make room for production of the Optimus humanoid robot at Tesla’s factory in Fremont, California. That will leave just the Model 3 and Model Y in Tesla’s consumer car lineup until the brand’s next rolling publicity stunt, the high-flying Tesla Roadster, allegedly arrives in 2028.

#3194. Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG

It’s mostly bad news from EA lately, but preservation efforts are nice to see.

Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason, but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG, including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series.

Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games:

In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy, Privateer 2, and Road Rash.

It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past.

In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV‘s full-motion-video cutscenes.

The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.

The flagship offering of those remasters is much, much higher-quality full-motion video sequences than have ever been available before, but other enhancements include 60 frames-per-second gameplay, a plethora of newly available .INI tweaks, and full controller support (though looking at the Steam forums for the games, some folks are having trouble with said controller support).

For Privateer 2—the little-remembered sequel to Wing Commander: Privateer—the crew couldn’t find the original, high-quality remasters of the FMV scenes, and ended up getting in touch with the game’s original cinematics director, Steve Hilliker, who had the tapes in his attic. Hilliker had always wanted to take a new color-grading pass, and he did just that, while also remastering and upscaling all of the cutscenes.

Similar updates were given to Wing Commander Prophecy. The blog post also details GOG’s involvement in restoring and remastering Prophecy and Road Rash. For the latter, EA re-licensed the entire original soundtrack for re-release.

The e collection is on sale on GOG and Steam right now; previous owners of the old versions of the games on GOG and the EA storefront get these remasters for free. None of the games cost more than $5 each.

One good story doesn’t undo a lot of bad news and questionable decisions from EA, but this shows that a few passionate people can do something remarkable for game preservation, even if some of the work was done on a volunteer basis outside normal working hours. (EA committed some resources to the restorations as the project progressed, though.)

While the remasters aren’t perfect, the gaming industry could use news like this. It’s worth reading the full story in the blog post for a journey down memory lane and a look at how involved a restoration process like this can be.

#3193. American Express Has Cut Its Share Count by 27% Since 2016. Here's What That Did for the Stock.

Investors have benefited from market-thumping returns in the last decade.

Companies that generate positive operating cash flow can allocate their capital in various ways. Of course, reinvesting in the business is what many long-term investors appreciate, as it can boost intrinsic value over time. There are also mergers and acquisitions, as well as paying down debt.

When it comes to returning capital to investors, companies can direct cash to dividend payments. Stock buybacks are another avenue to put money back into shareholders' pockets, particularly in a more tax-efficient manner.

American Express (AXP -1.23%) has been a leader in the latter category. The premium credit card enterprise reduced its outstanding share count by a notable 26.8% from Q3 2016 to Q3 2026 (ended Sept. 30). Here's what this did for the financial stock.

Over the past decade, American Express has been a wildly successful investment asset. The stock produced a total return of 471% during that time (as of Nov. 4). This gain easily outpaced the S&P 500 index.

Profit growth is a critical catalyst that supports stock performance. From the third quarter of 2016 to the most recent quarter, American Express's diluted earnings per share (EPS) increased by 352%. This reveals major fundamental strength for the business.

The company's diluted EPS rose at a faster clip than net income, which was up 228% in the last 10 years. Share repurchases make up the difference. Every time the business chooses to conduct stock buybacks, it boosts the per-share profits attributable to each existing investor. In other words, shareholders see their ownership stakes steadily increase over time. This is a key part of the management team's capital allocation policy.

Investors shouldn't only buy a stock because the business is constantly repurchasing shares. There is always more to the thesis. That being said, American Express is a high-quality company that's worth looking into.

The business has established a strong position in the credit card market, with a wide economic moat supported by its robust brand, which attracts affluent customers, and its powerful network effect, which creates a positive feedback loop that improves the value proposition for consumers and merchants. These traits defend American Express's competitive standing.

At a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 16.2, I believe the large-cap stock is reasonably valued right now. It's not necessarily cheap or expensive.

However, the leadership team is aiming for EPS to rise at a mid-teens annualized pace in the long run. That's a realistic outlook. And should it prove to be true, it presents a durable tailwind for the stock price.

#3192. Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump

Iran threatened to attack subsea cables if US escalates military strikes again.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.

The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.

Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable, is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.

Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.

Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.

Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.

Since the US and Israel first launched a major war with Iran in February 2026, Iran’s response beyond targeting US military bases, ships and aircraft has included attacking commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and hitting oil refineries and other energy infrastructure along with airports in various Gulf countries.

Iran has also made a point of threatening or attacking US Big Tech infrastructure in the Middle East, including launching multiple drone strikes on Amazon data centers. In May 2026, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Iran would “impose fees on Internet cables” belonging to US tech companies and other owners.

But more recently, multiple Iranian officials and commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have warned that they could directly attack the undersea cables running through the Strait of Hormuz. This came after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to renew major US military strikes on Iran and warned he could “annihilate” the country during a speech at the United Nations in New York on September 22.

“Seven major cables run through the Strait of Hormuz, supporting global Internet operations and commercial data transmission,” one IRGC spokesperson said on October 20. “We remind the enemy of this.”

The latest phase of the war has involved more limited US military strikes against Iranian targets, even as Trump has alternated between threats and touting the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough. Meanwhile, Iran has increased drone strikes and other attacks on commercial ships to exert its own pressure on the United States, with October marking the highest number of ship attacks since the war began.

Much damage has already been done. The limited fleet of cable-laying ships used for installation and repair has not been able to venture safely into the region since the war began, which forced the Meta-backed 2Africa cable to pause its planned expansion. The war has also compelled US tech companies and Gulf countries to accelerate efforts to develop alternative cable routes bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

The Middle East is not the only part of the world where threats to the Internet’s undersea backbone have intensified. Subsea infrastructure is increasingly at risk from sabotage and gray-zone warfare from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.

You’ll also get an in-stay credit when you book a vacation home through The Edit for four nights or more.

Starting in 2027, Chase’s The Edit collection of upscale hotel and resort stays will broaden to include more than 10,000 vacation homes. If you carry the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, that means you’ll soon have more ways to use The Edit credits on those cards.

This addition will significantly expand The Edit’s footprint — currently at more than 1,500 hotels and resorts — although its usefulness will depend on your travel style. The new properties are curated in partnership with Plum Guide, a vacation-rental booking platform.

Plus, when you book a stay of four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use at your vacation home.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming changes to The Edit.

Eligible Chase cardholders can currently book vacation homes through the issuer’s travel portal. However, those bookings are not eligible to receive The Edit benefits. That changes Jan. 1, 2027, with select listings.

If you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, here’s what you can expect when you book a vacation home through The Edit:

Up to $250 in statement credits on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardholders are capped at $500 in credits a year, while Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders get up to $1,000 (starting Jan. 1, 2027).

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

Compared to booking hotels and resorts with The Edit, you’re losing out on perks like a $100 property credit (which doesn’t have a four-night minimum), complimentary breakfast and room upgrades.

While cardholders will be able to redeem points toward vacation-home stays, Chase told NerdWallet that these bookings will not be eligible for Points Boost at launch.

You’ll also need to book vacation homes at least seven days in advance — a requirement that’s currently in place with standard vacation homes available in Chase’s travel portal. Chase said it plans to reduce that requirement in the near future.

Chase’s addition of vacation homes to The Edit follows American Express’ recent move to add Airbnb Luxe properties to its own lodging credit for eligible cardholders.

When you book a vacation home for four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use on services like massages, a private chef, dry cleaning and airport pick-ups.

Options vary by property, but you’ll see a list of available offerings prior to booking your stay. You won’t be able to see pricing, but you can reach out to a Reserve travel designer — a travel concierge who can help plan your trip — to get pricing estimates prior to booking. (You won’t be able to contact the vacation home host until after you’ve booked your stay.)

While it’s nice to get the credit, the four-night minimum could be frustrating for cardholders. When you book hotels through The Edit, there isn’t a stay minimum to get the $100 property credit (although you must stay two nights to use your eligible card’s $250 prepaid stay credit).

By comparison, AmEx offers a $250 Airbnb Experiences credit on the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express each calendar year when you book a prepaid Airbnb Luxe property through its travel portal. Terms apply. That statement credit is good for the rest of the calendar year in which the booking is confirmed. However, you can only unlock one $250 credit a year, even if you make multiple bookings.

Booking a vacation home through The Edit makes the most sense for longer group trips.

One of the best perks of booking a vacation home is that everyone gets to stay together in a shared space — something that’s difficult to do in a traditional hotel. If you’re able to get a larger group, you’ll also have more people to split the booking cost with.

Plus, you’ll want to stay at least four nights to benefit from the $150 in-stay credit.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

As Hilton noted, in Q4, acquired station expenses should be down materially from the $52 million we reported during the third quarter. Jeff will now address the key financial developments since the last call. Jeff?

Jeff Gignac: Thanks, Pat. I'd like to spend a minute on our balance sheet and our leverage. As most of you have seen, we've been exceptionally active in the capital market since our last call. In July, as we previously discussed, we repurchased $120 million of our secured and unsecured notes using cash and revolver borrowings. On October 21, we issued $750 million of 7.5% first lien notes due 2034, with most of the proceeds used to redeem $675 million of our 10.5% 2029 notes. Political cash allowed us to fully repay our revolver by the end of the quarter. In October, we issued a $675 million Term Loan G due July of 2030 at SOFR +350.

The Term Loan G proceeds and cash were used to pay down all but $150 million of our Term Loan D that's due in December of 2028 and to redeem an additional $150 million of our 10.5% notes. In October, we also extended our revolver from -- to July of 2030 from December of 2028, and we reduced the commitments to $680 million. This past Monday, we prepaid $25 million on the Term Loan G, satisfying all scheduled amortization payments through maturity. Just yesterday, we closed on an upsize of our AR securitization facility to $450 million. We also reduced the pricing on that facility to SOFR +115 and extended the maturity to November of 2029.

Finally, as noted in our release, we intend to use our political cash to further reduce debt by another $175 million to $200 million between now and the end of the year. That's almost $2 per share of value as we reduce debt. The net result of all of these actions is that our nearest maturities are now $150 million on the Term Loan D due in December '28, $200 million of our 10.5% first lien notes due in July of '29. We incurred $65 million of transaction costs related to these refinancing transactions, which includes about $43 million of call premiums on the 10.5% notes.

While the breakage costs work against us on near-term debt and leverage reduction, the lower debt coupons, together with additional debt repayments, are expected to reduce our annual interest cost, as Hilton noted, by at least $40 million next year. Remember, too, that the preferred equity redemption earlier this year reduced our annual preferred dividends by $4 million, and that was $50 million of face value that we reduced earlier this year. All of this enhances our discretionary free cash flow as we move into the nonpolitical year next year.

Our leverage metrics at the end of the quarter under our amended senior credit agreement definitions were 2.54x consolidated first lien net leverage ratio, 3.7x consolidated secured net leverage ratio and 5.7x consolidated total net leverage ratio. A few things I'd like to mention related to our release in the 10-Q. Our third quarter '26 results included a full quarter of the stations that we acquired and swapped earlier in the year. All key third quarter revenue metrics exceeded our updated guidance, and our expense items all fell within the updated guidance ranges. We're progressing as expected on our acquired station integrations, and you're seeing that show up in our reported results.

Net retrans revenue was $150 million for the quarter. That included $9 million of the contribution from our '26 acquisitions. And this is the second straight quarter in which net retrans revenue benefited our leverage ratio denominator, rather than being a drag on that on an 8-quarter basis. We expect net retrans revenue to be a growing contribution and to accelerate into 2027. We lowered our company-wide CapEx estimate to $110 million to $120 million from a prior $120 million to $130 million for 2026. It's mainly due to a couple of our station construction projects moving to 2027. We also lowered our full year tax guidance to a range of $75 million to $80 million.

And with that, I'll turn the call back over to Hilton.

#3189. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.
