#3188. SAB Biotherapeutics (SABS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Full enrollment in adult and adolescent SAFEGUARD cohorts sets up a pivotal 2027 data readout.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

SAB Biotherapeutics, Inc. (SABS +3.06%) reported a fiscal transition in the third quarter of 2026 as it increased research spending to advance its lead clinical programs. Management reported that the company achieved full enrollment for its adult and adolescent patient cohorts in the SAFEGUARD trial and received FDA Fast Track designation for its primary immunotherapy candidate. The company maintains a multiyear cash runway intended to support the development of treatments for Stage 3 type 1 diabetes through the release of topline data in 2027. Strategic focus remains on leveraging the proprietary Tc Bovine platform and expanding the addressable patient population through the initiation of additional clinical studies.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to SAB BIO's conference call to discuss third quarter 2026 financial results and business updates. Listeners are invited to review the full text of the forward-looking statements from this morning's quarterly earnings press release. Company management may provide projections during this call, and actual results could differ materially due to several factors, including those outlined in the company's latest filings with the SEC. [Operator Instructions] This call is being webcast live and can be accessed on the Investors section of SAB BIO's website at ir.sab.bio, where a replay will be available. I'll now turn the call over to Samuel Reich, Chief Executive Officer of SAB BIO.

Samuel Reich: Thank you, operator. Good morning, and thank you to everyone joining us for our third quarter 2026 earnings call. I'm joined today by Lucy To, our Chief Financial Officer, who will review the third quarter financial results. I'm also joined by Eddie Sullivan, our Co-Founder and President, and Alexandra Kropotova, our Chief Medical Officer. As we begin November, we recognize Diabetes Awareness Month and focus attention on the millions of people living with type 1 diabetes. We remain committed to advancing new medicines with the potential to change the course of the disease and improve the lives of those affected.

That focus continues to drive our work at SAB BIO, and we're pleased to have you with us today to review the progress we made during the third quarter. We continue to execute on our priorities for SAB-142 with strong momentum in SAFEGUARD enrollment and the FDA granting Fast Track designation to SAB-142 for the treatment of new-onset Stage 3 type 1 diabetes. For context, SAB-142 is a fully human anti-thymocyte immunoglobulin designed to preserve insulin-producing beta cells in order to slow disease progression in autoimmune type 1 diabetes. It was developed using our proprietary Tc Bovine platform, which allows us to generate fully human, multi-specific antibodies without the need for human donors.

Because SAB-142 is fully human, it has the potential to overcome key limitations of non-human approaches and enable safe redosing over the long term. We believe SAB-142 represents an opportunity to help people with type 1 diabetes redefine what a Stage 3 diagnosis can mean. SAB-142 is currently being evaluated in 2 clinical trials, the registrational Phase 2b SAFEGUARD study for those newly diagnosed with Stage 3 T1D and the investigator-led Phase 3 PRISE study for people up to 2 years from a Stage 3 T1D diagnosis. Let's start with an enrollment update for SAFEGUARD. The performance of our clinical team this quarter has been exemplary.

In September, the study's Data Monitoring Committee approved the final step-down to children ages 5 to 11, helping to further accelerate enrollment. We continue to see strong interest in SAFEGUARD from both patients and investigators, and we're excited to share that the adult and adolescent cohorts are now fully enrolled and closed for screening. With that, we are reaffirming our guidance to complete enrollment of SAFEGUARD in Q4, with topline data expected in the second half of '27. Building on that progress, the PRISE study expects to dose the first patients this quarter. There are 7 clinical sites planned across the United States, Europe and the UK.

PRISE is an important extension of the SAB-142 clinical program as it would potentially allow a future label expansion for SAB-142 to T1D patients up to 2 years from a Stage 3 diagnosis. As a reminder, PRISE is an investigator-led study supported by a grant from Breakthrough T1D and co-funded by SAB BIO. We are grateful to Breakthrough T1D for its support and to Dr. Michael Haller at the University of Florida, who serves as the study's principal investigator. We also want to recognize Dr. Chantal Mathieu at UZ Leuven and Dr. Timothy Tree at King's College London as co-principal investigators for their important contribution to the study.

Beyond our clinical progress, we reached an important regulatory milestone in October when the FDA granted Fast Track designation to SAB-142 for the treatment of new-onset Stage 3 type 1 diabetes. This designation is intended to facilitate the development and expedite the review of therapies for serious conditions where there is an unmet medical need, with the goal of bringing important new treatments to patients earlier. For SAB-142, this designation gives the program some serious aura. And importantly, it provides valuable procedural benefits as we advance our program.

These include opportunities for more frequent meetings and written communications with the FDA, eligibility for rolling review of the future BLA and potential eligibility for Priority Review if the applicable criteria are met. While Fast Track designation does not change the FDA's standards for approval or ensure that SAB-142 will ultimately be approved, we believe the benefits are meaningful as we move toward topline data. We will continue to work closely with the FDA as we advance the SAB-142 clinical program. And we believe this designation represents meaningful progress toward our goal of bringing SAB-142 to people living with type 1 diabetes as quickly as possible.

And with that, I will hand the call over to Lucy To, our Chief Financial Officer, for a recap of our third quarter financials.

Lucy To: Thanks, Sam. We ended the third quarter with $205 million in cash, cash equivalents and investment securities as of September 30, 2026. We maintain a strong cash position and project that our existing cash balance will fund our operations through 2028. This total includes $13.4 million in gross proceeds received in the third quarter from the exercise of our previously issued enrollment and data release warrants from our July 2025 PIPE. R&D expenses were $18.1 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $9 million for the same period in 2025. The increase is primarily driven by ongoing clinical trial costs and related headcount to support the advancement of SAB-142 through the registrational SAFEGUARD study.

R&D expenses include non-cash stock-based compensation expense of $3.9 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $0.5 million for the same period in 2025. G&A expenses were $7.8 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $3.7 million for the same period in 2025. The increase is primarily driven by personnel-related costs, including non-cash stock-based compensation. G&A expenses include non-cash stock-based compensation expense of $3.6 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $0.3 million for the same period in 2025. Other income was $3.6 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $58.1 million for the same period in 2025.

The decrease primarily reflects the change in fair value of warrant liabilities recognized in 2025. As a result, net loss was $22.3 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to the net income of $45.4 million for the same period in 2025. Overall, we reaffirm our position to support SAB-142's clinical development in the SAFEGUARD and PRISE studies through key milestones while preparing for commercial readiness for SAB-142. And with that, I can turn it back over to Sam for closing remarks before we open the call for questions.

Samuel Reich: Thanks, Lucy. We're pleased with the progress we made during the third quarter and enter the final months of the year with a clear focus: completing enrollment in SAFEGUARD and continuing to advance SAB-142 toward topline data. We are incredibly grateful to our team, our investigators and clinical collaborators, the patients and families participating in SAFEGUARD and the broader diabetes community. Their commitment and engagement continue to drive our work and reinforce the importance of developing new therapies for people living with type 1 diabetes. As we look to 2027, we're excited to move toward topline data from SAFEGUARD while continuing to build the capabilities and infrastructure needed to support SAB-142 over the long term.

We believe SAB-142 has the potential to meaningfully change the treatment of type 1 diabetes and we are focused on delivering on that promise. We look forward to sharing our progress as we continue advancing SAB-142 across our clinical programs and executing on our strategy. And with that, we're ready to take any questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question is from Michael Yee from UBS.

Michael Yee: Congrats on the progress on enrollment. As we think about the data ahead next year, could you sort of comment or reiterate your framing of expectations on that result in terms of C-peptide and A1C, and how important each of those are to hit for differentiation to Tzield? And secondly, given that Tzield now has a new Stage 3 indication, while we've been talking with different docs, what are you hearing out there? What are you seeing? And is that perhaps a pretty good indication of what the opportunity could be, although it's still early there?

Samuel Reich: Thanks, Mike. I'll answer the second part first and then hand it to Alexandra to answer the first question. So the second part on Tzield, we're very encouraged by what we're seeing with Tzield. The uptake in the community shows the importance of new medicines, and it's paving the way and establishing a pattern with doctors and patients to get treatment, to get a prescription to preserve the pancreas when a patient is diagnosed. So we're encouraged by what we're seeing and I think it bodes well for SAB-142 as it's -- as we believe strongly that it's a competitive product with fewer days of dosing.

We'll see where the results are on the efficacy, but also will overall have a better profile. So I think everything we're seeing with Tzield is good news for the field and for SAB-142. And for the first part, I'll hand it over to our Chief Medical Officer, Alexandra, to answer the question.

Alexandra Kropotova: Thank you very much, Sam. We are very hopeful about our upcoming data release next year. Of course, the primary endpoint of the preservation of the beta cell function as measured by the area under the curve C-peptide is our primary endpoint, and we'll be reporting the results on that, where the statistically significant results versus control arm will guarantee us the accelerated path to the approval for the product.

Now ATG is a clinically validated mechanism of action where previous multiple clinical trials showed the important improvement in the glycemic control needed for the full approval of the medications in the disease-modifying therapies, and we will be releasing the data on the glycemic control as well based on the HbA1c and the continuous glucose monitoring.

Now third component of a very important differentiation profile of the SAB-142 versus Tzield is the low immunogenicity due to the full human nature of the antibody that will allow the drug to provide the disease-modifying therapy over a lifetime of the disease of the patients, where the product can be redosed to continue maintaining the C-peptide and preserving the residual beta cells, not only over 1 or 2 courses but for over a much longer period. So immunogenicity data and the safety data associated with the long-term redosing will be part of our topline as well.

Operator: The next question is from Ellie Merle from Barclays.

Tejas Wein: This is Tejas on for Ellie. My first one, just for the study in the patients 2 years from diagnosis, could you expand on just some of the different cohorts of patients across that 2-year timeframe and what you're looking to see in each of those? And then I have a follow-up.

Samuel Reich: Sure. So it's a sister study to the SAFEGUARD study. The protocol is exactly the same with one exception, which is the time from diagnosis. One cohort is age-matched from the SAFEGUARD population that's effectively the control, and that's patients within 100 days of diagnosis. One cohort is from 100 days to 365 days, which is that window out to a year. And what we call Cohort 3, or the third cohort, is from 1 year to 2 years. And the importance of that and that data is to prove that the thing that matters most with a patient is the amount of beta cells they have and our ability to preserve those.

And the T1D community and SAB want as many patients as possible to be able to get access to SAB-142. And the PRISE study is designed to show that we can provide a benefit to patients up to 2 years from diagnosis.

Tejas Wein: Great. And then just a quick follow-up on timing. When could we expect to get data from any of these cohorts, and how could that be used to support a label expansion or inform a registrational trial in those various populations?

Samuel Reich: Well, so on the timing, I don't know that we're guiding to a specific time yet as it's an investigator-led study. I think we would expect it to be subsequent to SAFEGUARD data, but we'll see and we'll keep you posted on that. As far as the label, pending good outcome we would hope to and have the potential to have time not be a basis for diagnosis and just beta cells. So if a patient with type 1 diabetes has adequate beta cells for preservation, there's a possibility that might be all that's required for being able to get treated and covered.

And maybe if you step it back to just one step more conservative, perhaps it's up to 2 years from diagnosis, which will markedly expand the available total addressable market as well as have the ability to increase market penetration by not having this kind of a gun to the head of a patient with, you have to get it now or you're not going to be able to get it.

Operator: The next question is from Roger Song from Jefferies.

Cha Cha Yang: This is Cha on for Roger. I was hoping that you could give us more color in regards to the September DMC approval. Can you share more on what safety parameters were particularly important in supporting the expansion to the pediatric population?

Samuel Reich: Sure. I'll let Alexandra answer that.

Alexandra Kropotova: Thanks, Sam. So we have the independent Data Monitoring Committee that has been a part of the SAB-142 development program for over the last 2 years. The DMC consists of the 1 adult endocrinologist and 2 pediatric endocrinologists along with the independent biostatistician. For pre-scheduled, predefined DMC meetings, cumulative data for the SAB-142, which means that all data that were accumulated from the beginning, the very first patient enrolled in a trial, all the way until the DMC scheduled meeting were provided, the data were provided to the DMC in an unblinded fashion. It means that the DMC committee saw the data by treatment arm versus control.

And it's all available safety data across populations, broken also down by the age groups, adult versus adolescent and versus pediatric population. We had the DMC meetings that approved the step-down as planned without any delays, indicating that the product behaves very consistently and there is no new safety signal identified in the ongoing SAFEGUARD trial. So we're very, very pleased with how the product behaves. And it's again a very, very consistent safety profile across all age groups.

Operator: The next question is from Yatin Suneja from Guggenheim Securities.

Hanxing Gao: This is Iris Gao on for Yatin. Congratulations on the progress with both studies. So my first question would be like, is there an update on how many patients have been redosed so far, and is the drug still clean on ADAs? And my second question would be about like, how does the PRISE study affect the burn rate going forward?

Samuel Reich: We haven't disclosed to date how many patients have been redosed, but it's going according to plan. And then the second part was -- I'm sorry, could you repeat it? I didn't hear it.

Hanxing Gao: Oh, yes. It's how do you expect the PRISE study to affect the burn rate going forward?

Samuel Reich: We had included that study in our budgeting process. So the burn as guided has accounted for the PRISE expenses and doesn't change.

Operator: The next question is from Thomas Smith from Leerink Partners.

Brian Conley: This is Brian on for Tom. Congrats on all the progress. So first, given adult and adolescent cohorts here are fully enrolled in SAFEGUARD, can you comment on if there's anything notable on the baseline characteristics of the patients in these cohorts relative to your expectations? And then we have a quick follow-up.

Samuel Reich: I'll let Alexandra answer that.

Alexandra Kropotova: Our baseline characteristics for both cohorts are comparable to the baseline characteristics of the respective age cohorts in previous trials, TN-19 and MELD-ATG. So the data is very consistent, again, even at the baseline.

Brian Conley: Got it. And our second question, just on the PRISE trial understanding that in SAFEGUARD we needed to have that step-down from adults to pediatric patients, can we expect a similar dynamic in PRISE given at least some of the overlap in patient population? Or can you begin enrolling those pediatric patients once the study begins recruitment given the safety data you've generated to date?

Alexandra Kropotova: Yes, excellent question. And yes, we are starting enrollment in the PRISE-hATG study with the early age cohorts considering that we already have a very significant amount of the safety data accumulated through SAFEGUARD, and the DMC, independent DMC committee across the program. So it's the same DMC who already has seen all the data from the SAB-142 in previous trials who will be guiding and monitoring the safety in PRISE.

Operator: The next question is from Samantha Semenkow from Citi.

Unknown Analyst: This is Ben on for Sam. Can you describe the level of physician interest in the PRISE study? What kind of feedback are you receiving based on the site interactions? And then I have a separate question, if I may.

Samuel Reich: Yes, physician interest is very high. I think that we mentioned that Dr. Haller at University of Florida, Dr. Mathieu in Belgium and Dr. Tim Tree at King's College proposed this study design because of the tremendous interest. If you can imagine that both all the clinical research done with immunomodulation as well as now the first approved therapy, Tzield, limits a patient's ability to get dosed to the first up to 8 weeks, SAFEGUARD has been the most inclusive, up to 100 days so far. There's a huge pent-up demand and frustration both at the physician level and the patient level of people who are being excluded from the ability to get therapy or participate in clinical research.

So interest is high, demand is high, and it really is inbound interest from the T1D community and the academic community to SAB that we're gladly collaborating with and accommodating.

Unknown Analyst: And then turning back to SAFEGUARD, what is the pace of the pediatric screening and enrollment? Is it tracking with your expectations?

Samuel Reich: Yes, it's good. We're pleased by how it's going. And we're reiterating that we expect to complete enrollment this quarter.

Operator: The next question is from Keay Nakae from Chardan.

Kaey Nakae: With respect to PRISE Cohort C patients, how do you -- it's not clear to me from the inclusion/exclusion, how do you best handicap which patients at that duration of onset might be best suited to show a positive result?

Samuel Reich: I think it's all about C-peptide at baseline. It's the same study design as SAFEGUARD. The only difference is that time from diagnosis. So the amount of C-peptide which meeting the inclusion criteria for baseline C-peptide is that. And Alexandra, do you have anything to add?

Alexandra Kropotova: And then the additional parameter is the age groups. Similar to SAFEGUARD, we have predefined parameters for the sample size across the adult, adolescent and pediatric population in approximately similar 1/3 of each population fashion, since the disease progression may be dependent on the age as well. So baseline C-peptide and age are 2 parameters that participate in the stratification randomization at the baseline of the PRISE-hATG participants.

Operator: The next question is from Seema Sheoran from Rodman Financial.

Seema Sheoran: Congrats on the progress. So in April you presented impressive 4-patient data where 3 patients were described as super-responders, showing C-peptide levels above baseline at 120 days, or 4 months. My understanding is that this cohort is not receiving additional doses whereas SAFEGUARD includes redosing. I'm just curious to know how C-peptide levels have evolved with longer follow-up in these 4 patients and what that suggests about the durability of response without redosing.

Samuel Reich: So the data we presented from the Phase 1 study was the complete dataset. The study was 120 days long. That was the last study visit. And so we have not collected data beyond that.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session as well as today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.

#3187. AI Voice Agents Are Easy To Demo; Production Is Where The Engineering Begins

Alexandro Picolini is a technology executive and software architect focused on telecom, cloud and AI.

Voice AI demos have become surprisingly easy to build. With a real-time model, a microphone and a good prompt, a team can create something impressive quickly. But a demo is usually a controlled environment: clean audio, a stable network, cooperative users and readily available data.

A real telephone operation is very different.

I am a CTO and software architect with more than 25 years of experience in telecommunications and software development. My company develops contact-center platforms that connect telephony, digital channels and customer management. Our work integrating voice AI into these environments has shown me how much production depends on systems beyond the model.

One of the first problems we faced was telephone audio quality. As a call passes between carriers, its audio may be compressed and converted along the way. Receiving it in a higher-quality format at the final connection does not restore detail already lost. A person may still understand the conversation while a speech-recognition system struggles.

Speakerphone calls add background conversations, television and traffic. Voice activity detection—the technology that detects when someone is speaking—does not always distinguish the caller from surrounding voices.

It’s important to test through the actual telephone routes customers use, not only a headset connected to a computer. Teams should include mobile phones, speakerphones and noisy environments. They should listen to the audio reaching the agent, not just the voice it generates.

Human conversations include brief acknowledgments: “Uh-huh.” “Okay.” “Right.” These do not always mean someone wants to take over the conversation. If interruption detection is too aggressive, a simple “okay” stops the agent mid-explanation. If it is too conservative, customers must speak over the agent before it stops.

In some of our implementations, around two seconds has been a workable compromise. It is not a universal setting: Turn detection requires more than detecting sound.

It’s critical to test acknowledgments separately from deliberate interruptions. The goal is not to eliminate every overlap but to let customers interrupt when they need to without making ordinary listening behavior break the conversation.

An API taking three or four seconds during a WhatsApp exchange may barely register. On a phone call, those same seconds feel long.

You can ask customers to wait or provide subtle audio feedback. We have experimented with sounds that simulate typing while information is retrieved. That may work once; repeated pauses quickly become frustrating.

Whenever possible, information the agent is likely to need should be available through a fast data layer. In some implementations, we use Redis to cache customer information and reduce slow backend requests.

Teams should identify which lookups must happen during the call and which can happen beforehand. They should set a waiting limit for each dependency and decide what happens if it fails. A reassuring phrase is not a substitute for a responsive integration.

When someone shows me a voice AI demo and says it is production-ready, I ask: “How do you dynamically deliver the contact’s data to the bot?” The system may already know the campaign, customer account, recent interactions or reason for calling. Making the customer repeat everything wastes that context. Retrieving each detail only when requested adds delays.

Start by defining the minimum information needed for each use case. Pass it into the conversation through a consistent structure rather than loading an entire customer record. Separate background information from data that must be refreshed before an action, such as confirming an appointment.

Define what the agent should do when a record is missing, outdated or inconsistent. Restrict information to what the task requires, and verify identity before disclosing sensitive account details. A recognized phone number should not, by itself, authorize disclosure. Test those failure cases as deliberately as the ideal scenario.

Human transfer is not merely a rescue mechanism for a failed AI. Customers may request a person, a situation may exceed the agent’s scope or an action may require human authorization.

Define these transfer triggers with the operations team before launch. Specify the destination queue, its operating hours and an alternative when nobody is available. Test busy queues, unavailable agents and failed transfers—not just a successful connection. The transfer should carry a concise summary: why the customer called, what has been verified, actions already attempted and what remains unresolved. Make that information available where the human agent actually works.

Do not tell the caller that a transfer succeeded merely because the system requested it. Confirm the outcome, explain any delay and offer the agreed alternative when necessary. The customer should not lose the conversation’s progress at the moment human help becomes necessary.

Many problems do not appear with one or 10 simultaneous calls. At thousands of concurrent calls, we have seen delays in audio delivery over SIP that were almost invisible at small scale. It’s important to test the complete path under realistic concurrency, including external APIs and human transfers. Measure the time callers wait to hear a response, not only the time a model takes to generate one. Include slow dependencies and provider interruptions in those tests.

A polished demo may prove that the model is capable. It does not prove that every connected system will remain responsive under load. A good demo proves the AI can talk. Production proves whether the whole system actually works.​

TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates fell today, possibly helped by post-midterm election clarity and a drop in oil prices.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.01% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is six basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.

In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

#3184. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3182. Delek US Holdings (DK) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management outlines a balance sheet shift and a raised logistics outlook heading into year-end.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Delek US Holdings, Inc. (DK +2.34%) reported record third quarter net income driven by operational reliability and the successful monetization of regulatory exemptions. Management emphasized a financial transformation underpinned by the Enterprise Optimization Plan and a disciplined capital allocation strategy that includes significant share repurchases and an 18% dividend increase. The company transitioned its stand-alone balance sheet to a net cash position while advancing a sum of the parts strategy aimed at the eventual deconsolidation of Delek Logistics.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Delek US Holdings Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Robert Wright, EVP and CFO. Robert, please go ahead.

Robert Wright: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us today. Participants joining me on today's call will include Avigal Soreq, President and CEO; Mohit Bhardwaj, EVP, Strategy and Investor Relations; as well as other members of our management team. Today's earnings release and management call presentation material can be found on the Investor Relations section of the Delek U.S. website. Before we get started, I want to remind everyone that our comments today may include forward-looking statements, reflecting management's current expectations and assumptions. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from those discussed today.

For additional information regarding the factors that could cause actual results to differ, please refer to our filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by applicable law, we do not undertake any obligation to update these forward-looking statements. I will now turn the call over to Avigal for opening remarks. Avigal?

Avigal Soreq: Thank you, Robert. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today. Third quarter was a landmark quarter for us. Given our performance, we finished the quarter in a strong financial position. We are taking incremental steps in Q4 to advance our financial transformation. Our transformation has been made possible by our strong operation and our surgical execution to capture the market opportunities. Our operations play an essential role in the communities we serve by providing reliable fuel supply that support everyday needs and economic activities. We take great pride in being committed community partner.

Highlights in the third quarter includes: one, we continue to successfully navigate the volatility in the crude and product markets caused by the events in Middle East and Eastern Europe. Second, we made further progress in increasing our free cash flow profile and have increased our EOP improvement guidance to at least $250 million. And third, we have also maintained our disciplined and balanced approach to capital allocation through balance sheet improvement, dividend increase and strong buybacks. As I've mentioned in the past, maintaining discipline is critically important during periods of strong margins. We maintain prudent approach reflected in our disciplined capital deployment, focused on creating sustainable long-term shareholder value.

As I mentioned during our last earnings call, the events in the Middle East and Eastern Europe have created many ripple effects in the markets. We continue to see elevated freight rates that impact crack spread and crude differentials. In the current environment, we believe that we have a key advantage through access to pipeline delivered inland crude, limited exposure to elevated freight cost, high distillate yield and most importantly, the ability to respond quickly to changes in the market conditions. This advantage are critical to maintaining operational flexibility and delivering strong performance. Now I will cover some of our third quarter highlights and strategic initiatives in detail. Starting with refining.

Our refining system operated reliably with all 4 refineries running well. Big Spring has shown strong operating performance since its turnaround. It's exceeding its value creation target of improved reliability, higher crude flexibility, improvement in overall product yield and higher octane and blending capabilities. I'm very pleased with this improvement, and I'm confident that the Big Spring team will further improve this important asset. With no planned turnaround for the remainder of the year, our refining system is well positioned to capture the continued strength in crack spread. Moving to EOP, enterprise optimization plan continue to drive significant value. We are again increasing our EOP target to at least $250 million on an annual run rate basis.

During the third quarter of 2026, we estimate approximately $60 million of EOP contribution to our P&L. We have come a long way from our initial target of $100 million of annual free cash flow improvement. And I'm proud of the continuous improvement culture that we have created. Our sum of the parts initiative also continued to progress with raising strength of our midstream business. DKL today raised its 2026 EBITDA guidance to $530 million to $560 million. DKL is also on target to add an additional $60 million in EBITDA in 2027 from its organic growth projects on a run rate basis. This is in addition to the $15 million that we have realized in 2026.

DKL has completed the construction of the first sour compressor station and AGI well and is in the process of commissioning the facility. The sour gas solution will provide DKL the ability to fully capitalize on its growth opportunity in the Delaware Basin and maintain its best-in-class EBITDA growth and yield. On a pro forma basis, we continue to expect DKL third-party annual adjusted EBITDA to exceed 80%. This level of economic separation is a cornerstone of our sum of the parts strategy and continues to bring us closer to our deconsolidation goal. DKL is on the right path, and we continue to work hard to write the next chapter in its growth story.

As I mentioned last quarter, we are pursuing a proactive strategy to manage our obligation under the RFS. The SRE provision of the RFS serves the important purpose of mitigating the impact felt on small refineries from the RFS burden. We have felt this burden in the past and are pleased to have received all 4 small refinery exemptions for 2025 period. This will allow us to reduce our 2025 RVO burden and expect to receive approximately $425 million in proceeds in the fourth quarter. We expect the EPA to continue to provide a relief to small refineries for the year 2026 and beyond.

We believe the current administration, Senate, Congress and EPA realize the importance of SREs, not only for the refineries which qualify under the program, but also to the local communities they serve. The final piece of our strategy is being shareholder-friendly and having a strong balance sheet. During the quarter, we paid approximately $16 million in dividend and $50 million in buyback. Our strong balance sheet, improved reliability, EOP and confident in our outlook continue to support disciplined approach to capital allocation to continuing dividend and buyback. We remain committed to balanced and disciplined capital allocation strategy and are dedicated to rewarding our shareholders. In this regard, we have increased our quarterly dividend by approximately 18% to $0.30 per share.

And after buying back $50 million worth of our shares in Q3, we expect to do approximately $100 million in shares buyback between now and the end of the year. In closing, thank you to our team for the hard work and dedication. I'm immensely proud of the progress Delek has made, and I look forward to building on this momentum for the remainder of the year and beyond. Now I will turn the call over to Robert, who will provide additional color on the quarter.

Robert Wright: Thank you, Avigal. For the third quarter, Delek reported net income of approximately $1.13 billion or $18.22 per share with EBITDA of approximately $1.64 billion. On an adjusted basis, net income came in at approximately $843 million or $13.55 per share, with adjusted EBITDA of approximately $1.28 billion. Turning to our investor presentation. On Slide 4, we show the breakdown of adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS for the quarter. Excluding the 50% RVO adjustment and the impact of small refinery exemptions or SREs, granted during the quarter, adjusted EBITDA was approximately $1.04 billion and adjusted EPS was approximately $10.53 per share.

On Slide 5, we walk through the bridge in adjusted EBITDA from the second quarter to the third quarter on the same basis, excluding the 50% RVO adjustment and the impacts of SREs. Quarter-over-quarter performance was led by stronger refining margins and higher capture rates. Supply and Marketing margin was approximately $37 million in the quarter, with wholesale marketing contributing $36.7 million, driven by continued success of our EOP efforts and strong market environment. Asphalt was a loss of $4.6 million, fully offset by a $4.6 million profit from our supply business.

Our Logistics segment continues to deliver strong results, posting approximately $143 million in adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter as momentum continued across our crude, gas and water offerings. Let's move to Slide 6 for a review of cash flow. Cash flow from operations was $567 million for the quarter. This reflects net income adjusted for noncash items, offset by a net working capital outflow of approximately $809 million. Excluding working capital, operating cash flow for the quarter was approximately $1.38 billion. As to the working capital outflow, the majority of this was related to SRE receivables of approximately $425 million, and we expect these proceeds to come in the fourth quarter.

The remainder of the impact is split between timing-related items of roughly $200 million, which we expect to normalize in the coming quarters and roughly $160 million, which is tied to other financing-related items. Investing activities were a use of $117 million for the quarter. This includes capital expenditures of approximately $111 million with $55 million associated with DKL. Of that $55 million, $48 million of that went to growth projects at DKL and the remainder supported scheduled maintenance and regulatory spending across our system, ensuring our ability to run safely and reliably in the current macro environment. Financing activities provided approximately $256 million of net cash during the quarter.

Inflows were approximately $415 million of net proceeds from our 0 coupon convertible notes offering and approximately $220 million of net proceeds from the DKL equity offering. These were partially offset by $247 million of DKL revolver payments, $50 million of share repurchases, $16 million in dividend payments and approximately $22 million in DKL distribution payments to public unitholders. In addition, as Avigal mentioned, we are pleased to announce we're increasing our dividend to $0.30 per share and are expecting to spend approximately $100 million on buybacks in the fourth quarter. Slide 18 breaks out our net debt position between Delek and Delek Logistics.

On a stand-alone basis, excluding Delek Logistics, Delek's net debt has improved $224 million versus the second quarter and has moved to a net cash position of approximately $22 million. Now turning to Slide 19 and our outlook for the fourth quarter. Our total throughput guidance is as follows: Tyler, 75,000 to 80,000 barrels per day; El Dorado, 67,000 to 72,000 barrels per day; Big Spring, 68,000 to 73,000 barrels per day; and Krotz Springs, 78,000 to 83,000 barrels per day. Taken together, this implies a total system throughput target of 288,000 to 308,000 barrels per day for the fourth quarter.

In addition to the throughput guidance for the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect operating expenses to be between $225 million and $235 million; G&A between $50 million and $55 million and D&A to be between $115 million and $125 million. As committed last quarter, we are also breaking out our interest expense between Delek and Delek Logistics. We expect total net interest expense between $52 million and $67 million, with DK contributing between $12 million and $17 million and DKL contributing between $40 million and $50 million. As shown on Slide 8, on a run rate basis post the term loan payout, we expect interest expense on a DK stand-alone basis to be around $10 million.

With that, we will now open the call for questions.

When we just look at that improvement, can you walk us through how much you would attribute to structural changes you've made in the system? And then how much has that been a function of some of the macro backdrop?

Avigal Soreq: Yes. So I'm so happy that you asked that question. That's a very important aspect in our structural change that we did in the company. And I would say the first reasoning for that is obviously EOP, enterprise optimization plan. And you have seen that Alexa, that our EOP is a lifestyle. It's someone that everyone in this company is taking pride of. It's someone that everyone in this company wants to be -- to excel. And there is no limit to our imagination around that and how far we can take it. We are very happy about the progress we have done. We have more than 90 projects we are running around that.

We are working on that on a daily, weekly basis. And I'm very proud. There is a small project, a big project and everyone is taking part of that. I think we raised the EOP target of a free cash flow basis mid-cycle like 6x -- 7x, sorry. And now it's at least $250 million. That's an extraordinary achievement. And I'm proud -- it's not me, it's the organization that I'm proud of and every one of our employees that take part that's important initiative.

I just want to say to take the opportunity to say thank you for all of you because Sean and our operation together with OP is a very key foundation of this company and something that we really -- our employees are leading, and we're really excelling in. So that's the essence of it.

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes. And Alexa, that's the structural change is why we have so much confidence in our mid-cycle free cash flow, and that's why we want to talk about that.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Matthew Blair with TPH Research. Matthew, your line is open. Please go ahead.

Matthew Blair: Avigal and Robert, congrats on the strong results. Maybe that's a good place to start. Your marketing and supply profitability took a big step up overall in the third quarter, very strong on an absolute basis. Could you talk about the moving parts in the third quarter that pushed that up? And what are you seeing so far in the fourth quarter?

Avigal Soreq: Yes. We -- Matt, first of all, thank you for joining the call. We really appreciate you. We usually don't give guidance on DKTS because there is a lot of market dynamics into that. But I will give you something. Some of the structural change that we have seen through are going into DKTS. That's the reason that over time, when you canceling the noise, you see an elevated number over there. Ismael and his team are leading a very good tight organization, very focused, very value chain optimization throughout the value chain, and I'm very proud of the progress they are doing. And they are not standing still.

Every day, I hear more ideas, more projects, more excitement around that. So while I'm not going to give you what you want in terms of guidance for DKTS, I'm telling you that I'm very happy and we see a structural progress around it.

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes. Matthew, as Avigal just mentioned, and I think Robert had it in his script that we had supply and marketing contributed around $37 million for the quarter. A lot of the contribution, as Robert mentioned, came from wholesale. Wholesale is where our focus has been, as we have said in previous calls. And we are very excited about the progress that we are making in that segment. There is some still market volatility in the segment. That's why we don't really provide any guidance. But we are very happy with the way the things are proceeding as far as supply and marketing and what we call our DKTS line item is.

Matthew Blair: Sounds good. And then in the third quarter, you recorded an SRE benefit of it looks like $335 million when RINs were above $2 a gallon. Slide 17 implies that full SREs should be worth about $760 million to Delek at $1.50 RIN prices. So at $2, let's just around that to $1 billion or so. So I guess, could you just help us understand why the SRE benefit wasn't larger in the third quarter? And ultimately, would you agree that, that $2 a gallon, the economic benefit to full SREs should be worth around $1 billion or so?

Avigal Soreq: Yes, absolutely. So Robert will give you the highlights of the accounting reconciliation of the SREs. But I'm very happy about the progress we have done around that. That's a good opportunity to thank Misty for the strong relationship we have in DC across DC and how important it is and how important that everyone understands that we, as a nation, we are lacking refineries.

And the first objective here is to make sure that we are maintaining the one we have, especially in the rural area that the fuel supply is so important, especially around the area that we are working in other 40 refineries in the nation, and that's something that it's in the essence of the law, and we are committed to keep working towards and to make sure that we have good jobs to our employees and supplying those communities. Robert, why don't you take it from here?

Robert Wright: Yes, sure. Thanks, Avigal. Yes, I think, Matt, if you look at it based on current RIN prices and the small refinery exemptions that we were granted, we will recognize a total accounting benefit of around $750 million to $800 million, and this is really tied to 3 main things. First, as outlined in this morning's release, and as you know, we recognized a realized gain from SREs of $335 million. Second, within the release, we also disclosed that we recognized an unrealized gain of approximately $274 million which represents the mark-to-market valuation increase of those RINs since 2025.

And then beyond those 2 disclosed items, we expect another $150 million to $200 million to come in through the next several quarters as we apply the excess RINs against future compliance obligations. So all in, it's a $750 million to $800 million mark at current prices.

Operator: Your next question comes from Manav Gupta with UBS. Manav, your line is open. Please go ahead.

Manav Gupta: Guys, hopefully, you won't mind. I wanted to pick your brain a little bit more on the diesel market. You have a higher leverage to diesel than many of your peers. I just wanted to understand, based on your crystal ball, what's your outlook for the diesel margins for the next 6 to 12 months?

Avigal Soreq: Yes. Thank you for that question, Manav. Your questions are always great. We -- big picture, you see that we have 3 events in the world that we are seeing, the Middle East one, the Eastern Europe and obviously, China. The China event is because you saw VLCC from the Gulf Coast to China is around $24, $25 today, maybe this morning, $24 for VL, which is like 5x more expensive versus what it used to be a year ago. So all in, we have like 5 million to 7 million barrels outside the market with tanker prices. Some of the changes that we have seen are going to be more structural.

We have seen even on the lead time of new VLCCs and it looks like 3 to 4 years, and there is a lot of booking of new VLCC in 2029, et cetera. So we might see some lingering effect on that very important of transportation cost because of everything we see, mainly the ship to ship. Bottom line on the diesel, you have seen the inventories are low in the U.S. It's probably across the globe. And it's something that's going to take a second to fix. We've seen the economy so far, the Main Street is doing pretty well. You see the job number this morning and the GDP is growing.

So that's -- all of that requires diesel and a lot of diesel. We are up to the winter. So that's another tailwind for diesel prices. It's more to come, but I don't see other than those 3 events that I don't have a crystal ball, something material change in the outlook of diesel.

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes, Manav, I'll add a few more things to this. So obviously, as you rightly pointed out, we have one of the highest jet and distillate yield across the peers. So it's something very important for us. And equally important for us to make sure that the communities that we serve like in Arkansas, the airports that we serve from a jet fuel standpoint and from a diesel standpoint, they are satisfied as well. As far as the cracks are concerned, as Avigal talked about, the freight rates are going to put a floor on overall crack, including the distillate crack, which is holding the entire crack together.

And the second point to understand is to meet the European grade diesel, you also have to blend some jet fuel from -- in the exports that happen out of the U.S. is going to create some shortening for jet fuel as well. And as a result, people like us, we have to make sure that our total liquid volume yield is sufficient so that we can supply locally as well as globally. So overall, we still are extremely positive about the outlook for distillate and jet cracks.

Manav Gupta: Perfect. My quick follow-up here is, as you now point out like your capture rates, and thank you for that. The 3 of the 4 refineries are mid-60 to approaching 70% and probably there's further scope of improvement. El Dorado is somewhere still in the low 50s. And I'm trying to understand what are the next steps to get this first towards mid-50s and then hopefully towards 60% or so, if you could talk a little bit about that.

Avigal Soreq: Yes, absolutely. So we have disclosed in the past that we have improved El Dorado $2 last year. And as part of EOP, you remember, we spoke about a few times that El Dorado is the jet and other initiatives that improved that by around $2. You have seen those numbers in El Dorado improving. I think there is even a slide that Mohit provided that showed the capture rate is going up. And down the road, we see additional improvement in El Dorado. In many areas, we are obviously going to disclose it in the future.

But the DKTS, the supply and marketing are working extremely hard to make sure that every barrel land and every gallon lands where it need to land with the right quality. and with the right tight operations that we have seen. El Dorado, as you can see very easily has improved the capture rate significantly, and we see another outlook to improve it even more by $1 or even more down the road. So stay tuned. You will see and hear more about it.

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes, Manav, just to add to what Avigal said, $30 million is what we have highlighted today and dollar per barrel improvement, just like Avigal said, a very strong team at El Dorado, and I think we are very excited to capture this improvement as well. Manav, are you? You sound a little...

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jason Gabelman with TD Cowen. Jason, your line is open. Please go ahead.

Jason Gabelman: I wanted to go back to the small refinery exemptions, if I could, and I appreciate the disclosure on the $425 million that you're going to monetize in 4Q, but it's still not really clear what the current RIN length is that you have. And I think there's a fear that maybe you're selling these RINs now, but are still going to have a short that you're hoping will be covered by future SREs. And your peers have been very straightforward that they are current on their RINs.

I think it would be helpful to the market and clear a lot of confusion up if you could kind of provide some color as to what your actual RIN length is after you've received these SREs.

Avigal Soreq: Yes, absolutely. So Jason, just to make it very clear, our strategy all along is stay in compliance. We stay in compliance all along, and that's going to be the strategy going forward. Obviously, we are managing -- proactively managing the position. We are happy about the way we manage the position. We have a clear view about the RIN market, and I will let Mohit finish the answer.

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes. Thanks, Avigal. So Jason, thank you for the question, and you and I have talked about this at length multiple times. So if you look at from a cash proceeds standpoint, first, let's just clear that part out. So $50 million or so were included in the third quarter and $425 million will be coming in the fourth quarter. Now based upon all of our SRE grants, what we have to do is to manage a few things. The first is the cash need for the business. So we just talked about -- you've actually not talked about on the call, but we highlighted that we will be taking out our term loan.

So part of the proceeds will go for that. Then we also have to manage our overall compliance. So part of the RINs will be used for that. And then we also have to think about how the company is doing from a flat price risk standpoint for the RINs and also the overall tax situations. Based upon that, we decide what RINs to monetize and how many of them we need to keep for compliance. And that is going to be our strategy, as Avigal focused on, that we always want to stay in compliance, and that is also going to be our strategy on a go-forward basis.

Jason Gabelman: Okay. So if I'm hearing you correctly, you're compliant but not necessarily current and then also the $425 million is going to be after taxes?

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes. I think, Jason, we can take that offline. But for us, as we have highlighted multiple times that we don't disclose our RIN buying strategy, but we also want to make sure that we always stay in compliance with our obligations. So that is our strategy, and that will continue on a go-forward basis.

Jason Gabelman: Okay. I'll leave that there. My follow-up is just there was some reporting out there that Delek was receiving Defense Production Act proceeds to expand refining capacity. So just wondering if you could touch on that point at all if you're receiving those proceeds and if you're pursuing projects to expand your capacity?

Avigal Soreq: Yes, absolutely. So we are still talking to the administration. But to make it very, very clear, Tyler is going to stay at 75,000 barrels a day of crude. There is no material CapEx that we need to disclose, and we are talking about shifting between different kind of products, and that's it. There is not much more to it. We're obviously very thankful for the administration for helping rural refineries in the U.S. We are obviously very thankful for the administration of understanding that small jobs in those areas are extremely important and the affordability is extremely important. But from a materiality standpoint, it doesn't meet our threshold at all.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Joseph Laetsch with Morgan Stanley. Joe, your line is open. Please go ahead.

Joseph Laetsch: I wanted to go back to the refining macro a bit. So you talked about the diesel cracks, but could you also just give us an update on the latest dynamics that you're seeing in Group 3 from both a demand perspective, margin, crude cost standpoint as well?

Avigal Soreq: Yes. So Group 3, as we look at it yesterday, working to our expectation. It's actually doing slightly better versus typical November. The high crack spread is obviously part of that equation, and we see that as a positive for us. So that's also going well to where we are. So that's on the tactical side. On the more strategic side, we obviously see the Western Gateway project coming down the road, which will support tremendously Group 3. So that's very helpful for our position. We see that line as very good news for Delek because it's going to clear most of the group, and we are not going to pay for the movement of those barrels.

So it's 2 wins for us. So on the tactical side, the group is working well at these 10 seconds. And on the strategic side, we've seen more and more barrels from the group going west to compensate closure of refineries in the West Coast. So both tactically and strategically, we're in a good spot.

Mohit Bhardwaj: Yes. And just to add, Joe, we also have the Magellan pipeline taking additional barrels into Denver. And we have seen some of those wells start to move, and there's scope for that pipeline to expand as well. And we have seen group clearing out very well. And as Avigal mentioned, we are pleasantly surprised by the lack of seasonality that we have seen in the past.

Joseph Laetsch: Great. That's helpful. And then I just wanted to go back to the balance sheet, if I could. So from a capital structure standpoint, after the term loan is paid off, the only debt left, I think, will be the converts. How do you think about the optimal capital structure for Delek? Is it a net cash position? And then you also mentioned no desire to hold excess cash on the balance sheet. Could you just remind us what the right level of cash balance is for the company to hold?

Avigal Soreq: Yes, absolutely. So let's start with the bottom line, right? The $10 million DKL interest rate in an increasing interest rate environment is an extraordinary achievement. and we are very happy about where we are. And as we said all along, our strategy is to reward investors by increasing buyback that we did today from $50 million to $100 million on Q4 and by doing dividend through the cycle that we are very confident on that, right? What got us here is a few things, one of them and the most important on the structural thing is the enterprise optimization plan that we are very proud, and you can see the capture rate improving. So that's where we are.

As we said, we didn't give a clear cash number on that we're going to hold on the balance sheet, but we have no desire to hold any excess cash, and we want to make sure that we are the cheapest. We've seen a few transactions lately in our space. And our best acquisition is ourselves because we are the cheapest refinery in the U.S., and that's what we did this quarter. And we maintain very disciplined to our capital allocation strategy, and I will leave it to that.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of John Royall with Piper Sandler. John, your line is open. Please go ahead.

John Royall: So my first question is on the sum of the parts unlock. You're currently at 58%, I think, DKL ownership. That's been coming down pretty steadily. Can you talk about your path to hitting below 50% at this point? Do you have a time frame in mind for when you may get there?

Avigal Soreq: Yes. First of all, I'm surprised that, that question hit the conference so late. So thank you for bringing it up. I'm really proud of what we did this quarter. I'm very proud of the primary that Robert and Mohit led, very nice, and I'm very happy about that. But let's take a step back and look at the progress we have done, right? We've done 2 very good acquisitions on the right timing before water became in the spotlight. We have done another -- we built another gas plant.

We said -- I said today on the call, and I'm saying that again that we might need to expand the capacity that we have in Libby even more to serve our producers and our customers. And we actually developed a very clear, clean strategy of providing crude, gas and water in the most prolific area of the Permian Basin, and that strategy is working very well for us. You can see if you are looking on each one of our assets and you are extremely smart and do the math, and you can see that our intrinsic value, John, is the number, it needs to have 9 handle on the DKL unit. We are not there just yet.

But with one of the best units in the space in terms of return and growth, I think it's actually the best one, but let's call it one of the best one. We are very happy about our company. We are very happy about the trajectory. Mark and his leadership team in DKL are doing a very good job, and we made it bigger. And it's going to be one way. One, for the right value, it's always -- we are always open to sell it. For the right value, we are open to sell assets like we have done in the past, we did a bolt-on acquisition that was very good for us.

And we did also tax-efficient buyback between DK and DKL. As you can see, we steadily smartly, not -- we didn't rush reduce our interest from 79% to 58% and stay tuned, more to come.

John Royall: Great. And then my follow-up is just on turnarounds. I know you're done with your '26 program at this point. I'm not sure if you're going to answer this, but do you have any early view on what '27 could look like from a turnaround perspective?

Avigal Soreq: Yes. So we are still putting our ducks in a row for '27. Usually, our cycle is to give guidance about it in the next earnings call, and we'll stick to our cadence.

Operator: We have reached the end of our Q&A session. I will now turn the call back to Avigal Soreq, CEO, for closing remarks.

Avigal Soreq: Thank you. Thank you for my colleagues around this table and the management team. I want to thank our Board of Directors in trusting us and mostly and to our employees that make this company as good as we all can. Thank you for our investors to sticking to our story and believing in us, and we'll talk again next quarter. Thank you.

#3181. What Does a ‘Blue Wave’ Mean for Mortgage Rates?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.
