#3179. Identity Governance And The Challenge Of AI Agents Moving At Machine Speed

Praerit Garg, CEO, One Identity, trusted leader in identity security, helping enterprises protect and simplify access to digital identities.

​An employee might spend an afternoon retrieving customer records or checking account details. Meanwhile, an AI agent might tick off those tasks within seconds, then repeat them thousands of times without pausing. We’ve reached a golden age of automation, where AI can do more than just automate—it can make decisions and act upon them at speeds that even a whole team of humans could fail to match.

But there’s a catch. While every individual action performed by an AI agent may fall within defined permissions and parameters, all it takes is one excessive entitlement or poorly designed approval process for an AI to cause significant damage. And because AI makes automation much simpler to achieve, allowing employees to turn existing permissions into powerful automated workflows with a single prompt, it’s becoming much harder to govern. With McKinsey reporting that up to 40% of organizations are already scaling an agentic AI system in at least one business function, this is quickly becoming one of the year’s defining security issues.​

Much of the industry’s response has focused on building entirely new identity and governance architectures specifically for AI agents, but they actually already have the right tools at their disposal in the form of identity governance and administration (IGA) and privileged access management (PAM). The same questions that are asked of humans should be asked of machines: Whose authority is the agent exercising? What information can it access? Which actions can it take, and when should additional approval be required? Instead of rebuilding governance architectures from the ground up, businesses simply need to refocus the tools and learnings already at their disposal, particularly zero-trust architectures.​

Microsoft made a significant investment in exploring a more code-centric approach with code access security (CAS) some 25 years ago, but the company later deprecated it and no longer treats CAS as a security boundary because too many paths can allow privileges to be elevated. Microsoft now directs developers toward enforceable operating-system boundaries, including user accounts, which reinforces the idea that creating a specialized control layer doesn’t necessarily provide stronger protection than applying established security boundaries consistently.​

I was recently introduced to an elaborate access governance system designed specifically to stop AI agents from taking actions their users never intended. The organization’s concerns were legitimate, of course, but the solution their team proposed, like Microsoft’s, added so much complexity that they didn’t even consider they may already have the answer.​

An agent acting on someone’s behalf should, at most, only be able to use the permissions granted to that user. If an employee can view a customer record but can’t export an entire database, an agent working for that employee should also have the same limitations applied to it. If the agent can approve a payment or gain access to another business function that the user could not, the first question should be why those permissions were available in the first place.​

The early internet created a similar “trust crisis.” As businesses began distributing software online, users had no easy way to know who had created a program or exactly what it would do once installed. Worms such as Code Red and Nimda showed how quickly malicious code could spread when software was allowed to move and execute across connected systems. That’s when the industry decided that a form of trust infrastructure should be built around digital signatures, certificates and policies, which governed which software was allowed to run.​

Step back into 2026, and the same story is unfolding. Organizations need to establish where an agent and its underlying model came from, authenticate the identity it uses, restrict the systems and data it can reach and require approval before any actions are performed. A trusted model may reduce the risk of deliberately malicious behavior, but identity controls (based on least privileged and zero trust principles) still provide the enforceable boundary when prompts are ambiguous, permissions configurations are flawed or an agent reaches an “unintended” conclusion.​

AI magnifies the consequences of every single entitlement decision. A permission that posed a manageable risk when exercised occasionally by an employee can pose a greater risk when an agent uses it continuously across thousands of tasks. It’s up to humans to assess whether those permissions are still appropriate, what limits should apply and when additional approval is needed. PAM already provides the means to control and audit privileged access according to those decisions, helping organizations put their assessment of business risk into practice.​

Each autonomous service simply needs to have its own identity, a clearly defined supervisor and permissions tied to its specific “role.” In a multi-agent workflow, one agent might retrieve customer data while another updates a business system. Giving both access through the same broad credential would make it difficult to determine which agent performed an action or revoke one agent’s access without disrupting the entire workflow. Existing IGA and PAM capabilities can provide that accountability, provided they’re equipped to govern all identities continuously and revoke access at machine speed.​

AI is new and exciting, but we need to move away from the idea that an agent’s ability to reason about an action gives it the authority to perform it. That decision must remain external to the model and enforceable through the identity infrastructure.​

There’s no escaping the fact that AI agents will become more capable, more autonomous and more deeply embedded in everyday business operations. Every one of those agents must act through an identity, exercise permissions and encounter moments when additional authority is required. As agents become more capable, every organization should be able to explain which permissions were granted, on whose authority and, ultimately, who is accountable for their actions.​

#3178. TOKEN2049: Fundamentals Are Shaping Crypto Investing

Discover why now is the perfect time for Foolish investors to seize opportunities in the digital asset space.

Two days at the biggest crypto conference in the world are exciting. It's also exhausting listening to and meeting with so many of the major builders and thought leaders from both the crypto and the traditional finance world. I took it in for you, and this article is to share some of my major takeaways -- many of which you're less likely to read anywhere else -- but that I think are very encouraging for Foolish crypto investors.

Let me present to you the story of why right now is exactly the right time for Foolish investors to enter the digital asset space. It comes in five chapters, plus a bonus for the truly Foolish investors.

Alliance's Will Robinson shared a few charts based on hundreds, if not thousands, of conversations with crypto founders. They depict what founders have in mind for building applications over time.

Nonfungible tokens (NFTs), for example, had the highest share in November 2021, with 37% of all founders. This dropped quickly and kept dropping to basically zero right now. The decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) had a peak later in December 2021 at 24%, dropping to less than 4% a year later and are at almost zero now. Other themes, such as play-to-earn, show virtually the same curves. One theme that may have just peaked and is already dropping sharply is prediction markets.

This is not surprising. New things cause hypes that then quickly subside. This may never change because it's human nature. We have to consider such cycles in our fundamental investing approach, being careful about when and how we buy into hype.

But something has changed in crypto that makes it easier for fundamental investors to succeed. Real Vision's Jamie Coutts pointed this out very well in his presentation.

The above-mentioned hypes led to massive investments into building and scaling infrastructure. In 2021, for example, $36.5 billion was raised, according to Coutts. This paid off in a sense because we now have massive blockspace available across diverse ecosystems, and it costs very little to use. Even the notoriously slow and expensive Ethereum (ETH +0.48%) blockchain went from a median fee of more than $10 in 2021 to just around $0.04 now.

Most other blockchains are even cheaper. This enables use cases that simply were not possible before. More on that below.

The challenge in the past was that a lot of the investments went into incentives. Read: token issuance. According to Coutts, typical token supply growth was 14% a year about five years ago, leading to an increase in token supply of 78% since January 2021.

What has this meant? Total crypto market capitalization, excluding Bitcoin (BTC +0.25%) and stablecoins, has grown from around $330 billion at the end of January 2021 to nearly $820 billion today. This is a decent 150% growth.

However, if you consider that 78% of this growth has come from new token issuance and not from price increases, you realize that, despite 150% growth in market capitalization, portfolios of passive investors who haven't participated in this new token issuance have increased only 40% over the past five years. Actually, it's even less because this analysis hasn't yet factored in the added market capitalization of completely new projects launched after 2021. This has been devastating for investors.

But this is also where the next good news enters. New token issuance is down by 87%, according to Coutts, so that typical token supply growth is down to 3% per year. These are inflation figures investors are familiar with. Beating a 3% inflation rate is a very different story from beating the previous 14% inflation rate!

If you've followed the digital asset space, you've noticed that suddenly people are talking about protocols that use the revenues they generate to do token buybacks. Hyperliquid (HYPE +1.83%) is the most well-known example of using 97% of its massive revenue to buy back its own token, but there are others.

These projects have started to outperform that market. Hyperliquid, Pump.fun (PUMP +0.69%), and Aerodrome Finance (AERO +3.33%) are currently the top three protocols measured by how much revenue has been used for buybacks over the past 30 days, according to DefiLlama. These tokens' year-to-date returns are 236%, 191%, and 105%, respectively, compared to a total crypto market capitalization that has declined by 6% over the same period.

I believe this shows that the market is starting to pay more attention to cryptos that actually do have solid, proven fundamentals. This hasn't necessarily been the case in the past.

Coutts has found the same. According to his calculations, a basket of cryptos that have passed a basic fundamental filter has returned a negative 35% per year between 2022 and 2025. If you held a basket of the market capitalization-weighted Top 200 cryptos, on the other hand, they would have returned a positive 3% per year over the same time period. In 2026, the same basket of fundamentally filtered cryptos has outperformed the market capitalization-weighted basket by 4 percentage points!

Everybody is talking about AI, and I believe fewer and fewer people doubt that AI agents will play a major role in the future. Most everyone is probably going to have several agents basically performing their work and other tasks.

I think the general public and general investors underestimate one thing that has been a topic of several presentations and discussions. What will be the financial layer all these agents use? Will they all get bank accounts? Or will they get connected to our bank accounts, which we give them permission to use?

I don't think this makes any sense. What makes much more sense is that these agents will have their own wallets with which they transact. Permissionless blockchain is the one technology that makes this possible. Coupled with the tons of now-existing low-cost blockspace available, it's not difficult to see a future where agents are the major users of blockspace in massive quantities.

But there's one more thing that excites me even more than all of the above.

One of the quotes that hit me only later during the conference was Akshay BD saying, "AI for discovery, tokenization for access." He made a great point that tokenization enables access to asset classes for people excluded from investing in them before. This is obvious if you think about it.

What I haven't realized before is what this does in combination with AI.

Not only does tokenization enable a world where you and I and everybody else can invest in hundreds of thousands or maybe millions of different stocks and other assets all over the world. But AI makes it possible for us to actually discover the few specific investing opportunities we may be looking for that otherwise we may not be able to find.

When it really hit me was during a conversation with an African start-up currently looking for investors. Africa is a very diverse continent where market participants are dealing with challenges you and I have long forgotten. According to materials provided by this start-up, inefficient cross-border settlements lock up billions of dollars in capital. There are hundreds of billions of outstanding receivables, with tens of billions of unmet demand and trillions of dollars of loan books that simply cannot trade today. According to the same presentation, Africa makes up 2.7% of world gross domestic product (GDP), but only 0.2% of world equity trading happens there.

These are massive numbers, and, in my opinion, they're a big reason why prosperity is struggling to find its way in Africa.

However, this may change. All the things discussed above, in combination with regulations being put in place in Africa that clearly define the frameworks about how crypto and blockchain technology may be used, for the first time ever make a solution for these challenges absolutely feasible.

The combination of all of this, in my opinion, is a perfect reason for virtually anybody to seriously consider investing in the crypto space -- and maybe for the first time ever.

But what I came away with from TOKEN2049 is even more exciting for truly Foolish investors.

Good fundamentals are a necessary ingredient for a successful investment. But if we want to be comfortable with a Foolish investing approach of buying and, ideally, holding for years, decent revenue and growth today are not enough. There are other special ingredients that differentiate a fundamentally good business from one that lasts. One of these special ingredients I personally value is a good company culture. I heard some encouraging words during presentations and conversations at the conference pertaining to this.

For example, Illia Polosukhin, founder of NEAR Protocol (NEAR +0.24%), made the point that "we need to build products that meet user experience expectations," and "Crypto hasn't achieved that in the past." Such focus on the customer was even more ingrained in Hyperliquid Co-Founder Jeff Yan, who said, "We're not really optimizing for revenue. That's a byproduct of providing value."

Such statements are music to my ears and tell me there are people working in the space who aren't in it just to get rich. At their core is building something that adds value to customers.

This differentiates great companies from good ones. They focus on providing value first, and business success is a natural result from that.

Of course, there are other things that have to come together for a great long-term investment. But these are the types of companies I'm looking for as a Foolish investor.

As I reflect on the discussions and data from TOKEN2049, it's clear: For Foolish investors, there has never been a better time to dive into the digital asset space. The infrastructure is robust now, capital is more efficiently managed than ever before, AI integration is rising, and fundamentals are just starting to matter. In my view, the tide is uniquely in our favor, and this year will be a pivotal turning point in crypto investing.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3175. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3174. If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation

Merlin Bise is the CTO of Inbenta. He has built conversational AI since before generative AI.

​A lot of the AI deployed into the customer experience over the past three years isn’t performing. That’s just the reality. And the default response I hear, over and over, is to start all over again, evaluating and paying for a new platform.

In most cases, that’s an expensive way to rebuild the same problem.

I’ve been building AI for customer experience since before generative AI showed up. I watched intent matching give way to generative layers, and now we’re into agentic systems that can reason and act on their own. The platforms keep changing. But it isn’t the model that causes the deployment to fail—it’s the knowledge underneath it. I’ve seen that pattern in nearly every underperforming deployment I’ve looked at, going back years.

And look, none of this is a knock on the decision you made three years ago. You made it with the tools that existed then. Those were very different tools.

Here’s what’s new. Fixing the knowledge layer used to be a multiyear, hand-built project. That’s why re-platforming seemed faster, even when it wasn’t. AI now does the heavy lifting up front. It reads, structures and tags your content before anything goes live, so what customers hear is approved, not improvised. Work that used to take a room full of contractors a full year can now get done in weeks, not quarters. If you wrote off your knowledge problem 12 or 18 months ago as too slow or too expensive, it deserves a second look and, honestly, a lot more optimism than it would have earned back then.

Before you run another evaluation, check three things. You can diagnose all of them without a new vendor.

Content written for someone browsing a help site does a different job than content a model has to parse. A model can have the right document and still give the wrong answer. Why? Because two records that aren’t the same can look the same to a system reading them. If a customer asks about one product configuration and gets information about another, that isn’t because the company chose the wrong model or the customer botched the prompt. It’s a structure and authorship problem, and no new platform is going to fix it for you.

Count them. Most organizations have more duplication than they think. As mentioned earlier, a lot of platforms started with intent matching, then added a generative layer later and kept the original intent base underneath. So, now you’ve got two copies of your content, two governance surfaces and two possible answers to the same question. Contact center stacks do the same thing by channel—one store for digital and another for voice. The answer changes depending on which door the customer walked through. If a policy lives in more than one place, you have a consistency problem, not an AI problem.

This is the one that kills deployments. If the subject matter expert who spots a wrong answer has to file a ticket and wait on an engineer, corrections will never keep pace with the business. The person with the knowledge can’t act. The person who can act has no way to judge whether the answer was right. Give that six months, and the system has drifted away from how the company is supposed to operate, without a single error in the logs. You don’t get an alert—you get confused customers.

In the end, you should have one knowledge store instead of several, content structured so a machine can find the right answer and the people who own the policies in control of the answers. And there’s no need to replace your platform.

The economics back this approach up. A full platform replacement is a six-figure commitment before you even count internal time, and moving off an entrenched stack can run several times that. Fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of it. And you keep the asset, no matter what you run on top. If you want to switch platforms later, fine. You’ll be moving a structured, governed knowledge base, instead of hauling the same mess to a new vendor and paying them to discover it.

There’s a second-order benefit, too. A consolidated, governed knowledge layer gives you an audit trail. When a regulator asks about a specific conversation, you need to show the question, the answer, the source and who approved it. It doesn’t matter what platform was used. If you can’t see why your AI said something, you can’t defend it.

Here’s my takeaway. Before you run another evaluation, figure out whether you have a platform problem or a foundation problem. Most of the time, it’s the foundation. And it’s more fixable today than it was when you signed that original contract.

#3173. Broadcom's AI Revenue Is Exploding. Here's What Investors Should Watch Next.

Investors shouldn't ignore the macro and regulatory headwinds.

Broadcom (AVGO +0.74%) is one of the fastest-growing AI chipmakers in the world, but it usually doesn't attract as much attention as Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%). Unlike Nvidia, which produces general-purpose GPUs for data centers, Broadcom produces customized AI accelerators (XPUs) for hyperscalers. When deployed at scale, Broadcom's XPUs can process AI inference tasks faster and more efficiently than Nvidia's stand-alone GPUs.

In fiscal 2025 (which ended last November), Broadcom's AI chip sales soared 65% to $20 billion, or 31% of its top line. In fiscal 2026, it expects its AI chip revenue to surge 186% year over year to $58 billion, or 55% of its projected revenue.

But that could just be the beginning. Broadcom expects its AI chip revenue to nearly double to $115 billion in 2027 and double again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Assuming it hits those targets, analysts expect its revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 62% and 78%, respectively, from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2028. Those are incredible growth rates for a stock that trades at just 18 times forward earnings -- but investors should keep a close eye on its upcoming challenges.

Broadcom's AI business is firing on all cylinders, and it's bundling its other products -- including chips for Ethernet switches, optical interconnect components, and infrastructure software -- with its XPUs. That stickiness gives it tremendous pricing power and widens its defensive moat.

However, Broadcom could face intense macro and regulatory headwinds over the next few years. On the macro front, high interest rates could force AI companies to rein in their spending. On the regulatory front, the Democratic takeover of the House and Senate -- as well as five flipped governorships -- could force data center operators to stop expanding.

Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa already plans to suspend construction of new data centers in the Lone Star State -- and other states could soon follow suit. That pressure, which already crushed many AI stocks, could force Broadcom to reduce its long-term estimates.

To reduce its dependence on the AI market, Broadcom converted VMware's business model (which it acquired in late 2023) from perpetual licenses to recurring cloud-based subscriptions. However, the expansion of its infrastructure software business (which accounted for 30% of its revenue in its latest quarter) probably can't offset an abrupt slowdown in its AI chipmaking business.

Broadcom's stock looks like a bargain, especially after it declined more than 30% over the past six months, but only if you expect the AI market to keep expanding. If you expect AI spending to slow as macro headwinds intensify and the Democrats tighten their grip on data centers, it might be smarter to wait a few more quarters to see if its stock gets even cheaper.

#3172. Sandisk Stock Has Lost About 64% Since June. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy It.

How many years of boom-time profits should a buyer be willing to pay for?

Sandisk (SNDK +3.55%) stock sank about 22% on Thursday, Nov. 5, adding to a painful stretch for the flash memory maker. At roughly $806 as of this writing, shares are down about 64% from their June 25 close of $2,335, a record.

Thursday's slide continued a sell-off in AI data center stocks that started after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as investors weighed whether the outcome might slow data center construction.

And it's been quick. Sandisk closed around $1,330 on Oct. 29, the day it posted fiscal first-quarter results and guided for even higher profits in this quarter. So the growth stock has fallen about 39% over the past week, even though the company's outlook calls for earnings to keep rising.

I think the sell-off has finally brought the stock to a price worth paying. And Sandisk's guidance is what I'd use to set it.

Showing how much the company has changed, Sandisk's earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis grew 26% sequentially, to $49.51 in its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (which ended Oct. 2, 2026). That followed sequential gains of 278% in fiscal Q3 of 2026 and 68% in fiscal Q4. Fiscal Q1 revenue came to $11.0 billion, up 23% sequentially and 378% year over year, and data center customers accounted for about $4.8 billion of it. For fiscal Q2, management guided to adjusted earnings of $55 to $57 per share, implying about 13% growth over fiscal Q1 at the midpoint.

Put simply, profits are still climbing. But the growth rate is slowing quickly, and it might keep falling from here.

After all, memory profits can swing fast. A year before, in fiscal Q1 of 2026, Sandisk earned just $1.22 per share on an adjusted basis, with a gross margin of around 30%.

And in the three months ended March 28, 2025, it had an adjusted loss of $0.30 a share.

True, the company looks different now. Data center revenue was under $300 million in the year-ago quarter, and the gross margin has since climbed to 85%. But flash memory is still a product whose price can fall when supply outruns demand, and Sandisk's earnings would probably drop with it.

Sandisk's guidance covers only one quarter, so the simplest way to use it is to annualize it. Four quarters at the $56 midpoint would total about $224 per share in adjusted profit. At around $806, the stock trades at under 4 times those annualized earnings.

In other words, a buyer at today's price is paying for less than four years of profits at the current pace. Even on actual results, shares sell for about 7 times earnings over the last four quarters.

By comparison, at the Oct. 29 close, shares traded for about 6 times annualized guided earnings.

With a valuation this low, investors seem to expect the boom's profits to fade within a few years. I think that's a fair worry for a memory company. It's also why I wouldn't pay much more than the stock goes for now.

My price is around $900 per share -- the point at which four years of earnings at the fiscal Q2 guidance pace would equal what I'd pay. Asking a company this cyclical for much more than four years of boom-level profits feels like too much to me.

The coming stock split changes how that number looks, but not what it means. Every shareholder of record on Nov. 9 gets seven extra shares for each one held. The new shares arrive after the Nov. 19 close, and split-adjusted trading is expected to start Nov. 20. Divided by eight, my $900 price comes to about $112, and the $56 guidance midpoint becomes $7 a share.

At roughly $806, Sandisk is under that price. Sure, a stock that has dropped this far this fast can keep falling. And if flash prices start to slip, the earnings behind my price might follow.

With that in mind, I'd consider taking a small position now, maybe adding to it over time rather than all at once. If the stock gets back above $900 (or $112 after the split) before I buy, I'd hold off.

#3171. 2027 Tax Brackets and Federal Income Tax Rates

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3170. ​The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure

Bill Wong - AI Research Fellow, Info-Tech Research Group.

​​In my previous article, we examined the emergence of a new data center asset, the AI factory, which is optimized to run AI workloads. Compared to traditional data centers, AI data center campuses require up to 10 times the total facility power capacity, driven by GPU server racks that consume 12 to 28 times more power per rack and thermal density that requires advanced liquid cooling to handle five times the heat generation.

This new industrial revolution is driving an unprecedented demand for power, transforming the utilities industry from a relatively stable and quiet industry to a growth sector.​ Nations and organizations alike will need to optimize their AI energy strategy in order to flourish during and after this revolution.

After reviewing several national AI energy infrastructure strategies around the world, four distinct strategies stand out. These strategies will shape how nations are planning to build the required energy infrastructure for AI workloads.

• Sovereign Regulation-Driven: These jurisdictions introduce legislation to ensure that AI developers must fund their own power requirements, maintain the reliability of the grid and provide the supporting water infrastructure required for these data centers to prevent rising utility costs. In Canada, the country’s recently published AI strategy champions their grid’s 83% investment in clean power. Australia will require data center providers to generate as much energy as they consume. The EU has introduced a sovereign AI compute platform, EuroHPC JU, which aims to “develop innovative energy-efficient HPC software technologies tailored to exascale and post-exascale supercomputers.”

• Market-Driven: These countries rely on the private sector to drive the building of data centers and leverage easily accessible energy resources. The U.S. has begun by reinvesting into nuclear power plants and the use of small modular reactors. The UK has accelerated AI projects through its AI Growth Zones, fast track permits.

• Localization-Driven: Rather than adding additional workloads to the existing energy grids, some countries are locating new data centers near clean energy sources. Japan’s new collaboration strategy leverages nine designated green energy zones. South Korea’s new strategy directs the movement of 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul to regional nuclear and small modular reactor clusters.

• State-Driven: China’s government is planning to connect renewable energy resources from its western region to its computing hubs in its eastern region.​

In order to assess a nation or organization’s AI energy strategy, one must examine its energy value chain. This involves identifying the source of its energy, determining how power is generated, determining how power is managed and deployed, understanding the nation’s thermal management and understanding the sustainability strategy the nation or organization has implemented.​

Meaningful metrics in this area focus on the total volume, dependability and carbon footprint of the electricity required by the organization in question’s compute infrastructure. Countries and organizations using clean and renewable energy resources will be able to differentiate their energy infrastructure in a positive manner. On the other hand, countries leveraging fossil fuels, like natural gas, may have the short-term benefit of accessing low-cost energy resources, but they will also encounter long-term emissions problems, which expose them to carbon regulation and creates cost volatility.​

Metrics in this area focus on an energy infrastructure’s capacity and its ability to connect, control and optimize high-density energy flow between the bulk electric grid (external) and its computing facilities (internal).

From a macro-grid point of view, which focuses outside of the data center, leaders can use ultra-high-voltage transmission lines, battery storage and AI-driven load-balancing software to absorb the violent swings in demand from GPU clusters, which can dramatically improve power management.

From a micro-grid standpoint, which focuses inside the data center, leaders have a few things to consider. Today’s AI racks demand 130 to 600 kW, and pushing that much power through legacy wiring can generate wasted heat and requires multiple inefficient conversion steps. Modern operators can implement ±400V or 800V DC systems and solid-state transformers to reduce internal heat loss and conversion steps.​

Legacy air cooling can no longer dissipate the heat generated by today’s AI factories. How a company handles this heat is becoming a competitive advantage for any organization running its own sovereign AI infrastructure. I’ve observed some leading operators switching to direct-to-chip liquid cooling in closed-loop systems, which can slash operational water consumption.

Embracing robust environmental stewardship can help nations and organizations keep their data center expansion efforts sustainable, minimizing ecological disruption while preserving critical local environmental resources. Beyond conservation, some advanced operators are turning thermal management into a revenue stream. By establishing facilities in colder climates (like Canada, the Nordics or Hokkaido, Japan) and capturing the 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat directly from server racks, those operators can sell that heat to municipal district heating networks.​

Which AI energy infrastructure strategy is the best for a given organization will depend on several factors, and not all options are available for a given country or geographical location, especially those strategies that can leverage a country’s colder climate to reduce cooling costs.

Countries and organizations need to prioritize and align their energy infrastructure architecture with their nation’s sovereign AI strategy. For instance, sustainability initiatives will likely have the best success in countries like Canada and Nordic nations.

Finally, organizations need to learn how to address the current backlash from people regarding AI data centers near their communities. Builders and operators should be prepared to address questions and concerns surrounding the AI energy value chain they’re leveraging, along with its regional costs and benefits. Leaders should focus on sustainability, environmental impact and delivering an accountability framework for the operations of their proposed AI data center.​

Record Q3 sales and a raised outlook, plus a sharp jump in cash generation.

This quarter adds another important element to that story, consistency. Our third quarter results exceeded our outlook as we delivered higher sales, earnings and cash flow compared to the prior year. In sports, only a handful of professional teams have ever achieved a true 5 Pat. The New York Yankees won 5 consecutive World Series titles, the Montreal Canadians captured 5 straight Stanley Cups and Real Madrid claimed 5 consecutive European Cup championships. Those accomplishments were never about the streak itself.

They were the result of strong foundations, disciplined execution and organizations built to sustain success over time. That same aspiration is at the heart of the core strategy. While we are still in the relatively early stages of our journey, our 5 consecutive quarters of double-digit pro forma sales and adjusted earnings per share growth provide encouraging evidence that our Helios Business System is building the right foundation. We remain focused not on extending the street, but on creating a stronger company through disciplined execution, strategic investment and operational excellence that can deliver sustainable, profitable growth and long-term shareholder value creation for years to come.

We achieved record third quarter sales of $230 million with both of our segments contributing to our outperformance. That breadth matters. It reflects contributions from established customer relationships, recent business wins and the investments we have made in our commercial capabilities. It also reflects our sustained commitment to delivering product innovations to meet customer demands. In the most recent quarter, Sun Korea developed new common cavity valves, Enovation expanded no roads with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and partnered with SMA to enhance marine capabilities to the platform, while Balboa contributed to a luxury spa and pond scrap designed by Studio FA Porsche. Within Hydraulics, we saw growth from business wins and share gains. We also continue to benefit from demand across construction, industrial and smaller agricultural equipment, although large ag remains challenged. In Electronics, strength in recreation led to record third quarter sales for Enovation Controls, and we saw year-over-year growth in the marine end market for the first time in 7 quarters. The health and wellness end market was also up double digits in the third quarter. We did see some customers place orders ahead of price increases announced in the quarter that resulted in some sales being accelerated into the third quarter in both segments.

Considering the solid quarter, our September acquisition and continued order strength, we are raising our full year 2026 sales outlook and expect fiscal year 2026 sales to be the highest in Helios' history. However, the operating environment remains challenging with ongoing cost pressures, tightening supply chains, uncertainty around interest rates and a volatile geopolitical and trade backdrop. We cannot control those factors, but we can control how we execute, and that's where our focus remains. We continue to take actions to offset these dynamic macro factors. The timing of these actions, combined with when we will fully capture synergies on the Radio Sound acquisition have been factored into our updated outlook ranges.

When we introduced the core strategy, we laid out a clear road map for Helios' next phase of profitable growth, one built on stronger customer relationships, differentiated innovation, operational excellence and disciplined capital allocation. The plan draws on the deep legacies of the Helios portfolio companies, exemplified by Schultes Precision's recent 80th corporate anniversary. Across electronics, we are progressing production transfers within our global footprint, including moving manufacturing lines from Tulsa to our Tijuana facility to better align capabilities, costs and regional customer requirements. The transaction adds audio and communications capabilities that complement our existing electronic solutions and can support additional customers in adjacent markets. While financially modest, it is strategically aligned with our approach to acquire technology and capabilities that can be built as a platform and leverage across the portfolio. Over the last 18 months, the team has moved through market research, R&D, product development, prototyping, testing and qualification to get to an initial customer order. Together, these 3 areas are building a stronger foundation for long-term value creation. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jeremy to review the third quarter financial results and our updated 2026 outlook.

Higher volume and the benefits of our operating and portfolio actions helped offset continued inflation in material and component costs, freight and utilities. Operating income was $28 million compared with $1 million in the prior year quarter, which included a goodwill impairment charge of $26 million.

Adjusted operating income grew 4% to $38 million and adjusted operating margin was 16.6%, consistent with the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA increased 3% to $47 million with adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.3% compared with 20.5% last year. Although adjusted EBITDA was up $1.4 million, adjusted EBITDA margin was pressured due to our increased investments in R&D, fast-moving inflationary costs, higher incentive compensation expense driven by our year-to-date performance and a continued high run rate for employee benefit costs. We continue to manage spending carefully while protecting the engineering, commercial and operational functions that support future growth. Diluted earnings per share increased 71% to $0.53.

The prior year third quarter was impacted by a goodwill impairment, which was partially offset by the gain realized on the CFP divestiture. Adjusted diluted earnings per share increased 11% to $0.80, $0.03 above the high end of our outlook. Turning to the segments. Please refer to Slide 9. Hydraulics sales were $143 million, up 1% as reported and 15% on a pro forma basis. Sales increased in the Americas and EMEA, while the reported APAC comparison was affected by the divestiture. Growth reflected continued commercial execution and share gains as well as distributor partners restocking ahead of our announced price increases. Order activity softened following those increases, but appears to have normalized.

It is important to distinguish replenishment of channel inventory from the underlying rate of end market consumption. We are monitoring distributor inventory and regional order patterns closely. Hydraulics gross profit was $46 million, essentially unchanged from last year, while gross margin declined 20 basis points to 32.3%. Gross margins were impacted by higher freight and utility costs as well as additional expenses associated with the faster North America consolidation. Segment operating income increased 2% to $25 million, and operating margin improved 10 basis points to 17.3% as leverage on operating expenses as a result of higher sales more than offset the gross margin decline. Growth in the Americas and APAC more than offset lower sales in EMEA. Our performance reflects ongoing customer program activity and new business wins even as conditions across certain core markets remain challenged. We continue to target opportunities where our controls, displays and integrated technologies can deliver greater value to customers. Electronics gross profit increased 11% to $30 million and gross margin expanded 40 basis points to 34.7%. Gross margins benefited from leverage on overhead expenses as a result of higher sales, which more than offset higher input costs. Segment operating income was $12 million with an operating margin of 14.3%. The prior year third quarter operating margin was impacted by a goodwill impairment.

Excluding the goodwill impairment, operating income was flat with the prior year, reflecting incremental investments in research and development. Electronic component availability and pricing remain areas of attention, particularly for memory chips and circuit boards. We are working with suppliers and selectively positioning inventory to support customer requirements. We also continue executing production transfers and other initiatives intended to improve our cost structure and manufacturing flexibility while routinely evaluating pricing-related actions to help offset inflationary pressures. The Radio Sound acquisition integration is underway. Our near-term priorities are supporting the Indian motorcycle relationship, integrating the operations and identifying additional applications for the acquired capabilities across our customer base. We expect it will take about 1 quarter to capture the cost synergies.

The acquisition represents a high-reward opportunity that expands our audio solutions offering and establishes a relationship with a new OEM. Turning to Slide 10. We generated cash from operations of $40 million, up 59% from the prior year period and a record for our third quarter. Free cash flow in the quarter was $32 million and capital expenditures were $8 million as we continued investing in the business. This reflects our continued focus on driving timely customer collections, extending terms with our partners and managing inventory held within Helios.

We maintained our days inventory on hand, although our inventory balances increased year-over-year and sequentially as we increased stock to support higher sales while selectively taking an inventory position on electronic and thermal management components to support customer requirements and manage supply availability. On Slide 11, you can see our balance sheet continues to provide flexibility. We ended the quarter with total debt of $328 million and cash of $73 million, resulting in net debt of $255 million. Our capital allocation priorities remain in this order.

First, organic investment, followed by returns to shareholders, strategic acquisitions and then debt repayment. Our capital deployment in the quarter reflected this as we increased CapEx and R&D investments over the year ago period, repurchased our highest amount of common stock within the quarter, extended our cash dividends to 119 consecutive quarters and deployed $1.7 million on the acquisition of certain assets of Radio Sound. Slide 12 summarizes the financial priorities we established at the beginning of the year. We made consistent progress across all 4 priorities this year, executing our growth plan, improving gross margins, maintaining earnings momentum and optimizing capital allocation.

We are focused on ending the year strong, delivering a new sales record and converting the sales growth into earnings and cash. Turning to Slides 13 and 14. We now expect 2026 sales of $895 million to $902 million or 13% pro forma growth at the midpoint over the prior year period. The low end of the range eclipses our previous record of $885 million, so we are on pace for the highest annual sales in Helios' history. The top end of the range has increased as a result of anticipated sales from the completed acquisition.

For the full year, we expect Hydraulics sales of $564 million to $568 million, 15% pro forma growth at the midpoint and electronics sales of $331 million to $334 million, 12% growth at the midpoint. We expect consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.2% to 20.4% and adjusted diluted earnings per share of $3.08 to $3.15. We are tightening both the margin and earnings ranges from our prior outlook to reflect the current cost environment, along with the impact of the Radio Sound acquisition. The new adjusted diluted earnings per share midpoint reflects a 22% annual growth rate, approaching twice that of our expected midpoint top line growth of 13%.

For the fourth quarter, we expect consolidated sales of $205 million to $212 million. This includes hydraulic sales of $135 million to $139 million and electronics sales of $70 million to $73 million, reflecting current order visibility, component availability and the benefit from the acquisition. We expect fourth quarter adjusted EBITDA margin of 18.5% to 19.5% and adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.60 to $0.67. As a reminder, the fourth quarter of 2025 included an interest expense benefit of $5.4 million related to an interest rate swap that was originally due for maturity that quarter and was terminated as a result of our debt refinancing in 2024, which favorably impacted earnings per share by approximately $0.12.

This impacts the year-over-year comparison in the fourth quarter. There are several considerations behind this outlook. First, we expect the fourth quarter growth rate to moderate from the third quarter pace as we are lapping tougher compares, combined with the fact there was a full extra week in the shipping calendar in the fourth quarter last year. Last year, in the fourth quarter, we reported 17% sales growth and 29% pro forma growth without CFP. This is part of those tougher compares mentioned. Second, we remain in an inflationary cost environment. And although we have taken targeted pricing actions, we believe the benefit will start to show more in 2027.

Third, we will incur integration costs in the fourth quarter related to the acquisition, which were not originally anticipated in our prior outlook, while expected synergies will start to be reflected in early 2027. Our outlook, therefore, balances the strength of our year-to-date performance and commercial pipeline with a measured view of the orders for the balance of the year while layering in timing of initiatives to offset cost inflation as well as the recent acquisition. Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

With regulatory approval secured for its pending merger and fee businesses performing steadily, the bank is positioned to build on its regional momentum.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Jackson Financial (JXN -0.78%) announced retail annuity sales of more than $6.5 billion. The insurer is expanding into spread-based products, which earn income on interest rate spreads, to build a predictable earnings stream.

Management offers three key insights into how the company is driving this transition.

Jackson Financial is shifting its sales mix away from traditional variable annuities, contracts whose payouts fluctuate with market funds. It is expanding spread-based offerings like registered index-linked annuities (RILA), which shield retirement savings with capped downside protection, to lower reliance on equity market fees.

Jackson Financial secured an exclusive partnership with AARP to offer digital annuities directly to members starting in late 2026. This direct-to-consumer model gives the insurer access to self-directed investors without relying on traditional advisor networks.

Jackson Financial manages market volatility through Brooke Re, a Michigan-based captive reinsurer created to isolate variable annuity risk. The structure aligns accounting reserves with market economics, preventing costly non-economic hedging during rising interest rate cycles.

Sales momentum is building across spread-based retirement products, and free cash generation continues to cover capital return targets. Jackson Financial leverages strong distribution relationships, broad product choices, and internal investment capabilities to generate steady operating returns while watching policyholder lapse trends.

A disciplined hedging program and expanding direct sales channels provide a foundation for long-term growth across changing market environments.

#3163. ​Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows

Corey Ercanbrack is CTO at Vasion, leading the AI-native transformation of a cloud-native platform under FedRAMP High.

A state agency mails benefits notices to citizens, with personal data on the page and legal rights tied to what’s printed. When I asked the administrator responsible for its 30,000 endpoints what governs that output process, he said it runs elsewhere, on infrastructure owned by a different team.​

He wasn’t dodging me. That’s how these environments get built, and it produces a blind spot most leaders inherit rather than create. Information is governed where the data lives. Output is governed where the devices live. Those are two teams with different budgets, reporting lines and definitions of accountability, so the artifact carrying the heaviest legal obligation sits furthest from the controls protecting the information inside it.​

The same split appears across other organizations I work with. Major American cities operating under state public records law must produce any official communication upon request, whatever the medium. Their digital channels are instrumented. Paper isn’t. The specialist responsible for its endpoint estate acknowledged that if he sent a printed memo, someone would still have to find it.​

That gap has been survivable because a person stands in it. The employee who printed the memo knows he printed it, and if a request arrives two years later, someone can ask him. In audit terms, he’s a compensating control: what you document and test when the designed control can’t be implemented. Nobody documented this one. It’s been load-bearing for 30 years without appearing in a control matrix, which is why removing it looks costless.​

Agents remove it. Deloitte’s 2026 “State of AI in the Enterprise” report surveyed 3,235 business and IT leaders across 24 countries. Nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Among the capabilities Deloitte names as crucial are audit trails capturing the full chain of agent actions.​

When an instruction comes from a system rather than a person, there may be no human intent to reconstruct later and no awareness that a records obligation was triggered. Unless the workflow was designed to capture that context, automation can generate unaccounted output far faster than the informal human process it replaced. Leaders may be automating away a control they never knew they depended on.

Most AI governance programs are scoped to the application: which model acted, what data it reached, what it was authorized to do and what it produced. That work is necessary, but it is not sufficient, because operational documents don’t stay inside one application.​

I have watched a prior authorization request move from a medical record to paper, to a fax machine, to an insurer and return days later as an email. Each system recorded its portion and completed the step it was designed to handle, but none held the thread connecting them: the only view from which the organization could reconstruct the full event. The application finished its task. The business did not, and governance was scoped to the first while the obligation attaches to the second.​

An IT leader at a global distributor gave me a paperless example. More countries where his company operates now require documents to be deposited with a government authority. The regulation specifies where the document must be sent without specifying how it gets there. Treating the output boundary as a printing problem misses the broader obligation to govern the document throughout its journey.​

If an auditor picked up an AI-generated document tomorrow, what could you prove about it? Four questions help determine the answer.

1. Identity: Who or what produced it? Once a document is printed, exported or faxed, the chain of identity breaks. The artifact no longer shows which agent created it, who initiated the action or where the information came from.​

2. Authorization: Who approved its release? Knowing who generated a document is not the same as knowing whether release was authorized. A finished document proves neither.​

3. Audit: What happened between input and output? An agent extracts information, changes content and generates instructions. Record only the finished document, and you can’t show what it did. The record has to replay what went in, what changed, who acted and where it went.​

4. Retention: Can you find and classify it? Without the first three, you accumulate documents you’re obligated to protect and unable to trace, turning a governance gap into a storage liability.​

Miss one, and you don’t have end-to-end AI governance. Instead, you have a partial record of an action that continued without you. I recommend running these four against a live workflow before expanding agent authority. The gaps you find are the ones an agent will only widen.

The instinct is to connect every system, but these integrations are often fragile and require ongoing maintenance whenever one side changes.

Start with the work instead.​ Pick one operational document this week and follow it from creation to final disposition. Mark every point where somebody prints, exports, faxes, signs, scans or retypes information, and keep going after the data leaves the application. The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it. Test the four questions at each one. Wherever context breaks, you’ve found the real boundary of your program before an auditor does.​

The workflows that hold up often share one trait: The record was designed before the agent was deployed, rather than reconstructed after someone asked for it. That means someone decided where human review belonged and what needed to be recorded at every step, including the agent’s actions. You can’t deploy first and gather the evidence later. The record has to be created when the action occurs, or it may not exist at all. And the destination is rarely as modern as the agent. I’ve watched sophisticated automation end with a fax because that’s what the recipient accepts.​​

Governance has to follow the information through every handoff. The practical perimeter is everywhere the information goes.​​
