#3124. 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow

Startups often move quickly because they have to, making the most of limited resources and adapting as circumstances change. As tech companies scale, added layers of process, approval and hierarchy can gradually slow decision making and erode the flexibility that helped them grow.

The good news is that companies don’t have to abandon the habits that fueled their early success as they expand. Here, Forbes Technology Council members share startup habits established tech companies should preserve—or relearn—to maintain their agility as they grow.

Established tech companies should preserve the startup habit of staying close to the raw customer experience. As organizations scale, dashboards and layers of interpretation can obscure what people actually struggle with. Leaders should keep speaking directly with customers and empower small teams to act quickly on what they learn. Scale should improve execution, not distance companies from users. - Leah Wang, Karpo

The tech market in the AI era is changing super fast—the cycles for product demands, work methods and tools, and customers’ needs and requirements have all become very short. The one thing companies must preserve is agility within the boundaries of their focus. It is easy to get lost and try to achieve everything, only to end up with nothing. Being able to stay agile while knowing the problem your company solves is critical. - Yoav Amitai, Elsight

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Startups are great at prototyping new products and services and moving on quickly from ideas during the research and development phase. As companies scale, this “create fast, test fast, decide fast” capacity is often diminished. One way to keep it alive is to engage early with a customer or partner to confirm requirements or do testing. It puts healthy pressure on the development process while gathering valuable external feedback on pricing, functionality and positioning. - Eva Rudin, Thales Cybersecurity

Preserve the willingness to challenge assumptions. Startups move quickly because they don’t treat “this is how it’s done” as an acceptable answer. As companies scale, process can quietly replace curiosity. The best teams keep questioning their own products, decisions and assumptions, especially when something appears to be working. Scale should give you more resources to challenge the status quo, not more reasons to protect it. - Alissa Knight, Assail, Inc.

Keep saying no to the wrong business. When you are small, you cannot serve everyone, so you get good at turning down the wrong customers and use cases, and that focus is half of why you survive. At scale, every deal looks worth taking, and the muscle for walking away weakens. You must protect it on purpose. The companies that keep rejecting what does not fit stay sharp long after they could afford to lose focus. - Vytautas Savickas, Oxylabs

Solve problems close to where they occur. As organizations scale, issues often get escalated to the most senior person rather than the person best connected to the customer or the detail of the issue. That introduces delays to fixes being made and promotes permission-seeking rather than judgment and accountability. Push authority down and let the people closest to the problem make the call. - Rob Sloan, Zscaler

Knowing when to stop is crucial. Startups have to focus because their resources are limited. The ability in a startup to know exactly what is going on means not only decisions to invest but also decisions to divest are made faster. - Véronique Özkaya, DATAmundi

AI-first thinking is the biggest thing established players need to adopt from the startup realm. New ventures have the luxury of AI being the starting point, not something they need to bolt onto old, outdated processes. That blank slate is a real edge—no legacy systems standing between them and AI-driven gains. So, I’d begin every problem by asking where AI can make the biggest impact and build from there. That mindset will define the future enterprise. - Tarek Nseir, Valliance

Preserve the habit of testing before debating. Startups rarely have enough data to eliminate uncertainty, so they build something small, put it in front of users, and learn. At scale, debate can become a substitute for discovery. Established companies should relearn how to turn unanswered questions into fast, low-risk experiments, using evidence from the market to resolve what meetings cannot. - Melissa King, Paylocity

Let the people closest to a problem try things without asking permission first. In many cases, our team members have made our most impactful suggestions. We discussed it, tried it out and looked at the results together. Nobody wrote a proposal. Give teams a sandbox, clear data and security rules, and a few weeks to test. You’ll learn more than you would from a six-month planning cycle. - Merav Yuravlivker, Data Society

Keep communication lines efficient. The best startups have an uncanny ability to throw unnecessary hierarchy to the wind and flatten communication lines. That’s how startups home in on solutions rather than simply admiring the problem. - James Stanger, CompTIA

Cross-department talk is essential. In a startup, everyone can talk to everyone without wondering about politics and the org chart. You never know where the next good idea will come from—it often comes from an “unexpected part” of the org chart. If Joe from team X is afraid of talking to Mary from team Y just because they don’t have the same boss, the company’s capacity to innovate is severely impacted. - Stephane Donze, AODocs

Startups move fast because they accept higher risk, while large organizations slow down to protect reputation, revenue and investors. As companies grow, they must consciously balance risk appetite to keep innovating. Teams should also keep the startup habit of “relentless iteration”—sharing early “sh***y first drafts,” as referenced by Brené Brown—for fast feedback instead of waiting for polish. - Mandy Andress, Elastic

Ship things that aren’t ready and learn from real users instead of extensive internal reviews. Process exists to prevent mistakes, but it also prevents speed and discovery. Talk directly to users without a layer of research, summaries or account managers in between. - Amy Gu, Dynamsoft

Create rituals early and maintain them throughout your growth. Startup life is hard. One of the things that inspires and preserves team alignment is the rituals created in early startup life that create an identity, a battle cry and a touchstone to the mission. As new employees join the company, these same rituals become part of their orientation, which helps encourage unity. - Amy Brown, Authenticx

Preserve fast, reversible decision making. Let teams run small, bounded tests without routing every choice through layers of approval, then use the results to adjust quickly. Reserve heavyweight reviews for decisions that are costly or difficult to undo—not every experiment. - Nagesh Nama, xLM Continuous Intelligence

Share the full picture with everyone. In a startup, the whole team knows the revenue, the biggest customer problem, and what worries the founders most. As companies grow, that context gets held back at the top, and teams start working on tasks without knowing why they matter. People make better decisions when they know what the company is facing. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

Preserve the startup habit of a hard work-in-progress limit. Early teams cannot pursue 20 “top priorities,” so starting one thing means stopping another. At scale, portfolios expand faster than capacity, and coordination becomes the bottleneck. Force every new priority to displace an old one. Speed comes as much from limiting concurrency as from moving faster. - Akhilesh Sharma, A3Logics Inc.

Do it by hand before automating it. Startups run a new process manually for a few weeks and learn where it actually breaks. Larger companies jump straight to automation and lock in their guesses. In mature organizations we audit, roughly a third of flows either duplicate another or barely run. A month of manual work first is cheaper than a year of maintaining the wrong automation. - Sergii Grushai, Peeklogic

#3123. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#3121. Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at Age 65

At 65, most retirees face a permanent reduction in benefits because they haven't reached their full retirement age.

Age 65 is often a pivot point for retirement planning because it's when Medicare eligibility begins. However, for current near-retirees, it's not the finish line for Social Security. The average benefit for people who are 65 is $1,607.27 per month, according to December 2025 data from the Social Security Administration (SSA), the most recent figures available. This number is lower than the $2,088.79 overall average for all retired workers reported by the SSA as of September 2026.

While you're eligible for health coverage at 65, your full retirement age (FRA) is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later. Claiming Social Security at 65 results in a permanent 13.33% reduction in your monthly benefit.

The average benefit varies by gender, with men receiving $1,772.00 vs. women $1,457.40, a gap of about $314.60 per month. This difference generally reflects historical earnings gaps and variations in work history. For most retirees, these monthly payments serve as a foundation for their retirement income but are rarely enough to cover all expenses.

The dollar amounts in this table reflect SSA data as of December 2025. These figures provide a baseline for what people who are currently 65 receive, rather than a projection for those who claim at 65 in the future. Your personal benefit depends entirely on your own earnings history and when you choose to file.

If your full retirement age is 67, claiming at 65 is technically an early filing. The SSA bases your benefit on an average of your wages across your 35 highest-earning years, which are adjusted for inflation and run through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. Filing two years before your FRA prevents you from reaching that full baseline amount.

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. That adjustment will add about $58 a month on top of the overall age-65 average listed above. These adjustments are designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation, though they often lag behind the actual rising costs seniors face.

Social Security was designed to replace only 40% of pre-retirement income, a share that's well short of what most retirees need to cover their living costs. This makes it a supplemental source of income rather than a full replacement for a salary. Most retirees must bridge the gap with savings or other income sources.

Balancing your Medicare enrollment at 65 with a Social Security strategy helps ensure you don't lock in a lower monthly check than your long-term budget requires.

Claiming Social Security at 65 could make sense if you have a short life expectancy, you lack personal savings or a job to help you cover your living costs until your FRA, or if you just don't want to wait any longer for your benefits to begin.

But it's worth thinking through all your options before deciding which claiming age is right for you. Every month you delay increases your checks slightly until you qualify for your largest checks at age 70. Waiting until then could lead to a much larger lifetime benefit if you live into your mid-80s or beyond.

If you do decide to wait until you qualify for larger checks, keep in mind you'll have to pay for your Medicare Part B premiums out of your own pocket for the time being. Once you apply for Social Security, the government will start taking these premiums out of your benefits, so you don't have to pay a separate bill.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.

#3115. Stock Market Today, Nov. 6: AMD Surges 11% on Record Quarterly Revenue and Stronger Growth Outlook

On Nov. 6, 2026, AMD shares rallied as investors cheered its latest results and a forecast for faster growth through 2027.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +11.04%), a data-center CPUs, GPUs, and adaptive semiconductors provider, closed at $449.04, up 11.04%. Pre-market buying followed Thursday's drop after AMD topped revenue and earnings estimates, and investors are now watching data-center demand. Trading volume reached 45.2M shares, coming in about 101% above its three-month average of 22.4M shares.

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) closed at 7,379, up 0.34%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) finished at 24,579, up 1.09%. Among semiconductors spanning data-center CPUs, GPUs, adaptive computing, and embedded chips, Nvidia closed at $186.64, up 2.78%, and Intel closed at $56.28, up 7.71%, as chip buyers returned and AI demand stayed in focus.

AMD seems to be benefiting from a delayed reaction to its third-quarter 2026 earnings report, which came out on Nov. 4. Investors sold off the chip stock in Thursday trading amid concerns that the midterm election results would empower politicians to regulate the industry more tightly.

Today’s recovery suggests that traders may have overreacted on Thursday. Moreover, AMD delivered an objectively strong Q3 earnings report on Wednesday, reporting record revenues. The $13.4 billion in revenue was a 45% year-over-year increase, with data center revenue rising by 97% over the same period.

Additionally, analysts predict 50% revenue growth for the year, followed by an additional 79% in 2027. This suggests the AI boom is not going to end anytime soon.

Instead, where investors may have to worry is valuation. The 98 P/E ratio is well above that of its peers and may leave investors wondering whether that makes AMD stock a buy at that premium.

Indeed, buying the stock at current levels is arguably risky, as the valuation leaves investors vulnerable should unforeseen negative events occur. Nonetheless, AMD’s technology places it on the cutting edge of AI, implying its long-term growth story is far from over.

#3108. Plains (PAA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Silver Creek adds Rockies scale as Permian growth nears the high end of guidance.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Plains All American Pipeline, L.P. (PAA -2.49%) reported third-quarter adjusted EBITDA attributable to PAA of $711 million, reflecting the company's strategic focus as a premier crude oil midstream provider following the divestiture of its Canadian natural gas liquids business. Management indicated that production growth in the Permian Basin is trending toward the high end of previous estimates, while the Silver Creek acquisition provides immediate scale in the Rockies platform. The company stated it is on track to deliver $50 million in organizational efficiencies and has captured $50 million in synergies from its Cactus III acquisition. The company reported that recent capital structure optimization, including the redemption of preferred securities, will provide meaningful accretion to distributable cash flow moving forward.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Plains All American Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I'd now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Blake Fernandez, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Blake Fernandez: Thank you, Marvin. Good morning, and welcome to the Plains All American third quarter 2026 earnings call. Today's slide presentation is posted on the Investor Relations website under the News and Events section at ir.plains.com. An audio replay will also be available following today's call. Important disclosures regarding forward-looking statements and non-GAAP financial measures are provided on Slide 2. An overview of today's call is provided on Slide 3. A condensed consolidating balance sheet for PAGP and other reference materials are in the appendix. Today's call will be hosted by Willie Chiang, Chairman and CEO and President; Al Swanson, Executive Vice President and CFO, along with other members of our management team.

With that, I'm going to turn the call over to Willie.

Willie Chiang: Thank you, Blake. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. This morning, we reported strong third quarter adjusted EBITDA attributable to Plains of $711 million. Al will provide additional details on the quarterly results in his portion of the call. Our business is operating well, and we continue to demonstrate steady growth as we executed on the three initiatives that we established at the beginning of the year. First, we closed on the sale of our Canadian NGL business in May, which completes our shift to a premier crude oil midstream company and improves the quality of our cash flow and our opportunities for growth going forward.

Second, we have captured $50 million of synergies in connection with the Cactus III Pipeline acquisition. And third, we remain on track to deliver $50 million of efficiencies across the organization by year-end 2026. As we outlined on Slide 4, we have multiple levers to efficiently grow the business through a combination of organic and inorganic investment opportunities that complement our existing asset base. To further expand on the organic growth projects that we detailed in the second quarter, we're pleased to announce a 10-year agreement with a large integrated producer to further build out our Permian Midland gathering system.

This new agreement includes 270,000 dedicated acres, and it provides additional growth opportunities to the POP JV, bringing our total dedicated acreage in the Permian to more than 5.3 million acres. Outside of the Permian, we successfully closed the Silver Creek acquisition, which we have renamed Silver Spur on October 1. This further expands our presence within the Powder River Basin, where substantial drilling location with attractive economics support robust producer development into the future. Silver Spur is a strategic addition to our Rockies platform. The system currently transports approximately 125,000 barrels a day, underpinned by a diversified customer base and includes 915,000 dedicated acres with long-term contractual commitments.

By integrating these gathering assets into our existing network, we enhance our customer offering with long-term -- long haul connectivity to Cushing, creating commercial and operational synergies that support long-term cash flow growth. During the quarter, we also took steps to optimize our balance sheet with a successful junior subordinated notes offering and the subsequent redemption of our preferred securities. Al will provide more detail, but these transactions meaningfully simplify our capital structure and are accretive to distributable cash flow moving forward. On the macro front, the geopolitical landscape remains volatile with ongoing disruptions to global oil supply and damage to energy infrastructure.

Global demand has remained resilient and oil inventories, including strategic petroleum reserves, continue depleting, which is supporting the crude oil futures curve. Through this environment, North America remains critical to help meet global energy needs. More specific to the Permian, we expect production growth to be towards the high end of our previous range, about 200,000 barrels a day on a year-end exit-to-exit basis for 2026. Improving natural gas egress, higher rig counts over the past 6 months, continued developments of various formations in the Permian and continued advancements in drilling efficiencies and enhanced recovery techniques should and will provide momentum into 2027. We will provide a more formal outlook for 2027 Permian growth on our call in February.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Al to cover our quarterly performance and other financial matters.

Al Swanson: Thanks, Willie. Slide 5 contains adjusted EBITDA walks that provide additional details on our performance. Please note that 3Q reporting removes the NGL segment and includes one single consolidated segment for the entire company, which aligns with the sale of our Canadian NGL business that closed in May. For the third quarter, we reported adjusted EBITDA of $711 million, reflecting the benefit of operating efficiencies, annual tariff rate escalations and a reduction in environmental remediation expenses relative to the second quarter. As highlighted on Slide 6, we are on track to achieve our guidance targets for the year and narrowing the EBITDA range to plus or minus $50 million with a midpoint of $2.88 billion.

Based on prevailing macro environment, we would expect to be at or slightly above the midpoint of the range for the year. A summary of 2026 guidance and key assumptions are on Slide 7. We will provide guidance for 2027 on our call in February. Slide 8 illustrates strong distributable cash flow generation. In September, we successfully raised $1.5 billion of 30-year junior subordinated notes, which mature in 2056, consisting of $700 million of 6.75% Series A notes, which are callable in 5 years and $800 million of 7% Series B notes, which are callable in 10 years.

Subsequently, we used the proceeds along with cash on hand and commercial paper borrowings to redeem all of our Series A and Series B preferred units. This capital structure optimization is expected to increase annual distributable cash flow to common unitholders by approximately $60 million or $0.09 per unit while maintaining leverage within our targeted range. With that, I will turn the call back to Willie.

Willie Chiang: Thank you, Al. I'm pleased with our performance year-to-date and the continued execution on our key initiatives. Our crude oil business, with a more durable and predictable cash flow stream post-NGL sale, really positions us well for a variety of macro market conditions. As we show on Slide 9, we continue to execute our efficient growth strategy. The three announcements this quarter again demonstrate the multiple levers that we have to drive growth, including organic investments, inorganic bolt-on M&A and balance sheet optimization. We remain committed to capital discipline, maintaining a stable and flexible balance sheet and continuing to return cash to unitholders. With that, I'll turn the call back to Blake to lead us into Q&A.

Blake Fernandez: Thanks, Willie. [Operator Instructions] With that, Marvin, we're ready for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Manav Gupta of UBS.

Manav Gupta: I wanted to ask you a little bit more on the 270,000-acre Midland dedication. As you ramp towards the 225 target of volumes, how should we think about the earnings uplift that this opportunity provides?

Jeremy Goebel: Manav, this is Jeremy Goebel. We're going to give you some more guidance on that in February. But think of that as existing production. So it's not a ramp to production. It's just a matter of timing for connection. So that contribution will likely be late 2027, early 2028, when the connection is done, but we'll give you more guidance on capital and timing next year. But we're excited about the opportunity to partner with a top-tier producer and look forward to providing those services over a long period of time and expanding our Midland footprint.

Manav Gupta: Perfect, sir. The second question I wanted to ask you, I mean, we understand there's crude volatility, but what are you hearing from the producers generally in the Permian? When do you see to the point where these existing Permian pipes, even with the Cactus III expansion, are like almost 90% full?

Jeremy Goebel: Got it. Manav, that is a great question. What I would say is the volatility you experience every day in waking up and seeing a headline and crude move $8 to $10, they're experiencing the same. The pipes to the coast are close to 90% full now.

I think what you would see is the total basin will grow 200,000 to 300,000 barrels a day. The basin will clear for several more years. But I think your timing is appropriate for additional brownfield expansions in that '28 to '29 time period to see additional capacity come to market. So there's no need for a greenfield large pipeline at this time based on the ratable growth that we see and the smaller number of players driving growth, it seems like it's going to be orderly and that growth will happen over that time period. But your -- sometime in 2028 to early 2029, I think you'll see additional brownfield expansions.

But by and large, I think rates are constructive, dialogue is constructive with counterparties. We continue to re-contract the pipes that we have now and look forward to continue growing the business.

Willie Chiang: Manav, this is Willie. I just wanted to add one thing. Your question is spot on. It's very difficult to predict the exact timing of it because just of the global volatility. But as I sit back and we think about what's going on in the world, global demand has remained fairly resilient. There's a lot of noise in the supply chains. If you look at where the resources are and where the demand centers are for the world, it all points to North America really being an incremental producer. So the capacity that we've got out of the Permian is meaningful, and we've got the ability to expand Cactus III.

And as we've said before, we're going to match that expansion capacity to what the demand is to get to the water, but I think it really sets up for a strong macro environment going forward. Trying to analyze and pick exactly when it's going to happen, is very, very difficult, but we'll be patient, and we stand ready to be able to meet the needs.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Can you hear me okay?

Willie Chiang: We can hear you loud and clear.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Excellent. Look, a couple of things, maybe just zeroing in and nitpicking, just on the quarter itself, 4Q was implied here, how do you think a little bit about just implying down? Is there any specific drag here on the -- like forthcoming quarter? And then thinking a little bit more strategically to the last question here, what do you think the timing of evaluating that Cactus III expansion is vis-a-vis, you talk about that '28 timeline for a brownfield expansion? When do you start moving on that, and we're getting a little bit more detail on -- I presume that's the brownfield expansion you're getting at here.

Al Swanson: Julien, this is Al. I'll do the first part. Implied, obviously, in our guidance is about $700 million for the fourth quarter, down about $10 million from the third quarter. The real change is the market opportunities that we've experienced in 2Q and 3Q that's really driving the $10 million lower number plus the inclusion of Silver Creek for the fourth quarter. If you recall, our view is Silver Creek's an asset that's going to grow meaningfully over the next few years. 4Q included in our forecast is without the benefit of some of that growth, some transition services costs, integration costs, et cetera, and without the synergies.

So those two basically offset the step down in some of the market opportunities that we captured kind of as the war started for second quarter and third quarter.

Jeremy Goebel: Julien, for your second part, the shorter answer is we're continually evaluating them. Just as you saw this summer, we added 75,000 barrels a day. And then as contracts and rates are appropriate, we'll add the additional capacity. So it's not -- I don't think it's going to be one step change another 300,000 barrels a day.

I think you're going to see a series of expansions that go based on market demand.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Got it. Excellent. And you picked up what I was trying to put down on that 4Q and on the Silver Creek piece and the contribution. But maybe talking about the PRB more broadly here. I mean obviously, you're acquiring here. How do you think about diversification in that geography here, post midterms, et cetera? Anything that you'd flag in terms of just this is more strategic repositioning and adding on the margin maybe, but any points to complement your latest position there?

Jeremy Goebel: Thanks, Julien. We're very excited about the Silver Spur asset. I think the Powder River Basin is one that's been candidly evaluated for over some time period, and they're just starting to figure it out. So I think it's going to ramp into 2028. We have to continue to build out the system now through 2027, but there's a series of MVCs. There's 915,000 of acreage dedications. There's 4 to 5 producers that are already telling us that the wells are better and they cost less, and they're looking to potentially add a rig into the system. So we can see the Powder River Basin as the next growth wedge in the Rockies.

And that positions well for us not only on the Silver Spur asset from a gathering standpoint, but it also from a pull-through benefit to our pipelines and terminals in the Guernsey area headed south through to Cushing. So it's an integrated play for us. It's a growth on a stand-alone basis but also an integrated play. So we're excited about the opportunity to work with some of our large producers that are also there.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jeremy Tonet of JPMorgan Securities.

Francina Kolluri: This is Francina on for Jeremy. Just wanted to zoom in a bit more on that kind of Silver Creek contribution point in 4Q. How would you kind of maybe frame or size run rate contributions and then the kinds of projects that might be incremental to kind of reach that run rate in terms of thinking about capital needs to really capture that low-hanging fruit?

Jeremy Goebel: So think of the fourth quarter as transition. There's a transition services agreement, which has some additional costs that will go away. So typically, it takes us a few months to shed costs, so we'll go into next year. It will be inside that cost of capital very quickly at our long-term run rate. So we have to -- from a -- there's an investment that needs to be made between now and the end of 2027. So it will really catch its legs in the 2028 and forward. Like I said, a series of MVCs and acreage dedications, but we'll be shedding costs, adding market opportunities, doing some pull-through benefits on the asset through 2027.

So that will be the transition year, and it will really -- 2028 forward will be a great thing for the asset. But it's inside of 10x when we start, and it compresses well inside of our cost of capital outside of that. So it's not -- from an EBITDA standpoint, you can think of this as roughly 9 to 10x in the first 12 months. And after that, it gets well inside of that.

Francina Kolluri: That's very helpful. And then I just wanted to maybe talk more broadly about the M&A landscape. A lot of your peers have taken on packages this year. And so is there anything that's remaining, anything that looks interesting at this point?

Willie Chiang: Yes. I'll go ahead and take that one. This is Willie. Clearly, we've done a lot of bolt-on M&A or bolt-on acquisitions. So I'll speak about bolt-ons and then broader activities. We've actually been the ones that have been executing on a lot of these bolt-ons. We look at everything. I would tell you that I think the bolt-on opportunities are probably a little less than what the pace we've gone in the past. I think we've done 15 of these over the last 3, 4 years. So it's been very critical to our piece. A broader M&A is obviously an opportunity. But right now, we focus on our crude business. We've got -- anything we do focuses on returns.

So if we think about assets that we might bring in or things we may do, it's really focused around capital discipline and returns. And it's with that lens that we think about broader M&A, but look at everything, well positioned. Opportunities come our way, we'll be able to hopefully capture them.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of AJ O'Donnell of TPH Research.

Andrew John O'Donnell: I was just hoping if I could just sneak in one more question about the new Midland dedication. Just wondering, as far as the makeup of the volumes, are there any MVC components that are built into that? And then if you could talk about any of the volumes that are currently producing because I thought you said it was existing production. Are any of those volumes currently moving on your intra-basin or long-haul systems?

Jeremy Goebel: AJ, this is Jeremy. What I would say is these are acreage dedications consistent with the rest of the system on the contract structure. The vast majority of this would be going into existing systems just into the Midland complex to say whether a specific barrel's flowing through us. They're not providing any meaningful contribution to us today. And so this is just something that is a new contract from the gathering system for us.

Andrew John O'Donnell: Okay. Maybe just going back to the Permian macro. If we start to see this kind of compounding multiple hundred thousands of barrels of growth over the next few years, where do you see the most upside? Or what part of your system do you get most excited about? Is it like the incremental C3 expansions that you can do or market-based opportunities on your marketing affiliate? Or is the highest torque, maybe higher utilization on your northbound assets out of the Permian?

Jeremy Goebel: AJ, it's a great question. I'd say it's a bit of all of the above because filling the pipes is one thing. What we really get excited about is longer term, the additional improvements that the industry makes on recoveries, sustaining this for long periods of time, which is what we hear over and over again from our producer customers. The excitement around the surfactants, the excitement around the different completion techniques, the investments Exxon, Chevron, and the other integrators are made to extending the tail, that's what really gets us excited is that the long-term recoveries.

There's a lot of gas and a lot of NGLs, and there's a lot of excitement, but that's going to make those commodities worth a lot less. These still are going to be oil reservoirs driven by oil. So there's a real investment being made to continue to drive additional recovery. So on the oil side, flattening out the curve, having less capital to go chase this, big free cash flow generation and a stable balance and -- on the margin rates going out on the long-haul business is a plus, but the gathering business should be better. The long-haul business should be better, market-based opportunities around it.

So it's just an integrated platform that we have to serve our customers, and we look forward to expanding with them.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of John McKay of Goldman Sachs.

John Mackay: I'll go back to the Midland dedication, congrats on that. I just want to make sure we're thinking about it correctly. I know we'll get color later on kind of associated EBITDA and any associated spend. But given this is production that's already flowing elsewhere, I mean, is there an acquisition opportunity here for you guys over time on kind of whatever this production is touching right now?

Jeremy Goebel: John, I'd say at this point, that's inappropriate for us to talk about. But from our standpoint, we look forward to executing under the contract that we have today.

John Mackay: All right. Fair enough. And -- sorry go ahead. Please go ahead.

Willie Chiang: I'm sorry. John, this is Willie. I mean as I think about it at a high level, right, our whole business is integrated. So we've got gathering, intra-basin, long haul. So the thought of getting another 900,000 dedicated acres into the system, this is just what we do.

John Mackay: No, absolutely. That makes sense. Maybe I...

Willie Chiang: I'm sorry. I was quoting -- I misquoted the -- it's 270,000 acres here versus the 900 (sic) [ 900,000 ] was up in Silver in the Powder River. My apologies on that.

John Mackay: Absolutely. And maybe just on that point, you've probably increased the size of the dedicated acreage on the JV by looks like 30% since you kind of put it together about 5 years ago. I think we're just past that 5-year anniversary. Can you take this opportunity to give us your view on kind of the longer-term strategic plan here? Is there an opportunity to kind of buy in the other piece at some point? Is this going to be a kind of vehicle you can kind of continue to grow in? Maybe just give us an update now that we're kind of 5 years past the launch of it.

Jeremy Goebel: Sure. We've had a great partnership with Stonepeak and the Oryx team, and we'll continue to have a great partnership with them. That's their decision on when they decide to get out. But we've proven with them that we can grow, like you said, 30% growth over 5 years is really a 50% growth from where you started like when you think about it. So it's been a great run. It will continue to be a great run. We're happy for them to grow with us. But just like everything else, we've bought a lot of our partnerships in when that's the right time if that works, great. If they want to stay outstanding, great.

If a new partner comes in, we're prepared to work in any scenario. And we continue to grow as we've proven with them as a partner, we can grow with them or if the opportunity comes, we could do that. So I think there's no obligation to do it. There's an opportunity to do it, but there's no different than the opportunity to buy in other partners that we've had across our system.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Praneeth Satish of Wells Fargo.

Praneeth Satish: So I know it's still early, but maybe you can help us think through some of the puts and takes for 2027 EBITDA. I know you've got a few tailwinds here, $50 million cost synergies or cost efficiencies in the full year, Silver Creek, Cactus III, probably going to see volume growth on the oil side with the flush volumes coming in. So you put that all together, it does seem like you could see some reasonable growth in '27. So maybe what are some of the key headwinds that are kind of offsetting factors that we should think about when modeling '27 growth?

Al Swanson: Hi, this is Al. Yes, I mean, we've articulated kind of the four things, and I think you answered a meaningful part of our -- of the question. Clearly, PLA, we came in this year pretty highly hedged in the low 60s, we'll probably be in the low- to mid-60s by the time we exit with realized prices this year. Clearly, it's setting up for meaningful improvement there, $10 a barrel is a little over $40 million. So that's a definite tailwind. Clearly, the production growth, the $200,000 a day, that 1,000 (sic) [ 100,000 ] barrels a day that Jeremy mentioned, a lot of that came late.

We expect that to benefit '27 in addition to the excess rigs and the '27 growth itself. So we see the Permian volumes as a benefit. Clearly, the investment capital, whether it's our true investment expansion capital like the recent Cactus expansion, in addition, the Silver Creek acquisition as well. Those benefits will come to '27. And then the additional efficiency gains that we've talked about, the incremental $50 million, probably the one caveat or "headwind" we would point to, if you're taking that the last three quarters of this year, the crude is right around $700 million a quarter.

If you were just taking that, annualizing it and then putting all this growth on it, clearly, we've had some market benefits in those numbers. So we would encourage you to maybe dial in a little bit of taking out some of those market opportunities. Maybe we'll see the opportunity to get those in '27, but it wouldn't be -- we wouldn't come into the year expecting to see a repeat of some of that opportunities.

Praneeth Satish: Got you. No, that's helpful. And then there are several proposed Western Canadian egress projects that could bring more barrels into the Mid-Continent. I think at least one project that would go directly into Cushing. And I don't think they're expanding capacity from Cushing down. So I guess as you look across your asset footprint, and I don't know whether it's Capline or other systems, do you see any opportunities to participate or capture that incremental flow?

Jeremy Goebel: Praneeth, that's a great question. And certainly, any of the crude projects we're looking to see if we can benefit, complement, participate, so we'll keep you posted along the way, but we're constantly looking at opportunities to see if we can either partner with good projects, participate, create new projects. So we'll have more updates in the next 6 months if any of that comes to fruition. But certainly, things that complement us, we're actively looking at on the organic side as well as the acquisition side.

Operator: I'm showing no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn it back to Willie Chiang, Chairman and CEO, for closing remarks.

Willie Chiang: Great. Well, listen, thanks for your ongoing support questions, and we look forward to seeing you on the road soon. Have a safe day. Thanks.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

#3104. Stock Market Today, Nov. 6: Micron Technology Jumps as Chip Stocks Rebound From Thursday's Rout

Memory chip demand and bargain hunting lifted the stock today, Nov. 6, 2026, as traders looked past the prior day's sharp sell-off.

Micron Technology (MU +5.12%), a memory chips and storage solutions provider, closed at $690.00, up 5.12%. Shares surged as chip stocks bounced back from Thursday's rout, and investors are watching AI memory demand and the next earnings report.

Trading volume reached 44.5 million shares, coming in about 59% above its three-month average of 28.0 million shares.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) rose 0.31% to 7,377, and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.09%) climbed 1.09% to 24,579. Among semiconductor memory and storage solutions peers, Western Digital (WDC -1.44%) closed at $263.78, down 1.44%, while Seagate Technology Holdings (STX -1.19%) finished at $460.99, down 1.19%.

On Friday, Nov. 6, Micron Technology joined a broad semiconductor rebound after Thursday's rout, as investors realized shares were oversold yesterday. Micron, in particular, looks cheap. Its stock's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 3.8 is at a low point over the past year, and far below Seagate's 12.4, for example.

Wall Street has been hesitant to jump into Micron shares because the memory chip industry tends to follow a cyclical pattern. After memory became scarce this year due to the artificial intelligence boom, and prices soared, Micron announced efforts to expand supply. This tends to eventually lead to an industry downturn as the memory shortage abates and prices drop.

However, the AI sector is expanding around the world, resulting in data center buildouts that require memory for years to come. Micron's latest guidance points to tighter memory and storage supply-demand conditions extending into fiscal 2027 and 2028, which remains a key backdrop for the stock.

The AI infrastructure explosion seemed threatened by this week's U.S. midterm election, when the Democratic Party gained control of Congress. Investors were concerned that incoming Democratic leadership might drive tighter AI regulations and pause data center construction projects, leading to yesterday's sell-off.

Those fears were tempered by Micron's bargain valuation, and the company's strong success to date. On September 30, Micron reported record fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results, and that update brought the market's focus back on strong memory pricing and demand.

Robert Izquierdo has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Western Digital. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3103. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

#3102. 'The whole landscape changed': Gaming CEOs see new opportunities post-midterms

Midterm election results have created new openings for U.S. gambling expansion, while raising the prospect of greater political and legal pressure on prediction markets, according to gaming industry executives.

"The whole landscape changed," said Craig Billings, CEO of Wynn Resorts, during the company's earnings call Thursday.

Wynn has been closely watchng developments in the Middle East as it looks to open the United Arab Emirates' first legal casino in 2027. Billings said he suspects the election will have an impact on the "likely trajectory of the conflict in the region."

Closer to home, Billings sees opportunities in Texas. And he's not the only one. On the heels of reporting record third-quarter revenue and raising guidance for its brick-and-mortar business, Penn Entertainment CEO Jay Snowden called out specific opportunities made possible by state leadership changes.

Election Day was "a very good day overall for the industry, and certainly for Penn," Snowden said on Thursday's earnings call.

Texas, in particular, could be a jackpot for the casino industry. In a massive upset, Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated longtime Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who has been persistent in blocking gambling expansion in the Lone Star State.

"Texas is a fascinating market," Billings said, explaining how many consumers travel to Oklahoma to gamble at tribal casions. "So it's kind of a stealth market that is giant."

Penn has been building a position in Texas for years, Snowden said. It operates two of the state's three Class 1 thoroughbred racetracks and has established relationships with local leaders.

Penn plans to spend more time in Texas and, if lawmakers move toward legalization, Snowden said he expects the company is “positioned as well, if not better than really anybody in the sector.”

Las Vegas Sands also has invested heavily for many years to get casino gambling legalized in Texas.

"When Las Vegas Sands thinks about Texas and the Metroplex, it's really about an asset that will be both for business and future tourism," Sands Chairman and CEO Patrick Dumont told CNBC in an interview in October in Macao.

Dumont recently acquired the controlling stake in the Dallas Mavericks from his mother-in-law Miriam Adelson. He said there is the potential for a new Mavericks arena to incorporate a future casino.

"Whatever Las Vegas Sands can do in the future, that will be its own location, its own site and its own timeline," he said.

Houston Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta, currently serving as U.S. ambassador to Italy, owns Golden Nugget casinos, is Wynn Resorts' largest investor and is buying Caesars to take it private. Following a CNBC interview in Italy, he said, "Of course I want gaming in Texas!"

A new market would draw national sportsbook operators that would likely include DraftKings, Flutter-owned FanDuel, Caesars, Fanatics, and BetMGM, which is co-owned by MGM and Entain, among others.

Though the Texas' state election removed a major political obstacle, it didn't produce a deal. Legalizing casino gambling or sports betting would still require a constitutional amendment approved by two-thirds of both chambers and then voters.

Texas state control is now divided. While Democrats flipped the state House, Republicans kept the Senate. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governorship.

Las Vegas Sands spokesman Ron Reese told CNBC it's too early to speculate about what might happen with Texas gaming, but that the company will monitor developments closely.

Truist gaming analyst Barry Jonas wrote in a Wednesday note that he sees mixed implications from the midterm results.

"The Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton's support for regulated online casinos could improve the chances of iGaming legalization," Jonas said. On the other hand, Nebraska voters rejected ballot measures to legalize online betting.

Georgia, where Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship, could also provide an opportunity. She campaigned on letting voters decide whether to legalize casino gambling, with revenue expected to be earmarked to help fund education. Sports betting and casinos remain illegal in the state, and earlier sports-betting legislation failed in the House.

Penn could also benefit if lawmakers seek tighter regulations for so-called skill-based gaming machines, which compete with casinos and licensed video gaming terminals, according to Snowden. He said candidates who support skill-based gaming machines lost seats or influence in several states.

Penn operates four casinos in Pennsylvania as well as video gaming terminals in that state and other jurisdictions, and has three casinos in Missouri.

Snowden linked recent strong year-over-year gaming revenue growth to the shutdown of skill games in Pennsylvania in mid-October. Although he cautioned that it was too early to know whether Pennsylvania’s growth would last, he noted Missouri also saw strong revenue growth as its state attorney general pursued the machines there.

In Indiana, voters in three counties rejected a proposed casino license, which Penn sees as a benefit as it limits new competition for existing casinos in Indiana and neighboring Illinois and Ohio. Some gaming insiders speculate that a wave of left-leaning progressives in power could work to limit gambling businesses.

"There's no shortage of noise about where this industry is headed, and the election certainly turns up the volume," said Joe Maloney, president of Sports Betting Alliance. "What hasn't changed with the election is what works, and that's state-regulated sports betting and iGaming, built on accountability, consumer protection, and tax revenue for states. That's our lane, and we'll make that case to every new lawmaker willing to listen."

Democratic victories are likely to increase the pressure on prediction markets, even as industry supporters call out their predictive value in forecasting the election results.

"Every eligible customer should have access to these markets, which are federally regulated through our CFTC-registered Futures Commission Merchant," a Robinhood spokesperson said.

Democrats’ control of Congress gives them subpoena power and committee resources to investigate the president’s family and business dealings. That could put Donald Trump Jr. back in the spotlight as he is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket’s advisory board.

Congress could also consider legislation limiting the markets’ scope. The bipartisan Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act would bar Commodity Futures Trading Commission-regulated exchanges from offering contracts based on sports or casino-style games. But the bill had only been referred to committee as of the election. A veto-proof law would require two-thirds support in both chambers; no such vote is currently scheduled.

The American Gaming Association has been fighting prediction markets as unlicensed gambling.

"The prediction markets are facing a tsunami of criminal charges, major civil investigations and significant defeats in court," Bill Miller, the trade group's CEO, told CNBC. "In the aftermath of the election, we expect the bipartisan scrutiny of these platforms to further intensify."

"Our platform is an institutional-grade exchange with strong market-integrity and customer-protection programs," Polymarket told CNBC. A spokesman said the company welcomes the opportunity to work with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Repeated requests to Kalshi for comment went unanswered.

Jeff LeRiche, a partner at law firm Husch Blackwell, said he expects more scrutiny.

"Entities with robust compliance and surveillance infrastructure will be well positioned to navigate the increased attention," said LeRiche, who spent more than 20 years in the CFTC's enforcement division.

The state-level legal fight is already underway. Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected Kalshi’s request for a rehearing in its Nevada case, leaving the company exposed to state enforcement there.

New Democratic attorneys general in Ohio, Michigan and Nevada will also decide how to handle inherited disputes.

Ohio’s outgoing AG Andy Wilson helped lead a multistate effort to defend state gambling laws, Michigan’s Dana Nessel sued Kalshi and won a preliminary injunction, and Nevada’s Aaron Ford secured injunctions against prediction-market operators.

New AGs could also decide to follow Utah's lead in filing criminal charges, along with Arizona where criminal charges are pending.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#3101. If I Could Buy and Hold Only 1 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Through a Democratic Congress, It Would Be This One

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are plunging following the results of the midterm elections.

The 2026 midterm elections have introduced a layer of uncertainty for artificial intelligence (AI) investors. With Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress, lawmakers are preparing to introduce legislation addressing AI safety, electricity costs, and the expansion of data centers across the United States.

For companies such as Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%), Microsoft (MSFT -0.99%), Amazon (AMZN -0.35%), Alphabet (GOOGL +0.78%) (GOOG +0.78%), Meta Platforms (META +0.84%), Tesla (TSLA +4.23%), and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +8.62%), the implications could be significant.

Much of the AI revolution has been driven by investments in semiconductors, cloud computing, and data center infrastructure. There's one technology giant pursuing a different strategy. If I could buy and hold just one AI stock throughout the next two years of a divided government, I'd consider Apple (AAPL -0.52%). Let's dig into why.

Most of the largest AI developers are spending unprecedented sums of money building AI infrastructure. Nvidia supplies the graphics processing units powering these facilities, while Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta are investing hundreds of billions of dollars each year to expand their computing capacity. Tesla is also spending heavily on autonomous driving and robotics.

Apple is taking a different approach. Rather than competing to build data centers, Apple is focused on bringing AI capabilities directly to its existing products. This includes integrating generative AI features into the iPhone, the Mac, and Siri, while relying on partners for additional computing capabilities.

The financial implications of this strategy are compelling. During fiscal 2026, Apple's capital expenditures (capex) declined 29% to roughly $9 billion. Meanwhile, research and development (R&D) spending increased 32% to $45.8 billion, reflecting continued investment across software and AI.

The takeaway here is that Apple is investing heavily in innovation without committing nearly as much capital to physical AI infrastructure as its hyperscaler peers. That difference could become important if Congress pursues legislation that makes building new data centers more difficult.

Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, raising questions about utility costs, environmental impacts, and whether local communities should shoulder the financial burden of new development. Many Democratic lawmakers are indicating that they intend to pursue additional oversight when the new Congress convenes.

It's important to note that President Donald Trump retains veto authority, meaning sweeping federal restrictions are not guaranteed. Nevertheless, even the possibility of tighter regulation introduces uncertainty for big tech.

Slower data center construction could affect demand for Nvidia's chips. For cloud services providers such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet, new restrictions could hinder expansion plans and make budgeting more challenging.

By contrast, Apple already has a global installed base across billions of devices through which it can push AI-powered features. Rather than building an entirely new customer ecosystem, Apple can introduce updated capabilities to people who already own its products. This creates a unique opportunity to encourage device upgrades, strengthen customer loyalty, and potentially expand its budding services business.

While Apple's AI strategy is interesting, the company's underlying financial performance is what makes the investment thesis compelling. During its fiscal fourth quarter (ended Sept. 26), Apple generated $114.5 billion in revenue, representing 12% growth year over year.

iPhone revenue increased 17% to $57.6 billion, while services revenue reached $31.6 billion. These figures illustrate an important point: Apple does not need AI to become an entirely new business segment overnight.

The company's existing products and services already generate meaningful revenue, providing management with the financial flexibility to invest in emerging technologies without jeopardizing the core operation. Moreover, Apple's relatively modest capex profile allows it to preserve more cash for dividends, share repurchases, and future product innovation.

While the next two years could bring changes to the regulatory environment surrounding AI, Apple stands out because the company doesn't need to win the AI infrastructure spending race to benefit from the technology. It just needs to make AI useful enough that consumers continue buying its products and paying for its services.

For investors, that flexibility is especially valuable. That's why Apple is my top buy-and-hold AI stock in the current political landscape.

#3098. Family offices boost startup investments in October, backing women's health and caregivers

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

After a slow September, investment firms of ultra-wealthy families stepped up their deal-making last month. In October, family offices made 56 direct investments in companies, up about 30% from the month prior, according to data provided exclusively to CNBC by Fintrx, a private wealth intelligence platform.

Laurene Powell Jobs' Emerson Collective was the most prolific investor of the month, backing three healthcare startups according to Fintrx data. Her investment and philanthropy firm seeks to address health equity and other complex challenges like the energy transition.

Last month, Emerson Collective joined a $555 million Series G for Devoted Health, a healthcare provider and insurer of Medicare Advantage plans, alongside information technology billionaire Azim Premji's namesake family office. Devoted Health, which has counted Emerson Collective as an investor since 2021, announced that it will use the fundraise to expand to five additional states for a total of 34.

Powell Jobs' firm also participated in two fundraises for healthcare data startups BioStack and Collective X Health. BioStack, which raised $9.5 million in seed funding, analyzes patient records across different institutions to create training datasets for artificial intelligence healthcare models. Collective X Health, fresh off a $3.2 million pre-seed round, seeks to close the gender data gap by compiling and licensing peer-reviewed, female-specific data and research.

Emerson Collective is in good company as family offices continue to invest in healthcare innovations from telehealth to drug discovery. In a family office survey released by Citi Wealth in September, healthcare ranked as the second-most-popular sector for direct investing at 32%, only behind AI at 51%.

Melinda French Gates' Pivotal Ventures joined an $82 million Series C for Abby Care, an AI-enabled startup that trains and certifies family members as paid caregivers under Medicaid and Medicare programs.

Erin Harkless Moore, who manages investments at Pivotal Ventures, told CNBC that the firm looks for founders who have first-hand experience with the complexities of healthcare. Abby Care CEO and founder Havi Nguyen started navigating the Medicaid system at age 9 as a caregiver for her sisters and eventually her grandparents.

"We look for teams that understand the problem deeply and have a model built for the realities of the healthcare system as it currently exists. Abby Care is a great example," Moore said. "Their deep understanding of the market allowed them to both spot an unsolved problem and understand how to navigate the regulatory challenges in this space."

For family offices looking to invest in healthcare, Moore said overlooked markets offer a chance to back companies addressing needs that have long gone unmet.

"Women's health is a space that has been historically underfunded and under-researched. We have less data, less funding, and huge gaps to fill," she said. "That can make investing more challenging, but it can also point to where there's real opportunity."

#3096. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.

#3090. Montana votes to ban corporate political money. Next stop? Probably the Supreme Court

Imagine a corporation wants to spend $10 million to defeat a political candidate. Under the Supreme Court's landmark 2010 Citizens United ruling, it can spend as much as it wants provided it doesn't coordinate with the candidate's campaign.

On Tuesday, Montana voted to change that.

In a state President Donald Trump won by nearly 20 points in 2024, roughly 65% of Montanans voted to approve Initiative 194 — the "Montana Plan" — embracing a novel legal strategy to curb corporate political spending. If states cannot restrict political speech under Citizens United, can they instead strip corporations of the power to spend money on elections?

The vote follows a record $11.87 billion in political advertising nationwide this election cycle that was split about evenly between the two parties, according to media tracking firm AdImpact.

The voter-approved measure is set to become state law on Jan. 1 in Montana, where voters can make law via ballot initiatives. Montana's Republican-controlled legislature could amend or repeal it, though proponents have pledged that if that happens they will take the fight back to voters in 2028.

Now, Montana is poised for a constitutional showdown that could reach the nation's highest court. If the strategy survives, it could provide a replicable blueprint for restricting corporate political spending across the country. Similar measures are being explored in more than 30 states.

"If a single state can successfully deny corporate power over elections, it proves that Citizens United wasn't the final word on democracy, and we will continue battling," said Tom Moore, a former Federal Election Commission official and current senior fellow at the Center for American Progress who helped develop the Montana Plan.

The Montana Plan hinges on a legal distinction: Corporations may have constitutional rights, but their powers come from the states.

Under Initiative 194, Montana would strip corporations, trade associations, labor unions and nonprofits, including those headquartered elsewhere, of the legal power to spend money influencing elections in the state.

In practice, that should mean no corporate-funded attack ads, no trade associations bankrolling referendum campaigns and no politically active nonprofits spending their own funds to sway Montana voters.

Violators risk losing state-granted corporate privileges such as limited liability, which generally protects shareholders from personal responsibility for corporate debts, until all improperly spent funds are surrendered and legal conditions are met.

"The argument of the people supporting the initiative is, in theory, trying to be pretty simple. Keep your campaign cash out of Montana, or you run the risk of putting your shareholders' personal balance sheets on the line," said Kal Munis, a politics professor at Montana State University who is an expert in the state's politics.

The financial stakes extend well beyond Montana. Known corporate contributions to outside groups in federal elections surged from $13 million in 2010 to more than $600 million by September 2026, according to OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks such spending. That excludes money funneled through nonprofits that conceal their donors.

But there's an irony to the Montana Plan. It had high-dollar backers from corporate America.

State campaign finance data shows Samantha Walton, wife of Walmart heir Lukas Walton, gave $722,300 to groups backing the plan, while LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman contributed $150,000. The campaign's organizing nonprofit, Transparent Election Initiative, is itself a type of dark-money group that generally isn't required to disclose its donors.

And the new law wouldn't exactly take billionaires out of politics. It exempts individuals, political committees, government entities and bona fide news, commentary and editorial content.

Consider Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, the 2026 election's largest known individual donor, with at least $474 million in political giving, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records. Musk could still spend millions of his personal fortune influencing Montana elections. His companies, however, would face the new restrictions.

Moore argued that because corporations derive their legal existence from states, those states should have the power to restrict their political spending.

Opponents call the Montana Plan an unconstitutional end run around Citizens United. If states cannot directly prohibit protected political speech, they argue, they cannot accomplish the same thing by threatening companies' legal privileges.

And critics warn the restrictions would reach beyond corporate giants, silencing local trade groups, labor unions and community organizations on school bonds, tax measures and other local ballot issues.

"Why allow a media corporation to speak out, while denying a non-profit association of citizens the right to organize around clean water or lower taxes?" said Brad Smith, who leads the Institute for Free Speech and is a former FEC chairman. "Billionaires will find loopholes. All this really does is silence Montana's small- and medium-sized businesses."

The first legal test is already underway in Hawaii, where lawmakers enacted a similar law in May. Montana is the first state to embrace the strategy through a statewide vote.

The Hawaii law faces formidable legal opposition. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has sued to block it, and the Institute for Free Speech is representing the Grassroot Institute of Hawaii in a separate challenge. The national ACLU has also weighed in, arguing in a court brief that the law violates the First Amendment.

Legal and campaign finance experts told CNBC the dispute could eventually reach the Supreme Court, whose 6-3 conservative majority has repeatedly loosened campaign finance restrictions. Just in June, the justices struck down limits on political parties' spending in coordination with candidates.

"Shifting the prohibition into the corporate code is a distinction without a difference," said Michael Kang, a Northwestern Pritzker School of Law professor who studies campaign finance. "The courts will see right through it because the clear intent remains to bypass Citizens United. It seems like a legal sleight of hand."

Montana has lost this fight before. In 1912, voters banned corporate campaign spending after copper barons bribed lawmakers and dominated state politics. The law stood for a century before the Supreme Court struck it down in 2012 under Citizens United.

"The way we look at it, this is states' rights vs. Citizens United," said Moore, of the Center for American Progress. "That's the pitch once and if it makes it to the Supreme Court they're going to need to decide between one of their two favorite legal theories and things to fall back on."
